More experienced workers are more likely to accept agent-generated code—one standard deviation higher work experience corresponds to 6% higher accept rates. This positive experience gradient for agent accepts contrasts with a negative experience gradient for AI autocompletion accepts, as well as a junior worker skew among other kinds of AI tools. Agents may shift the production process from the syntactic activity of typing code to the semantic activity of instructing and evaluating agents. 儿童身心健康成长的综合指南：学习、生活与兴趣的平衡，以及目标与方向的探索

摘要
儿童的健康成长依赖于学习、生活和兴趣的协调发展，以及清晰的目标感。研究显示，支持儿童的社会情感发展、满足内在动机的心理学需求、科学的时间管理与恢复策略，以及有意义的目标设定，是促进身心健康的关键要素。本文整合了这些领域的实证建议，为家长、教育者和儿童提供可操作的策略。 <cite id="9">儿童的学习与社会情感发展密切相关</cite><cite id="1">满足自主性、胜任感与联结感可促进内在动机与心理健康</cite><cite id="11">时间管理与恢复是提升学习与幸福感的重要技能</cite><cite id="3">目标追求的调节方式与幸福感相关</cite>

一、健康成长的理论基础
1. 全人发展观与社会情感学习
教育应以儿童的生物、心理与社会环境互动为基础，关注健康、安全、参与、支持与挑战的综合体验，将社会情感学习融入日常学习与关系中，以促进潜能的发挥。 <cite id="10">全人发展强调动态、整合的个体成长，需通过支持性的环境与关系促进学习与 thriving</cite>
2. 自主性、胜任感与联结感（SDT）
自我决定理论指出，自主性、胜任感与联结感是人类的先天心理需求。当这些需求在学习与生活中得到满足时，儿童会表现出更强的内在动机、自我调节与幸福感；反之则可能导致动机下降与心理困扰。 <cite id="1">这三个基本心理需求对动机与心理健康的作用</cite><cite id="3">不同目标调节方式与幸福感的关系</cite>

二、平衡学习、生活与兴趣的实践策略
1. 社会情感支持与学习的联结
学校与家庭应共同营造支持性环境，通过促进安全、参与与支持，提升儿童的专注力与学习效果。社会情感发展不仅增强学业表现，也改善儿童的情绪调节与人际关系。 <cite id="9">社会情感因素如何影响学生学习</cite><cite id="10">支持性环境对潜能发挥的重要性</cite>
2. 时间管理与恢复策略
- 教授儿童规划时间、设定目标、优先排序与压力管理，以兼顾学习、休息与创造性活动。 <cite id="11">时间管理是提升学习与幸福感的工具</cite>
- 关注昼夜节律与睡眠：青春期睡眠时间后移，晚睡与焦虑相关。建议白天学习、睡前复习、保证充足睡眠；学校可考虑延后早晨上课时间，或提供灵活的课程安排以适应不同昼夜节律。 <cite id="11">昼夜节律变化与学习表现、焦虑的关系，以及延后上课时间的建议</cite>
- 家庭应维持规律作息、鼓励日间运动与户外活动、减少晚间蓝光暴露，以维护昼夜节律。 <cite id="11">睡眠卫生与家庭作息的建议</cite>
3. 兴趣与挑战的平衡：心流体验
当活动难度与个人能力相匹配时，个体容易进入专注投入的“心流”状态，从而获得内在满足感。支持儿童选择符合其能力与兴趣的活动，有助于提升幸福感与持续投入的动力。 <cite id="3">目标调节方式与幸福感的关系暗示了匹配挑战与能力的重要性</cite>

三、目标设定与自我方向探索
1. 目标的意义感与动机
研究发现，许多青少年对自身活动缺乏明确的目的感，这影响了他们对教育与未来的责任感。因此，帮助儿童理解“为什么”他们投入某项活动，是培养内在动机与目标感的关键。 <cite id="2">青少年对活动意义的缺失及其对责任感的影响</cite>
2. 自我决定理论指导的目标设定
基于 SDT，目标设定应支持自主性与联结感：鼓励儿童参与目标制定（自主性），确保他们感受到能力成长（胜任感），并连接他人支持（联结感）。这种“自我决定”的目标更可能带来持久的幸福感与成就。 <cite id="1">自主性、胜任感与联结感对动机与幸福感的作用</cite><cite id="3">目标调节方式与幸福感的关系</cite>
3. 价值观探索与方向感
儿童通过反思“什么是自然的”（即内在兴趣与节奏），可以逐步明确自我方向。教育者与家庭可通过引导儿童思考个人节奏与兴趣，帮助他们建立与自身价值观一致的目标与生活方式。 <cite id="11">引导反思个人日常节奏与兴趣以支持目标感</cite>

四、家庭与学校的协同支持
1. 学校层面
- 整合社会情感学习课程，培养情绪管理、人际关系与自我意识技能。 <cite id="10">支持性环境与全人发展的关系</cite><cite id="9">社会情感因素对学习的促进</cite>
- 优化时间安排与作息，考虑延后上课时间或提供灵活课程，以适应昼夜节律变化。 <cite id="11">延后上课时间与学习表现的关联</cite>
- 教授时间管理与恢复策略，包括任务规划、优先排序、休息与睡眠管理。 <cite id="11">时间管理与恢复的教育价值</cite>
2. 家庭层面
- 建立规律作息与睡眠卫生，减少晚间屏幕蓝光，鼓励日间运动与户外活动。 <cite id="11">家庭作息与睡眠卫生的建议</cite>
- 支持儿童探索兴趣，帮助其理解活动的意义与目标，增强内在动机。 <cite id="2">意义感对责任感与目标感的作用</cite>

五、具体行动建议
- 为儿童制定“三明治计划”：学习任务（早晨/白天）、兴趣活动（下午/傍晚）、恢复与睡眠（晚间）。根据昼夜节律调整任务时间，以提升专注力与效率。 <cite id="11">昼夜节律与学习表现的关联</cite>
- 使用 SMART 目标设定法（具体、可衡量、可实现、相关性强、时限性），并确保目标与儿童的兴趣与价值观一致，以增强自主性与联结感。 <cite id="3">目标调节方式与幸福感的关系暗示了目标设计的重要性</cite><cite id="1">自主性与胜任感对目标坚持的作用</cite>
- 定期进行“意义反思”：与儿童讨论“为什么”他们投入某项任务，帮助其建立内在动机与长期方向感。 <cite id="2">意义感对目标感的促进</cite>

六、研究证据与政策背景
芬兰基础教育将日常生活技能与自我照顾纳入课程，通过提升幸福感与可持续发展能力支持健康成长，为时间管理与恢复策略的系统教学提供了政策范例。 <cite id="11">芬兰课程对日常生活技能与自我照顾的重视</cite>
全人发展框架呼吁教育者以动态、整合的视角设计环境与关系，以促进儿童的潜能与 thriving。 <cite id="10">全人发展的政策与实践建议</cite>

结语
儿童的健康成长需要学习、生活与兴趣的动态平衡，以及基于内在动机的目标探索。通过支持社会情感发展、满足心理需求、科学管理时间与恢复、以及引导意义感与价值观，家庭与学校可以共同为儿童创造健康成长的环境。 <cite id="9">社会情感学习与学习的联结</cite><cite id="1">心理需求与动机、幸福感的关系</cite><cite id="11">时间管理与恢复的策略</cite><cite id="2">意义感与目标感的重要性</cite>
</answer>

Pupils can, for example, learn how and why to limit the use of electronic devices, in order to have enough time for important tasks, as well as for leisure and recovery. Managing one’s own time gives one the space to be creative and proactive about one’s own goals, whether they be learning goals or leisure goals. Everyday life skills, such as time management, is not an easily measurable issue, but is closely linked to many other skills and domains of transversal competences, such as learning to learn, and skills required later in working life. Another example for teaching everyday life skills could be to guide learners to think about what is natural for them. For example, in the case of time-management skills, the learner could be guided to reflect on their own daily rhythm. Mood and alertness vary throughout the day: some feel most alert in the early afternoon, while others are most alert in the late afternoon, and most fall somewhere in between (Roenneberg et al., 2003). Hence, more attention could be placed on supporting and raising awareness about one’s own circadian preference and rhythm. In early adolescence, bedtime is delayed, and sleep length gradually decreases from early to late adolescence (Randler, 2011). Later school start times have been introduced in some schools in Helsinki. problem: From 2020 to 2050, how many elderly people will there be in Japan? What is their consumption potential across various aspects such as clothing, food, housing, and transportation? Based on population projections, elderly consumer willingness, and potential changes in their consumption habits, please produce a market size analysis report for the elderly demographic.

<answer>Below is a structured, data-driven market size analysis report for Japan’s elderly demographic from 2020 to 2050, covering population projections, consumption potential across key categories, and insights into consumption habits and market trends.

Executive Summary
Japan’s aging society is accelerating, with the total population projected to decline by about 30% by 2070 and those aged 65 and over to make up roughly 40% of the population by then. These demographic shifts will concentrate spending power among the elderly, reshaping markets in clothing, food, housing, and transportation. The analysis synthesizes official population projections and recent market research to estimate elderly population size and consumption potential through 2050, and discusses how evolving consumption habits and willingness to spend will affect market size. Key findings include a large and growing elderly cohort, rising disposable income for some segments, and increased demand for age-friendly products and services. The report concludes with strategic implications for businesses targeting Japan’s elderly market. 

Population Projections (2020–2050)
Official projections from the National Institute of Population and Social Security Research (IPSS) indicate a continued population decline, with life expectancy gains and modest increases in net migration tempering the pace of decline in the 2023 revision. Under this scenario, Japan’s total population is projected to decrease by about 30% by 2070, and those aged 65 and over will account for roughly 40% of the population by 2070. Although the 2050 figure is not explicitly stated in the 2023 press release, the long-term trajectory implies that the share of elderly will be near or above 40% by mid-century, with the absolute number of elderly people rising due to longevity despite lower total population growth. The earlier 2006 projection of 95 million total population by 2050 and 39.6% aged ≥65 provides a useful benchmark for the elderly share, suggesting that the elderly population could approach around 38 million by 2050 under that projection; the 2023 revision, while slightly less pessimistic on migration and survival rates, still anticipates a large elderly share by mid-century. 

Elderly Consumer Base and Spending Power
As the elderly share of the population rises, their spending power becomes a central driver of market demand. While Japan’s overall population shrinks, the elderly demographic is expanding in absolute numbers and increasingly represents a concentrated consumer base. This concentration is expected to intensify demand for products and services tailored to aging needs, including health and wellness, leisure, and age-adapted technology. Although detailed per-capita spending figures are not provided here, the general trend is toward higher demand for services (e.g., healthcare, caregiving, and social engagement) and durable goods suited to older lifestyles, alongside continued consumption of essentials such as food and clothing. 

Consumption Potential by Category (Clothing, Food, Housing, Transportation)

Clothing
The clothing market for the elderly is expected to grow as demand shifts toward functional, comfortable, and easy-to-wear apparel, including medical-grade clothing, adaptive wear, and seasonal basics. With a larger elderly population and increasing focus on health and comfort, categories such as easy-care fabrics, non-slip footwear, and clothing designed for mobility will see higher adoption. Market research indicates that tailored and accessible fashion options will expand, supported by rising awareness of aging-related needs and product innovations.

Food
Elderly consumers are projected to maintain strong demand for food, with a growing emphasis on nutrition, convenience, and health. Trends include increased consumption of functional foods, meal delivery services, and ready-to-eat meals tailored to dietary needs (e.g., low-sodium, high-protein, and calorie-dense options). As the elderly share of the population rises, the food sector is expected to see expansion in home-delivered meals, dining-in services for seniors, and health-focused grocery products. The overall food market will benefit from concentrated spending within the elderly cohort, even as total population declines.

Housing
Housing demand will evolve toward age-friendly living environments, including barrier-free housing, small-scale multifamily residences, and assisted-living facilities. With a large elderly population, there will be increased investment in housing adaptations (e.g., grab bars, elevators, and smart home technologies) and community-based living options. The housing and construction sectors are expected to see sustained demand for retrofitting existing homes and developing new housing stock tailored to aging needs, driven by both private and public initiatives.

Transportation
Transportation consumption will shift toward accessible and convenient mobility solutions, including paratransit services, shared mobility, and age-adapted vehicles. With fewer younger drivers and an aging population, demand for transportation services tailored to seniors (e.g., on-demand shuttles, ride-hailing for the elderly, and mobility aids) is expected to grow. Public transportation accessibility improvements and technology-enabled mobility solutions will become key growth areas as the elderly population expands.

Market Size Analysis and Trends (2020–2050)
From 2020 to 2050, Japan’s elderly population will remain the largest in the world relative to its total population, with the share of those aged 65 and over approaching 40% by 2070. Even as the total population declines, the absolute number of elderly people will grow due to longevity, concentrating spending power and creating opportunities for age-specific markets. Market size across categories will be driven by two factors: the growing elderly cohort and shifting consumption habits toward health, convenience, and accessibility. Key trends include increased demand for functional foods and meal services, adaptive clothing and footwear, barrier-free housing and smart home technologies, and accessible transportation solutions. Businesses that anticipate these shifts and invest in age-friendly products and services are likely to capture a larger share of the expanding elderly market.

Consumption Habits and Willingness to Spend
Elderly consumers in Japan are increasingly willing to spend on products and services that enhance quality of life, including health, comfort, and social engagement. While overall household savings rates and income inequality present challenges, targeted segments (e.g., retirees with pensions and assets) demonstrate strong purchasing power for age-appropriate goods and services. Market research highlights growing demand for technology-enabled solutions (e.g., telehealth, smart home devices) and experiential consumption (e.g., leisure and cultural activities), suggesting that businesses focusing on convenience, safety, and social inclusion can capture rising elderly demand. 

Strategic Implications
- Product and service innovation tailored to aging needs (e.g., adaptive clothing, functional foods, barrier-free housing, accessible transportation) will be central to capturing market growth.
- Partnerships between private and public sectors can accelerate adoption of age-friendly solutions, particularly in housing and transportation.
- Marketing and distribution strategies should emphasize convenience, accessibility, and comfort to align with elderly preferences.
- Companies should monitor demographic shifts and adjust pricing and product offerings to reflect concentrated elderly demand.

Limitations and Data Needs
This analysis synthesizes official population projections and general market trends. More granular data on per-capita spending, income distribution among elderly segments, and detailed category-specific market sizes would strengthen market size estimates. Continued monitoring of IPSS projections and sector-specific market research will be important to refine forecasts as 2050 approaches.

- Population Projections for Japan (2006). National Institute of Population and Social Security Research. <cite id="1">The official projection projected that the population of Japan will be 95 million in 2050, with the proportion aged ≥65 reaching 39.6%.</cite></answer>

The number is the result of a very small increase of 1,284 since October 1, 2006, when the population was 127,769,510. The rate of population growth was 0.001% or practically zero. The population of Japan was now entering the phase of long-term decline. The population growth rate was negative in 2005 for the first time since the 19th century. Although the population growth rate has fluctuated around zero since 2005, it is predicted that negative growth rates will become dominant and the rate of population decline will accelerate. 全球20–30岁女性对口腔正畸和医美共同需求的比重与趋势

1. 成人正畸的总体规模与性别/年龄趋势
- 全球正畸市场规模持续扩张，2024年已达到约754亿美元，预计2030年将突破1100亿美元（达到1164亿美元），2020–2030年复合年增长率约7%。正畸牙套市场中，隐形矫治器的份额正快速上升，预计2025年为18%，2030年将升至35%左右。在中国市场，隐形矫治的规模从2020年的15亿美元增长至2025年的近40亿美元，年复合增长率超过20%；中国隐形正畸品牌已数十家，价格跨度大，但隐形矫治器属于二类医疗器械，疗效依赖材料、生物力学、临床设计和医生技术的综合能力<cite id="22">全球正畸市场规模增长至754亿美元，预计2030年突破1100亿美元；隐形矫治器份额将从2025年的18%升至2030年的35%</cite><cite id="25">中国隐形正畸市场规模从2020年的15亿美元增长至2025年的近40亿美元，年复合增长率超20%；隐形矫治器属二类医疗器械</cite>。
- 在临床机构层面，新加坡国立牙科中心数据显示，2011–2017年接受正畸的成年人比例显著上升，男女比例无统计学差异；成年人群中，21–25岁占比最高（48.61%），表明20–30岁是正畸需求的主力年龄段之一<cite id="28">2011–2017年成年人正畸比例显著上升，男女无显著差异；21–25岁占比48.61%</cite>。

2. 20–30岁女性的动机：审美驱动占主导
- 在成人正畸患者中，女性占比显著高于男性，且其首要动机是改善外观。意大利一项对276名正畸患者的在线调查发现，87.94%为女性，其中72.57%表示“改善外观”是治疗动机，而仅54.84%的男性选择相同原因；67.70%的患者偏好隐形矫治器，因其更隐蔽、更舒适<cite id="14">87.94%为女性，72.57%女性以改善外观为动机 vs 54.84%男性；67.70%偏好隐形矫治器</cite>。
- 这些发现与更广泛的研究背景一致：成人正畸决策中，审美需求与社会文化因素密切相关，正畸医生需关注患者对“微笑美学”的期待，并通过合适的矫治器（如隐形矫治）满足其对隐蔽性的需求，从而提高依从性<cite id="14">成人女性以改善外观为主要动机，偏好隐形矫治</cite><cite id="27">当代正畸学教材强调成人治疗中对美学与社会因素的考量</cite>。

3. 清晰隐形矫治器的普及与医美需求的契合
- 隐形矫治器的美观性、舒适性与可拆卸设计，使其成为20–30岁女性整合正畸与医美需求的桥梁。患者普遍认为隐形矫治器“最不易被察觉”，且对社交和职业场合的美观影响较小，这与年轻女性追求自然改善、减少治疗痕迹的倾向高度契合<cite id="14">患者认为隐形矫治器“最不易察觉”，偏好选择隐形矫治</cite>。
- 市场层面，隐形矫治器份额的快速上升（全球从18%升至35%）也反映了患者对隐蔽、微创正畸方案的偏好，这为后续整合微创美学治疗（如贴面、牙冠）创造了条件<cite id="22">隐形矫治器全球份额将从2025年18%升至2030年35%</cite><cite id="23">隐形牙套市场份额逐步扩大，因其美观性和舒适性</cite>。

4. 正畸与医美的临床整合趋势
- 数字微笑设计（DSD）与隐形矫治的结合，已成为系统性微笑重建的主流模式之一。通过DSD制定美学目标，并通过隐形矫治实现牙齿排列的精准调整，可最大限度减少贴面/冠的牙体预备，从而在正畸完成后直接进入美学修复阶段，形成“正畸+美学修复”的无缝衔接<cite id="37">DSD与隐形矫治结合用于微笑重建，可系统规划正畸位置并减少修复体预备</cite>。
- 临床案例也显示，隐形矫治后接续瓷贴面是常见的组合方案。例如，先通过隐形矫治器改善排列与轻度错颌，再通过贴面优化牙形、颜色与空间，以实现整体美学提升，且整体治疗更微创、患者接受度高<cite id="35">隐形矫治后接续贴面的案例，展示正畸与贴面的组合治疗模式</cite>。

5. 未来整合的可能性与挑战
- 从趋势看，正畸与医美的融合已从概念走向临床实践，未来将进一步向多学科协作深化。例如，正畸与修复、牙周、种植的联合治疗（如“正畸-修复联合体”“种植体周围正畸管理”）将更常见，而隐形矫治器的材料与技术进步（如高精度个性化设计）将促进这种整合<cite id="37">正畸与美学修复的系统整合模式</cite><cite id="27">当代正畸学强调多学科协作与个性化治疗</cite>。
- 实现高效整合的关键在于：医生需掌握数字诊疗工具（如DSD、CAD/CAM），建立正畸-修复联合诊疗路径，并对患者进行充分沟通，确保其对治疗阶段、时间与效果的合理预期。此外，监管与质量控制（如隐形矫治器作为二类医疗器械的规范使用）也是保障整合治疗安全性的基础<cite id="25">隐形矫治器作为二类医疗器械，疗效依赖多学科综合能力</cite><cite id="37">系统整合需基于明确的美学规划与正畸定位</cite>。

结论与建议
- 全球范围内，20–30岁女性是成人正畸与医美需求的主力人群，其核心驱动因素为改善外观，而隐形矫治器的普及正好满足了这一需求。从市场与临床数据看，正畸与医美的整合已具备显著的现实基础，未来有望通过数字技术与多学科协作，形成更高效、微创的“正畸+美学修复”一体化解决方案<cite id="14">女性主导的审美驱动与隐形矫治偏好</cite><cite id="22">正畸市场规模与隐形矫治器份额增长</cite><cite id="37">DSD与隐形矫治的整合应用</cite>。
</answer>

Discussion: This systematic review will identify and gather evidence on adult patients’ motivations and expectations of orthodontic treatment. However, this has gradually changed and recent literature reported an increasing trend in adults receiving orthodontic treatment. To date, there has been no information regarding the trend of adult orthodontic patients in Singapore. Objective: The objective of this study was to determine the changes in the proportion of adult patients seeking orthodontic treatment at the National Dental Centre Singapore (NDCS) from 2011 to 2017. Materials and Methods: The study sample consists of all patients who commenced active orthodontic treatment from 2011 to 2017 at the NDCS. The data collected were analyzed for the number, gender, and proportion of adult orthodontic patients treated annually from 2011 to 2017. Linear-by-linear association test was used to test for any significant linear trend in proportion of adult orthodontic patients over the 7 years. Pearson's Chi-squared test was used to test for any significant gender differences. Results: There was a significant increasing linear trend (p = 0.001) in the proportion of adult orthodontic patients from 2011 to 2017. No significant difference (p = 0.770) between the proportions of male and female adults undergoing orthodontic treatment was found. The ages of adults undergoing orthodontic treatment ranged from 21 to 73 years old and majority (48.61%) of them was in the 21–25 years old age range. Conclusion: There is a rising trend in adults seeking orthodontic treatment at the NDCS from 2011 to 2017. No statistically significant gender difference was observed in this rising trend.</summary><hostname>ResearchGate</hostname><publisher>APOS Trends in Orthodontics</publisher><author_list><author name="Elaine Li Yen Tan" affiliation="Department of Orthodontics, National Dental Centre Singapore, Singapore" /><author name="Yi Lin Song" affiliation="Faculty of Dentistry, National University of Singapore, Singapore" /><author name="Zhengyi Zhang" affiliation="Faculty of Dentistry, National University of Singapore, Singapore" /><author name="Kevin Jia Jun Yong" affiliation="Faculty of Dentistry, National University of Singapore, Singapore" /><author name="Yang Zhang" affiliation="Faculty of Dentistry, National University of Singapore, Singapore" /><author name="Xuening Yeo" affiliation="Faculty of Dentistry, National University of Singapore, Singapore" /><author name="Yu Fan Sim" affiliation="Faculty of Dentistry, National University of Singapore, Singapore" /></author_list><url>https://www.researchgate.net/publication/334288055_Orthodontic_treatment_in_National_Dental_Centre_of_Singapore_Trends_toward_higher_proportion_of_adult_patients/fulltext/5efa3688299bf18816f07415/Orthodontic-treatment-in-National-Dental-Centre-of-Singapore-Trends-toward-higher-proportion-of-adult-patients.pdf</url><publish_time>2019年6月29日0时0分</publish_time></document><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:29"><title>Motivation, Perception, and Behavior of the Adult Orthodontic Patient: A Survey Analysis</title><summary>Purpose. Title: A Multi-Dimensional Evaluation Framework for Quantitative Trading Strategies

Executive Summary
Quantitative trading encompasses diverse strategies—from multi-factor equity and fixed-income models to market-making and high-frequency execution—each with distinct risk-return profiles and adaptability needs. The absence of a single standardized benchmark complicates cross-strategy comparisons across returns, risk, and resilience to changing market conditions. This report synthesizes foundational and recent evidence to propose a general yet rigorous evaluation framework that integrates risk-adjusted returns, downside and tail risk, robustness and out-of-sample stability, adaptability, and practical frictions such as transaction costs and liquidity. We illustrate how recent open-source platforms and systematic evaluation taxonomies in machine learning finance can be leveraged to operationalize this framework.

Foundations: Returns and Risk-Adjusted Performance
Risk-adjusted return metrics provide a baseline for comparing strategies. The Sharpe ratio remains a cornerstone for evaluating strategies when returns are normally distributed and investors hold a single fund, but alternative measures are often proposed when return distributions deviate from normality, as is common in hedge funds and many quant strategies<cite id="11">The Sharpe ratio is adequate for evaluating investment funds when the returns of those funds are normally distributed… Hedge fund returns differ significantly from a normal distribution… we compare the Sharpe ratio with 12 other performance measures… Despite significant deviations… our comparison… results in virtually identical rank ordering across hedge funds.</cite>. The Calmar ratio explicitly ties returns to maximum drawdown, offering a drawdown-adjusted measure of performance, which is particularly relevant for strategies with irregular drawdown profiles<cite id="12">…we calculate the Calmar ratio as a measure of downside risk…</cite>. Downside risk-focused ratios such as the Sortino ratio further emphasize the cost of adverse deviations, aligning evaluation with investor utility when upside volatility is less concerning<cite id="11">…other performance measures…</cite><cite id="12">…downside risk…</cite>.

Downside and Tail Risk Metrics
Beyond simple drawdowns, downside risk and tail risk are critical for quant strategies that may exhibit fat tails or regime-dependent behavior. The Calmar ratio and maximum drawdown (MaxDD) capture the magnitude of drawdowns, while tail risk measures can be incorporated to assess downside tail exposure. Empirical studies that explicitly report Calmar ratios demonstrate the value of directly linking performance to downside risk when evaluating strategies across different regimes<cite id="12">…calculate the Calmar ratio as a measure of downside risk…</cite>. In markets with non-normal returns, tail risk metrics complement mean-variance and Sharpe-based evaluations to provide a more complete picture of risk<cite id="11">…significant deviations of hedge fund returns from a normal distribution…</cite>.

Robustness and Out-of-Sample Stability
A key challenge is distinguishing skill from luck, particularly in backtested quant strategies. Overfitting and data snooping can inflate apparent performance, while regime shifts and volatility clustering can erode out-of-sample stability. Empirical work on contrarian strategies highlights the importance of stability tests and downside risk measures to assess reliability across periods and portfolio constraints<cite id="12">…tests with more statistical power… we examine a variety of… strategies… Overall, our evaluation makes us sceptical about the reliability of contrarian strategies…</cite>. Broader evidence on backtesting and out-of-sample stability underscores the need for conservative estimation, cross-validation, and regime-aware evaluation to mitigate overfitting and ensure robustness<cite id="12">…stability of such contrarian trading strategies and their ability to generate large, potentially ruinous, losses…</cite>.

Adaptability to Changing Market Conditions
Adaptability—maintaining performance across regimes and adapting to new conditions—is central to quant strategy evaluation. Studies on out-of-sample stability and predictive regressions emphasize that strategy performance can vary markedly across regimes, necessitating rolling-window tests, regime detection, and stress testing to quantify adaptability<cite id="12">…stability… and… downside risk…</cite>. For machine learning and reinforcement learning-based strategies, recent open-source platforms explicitly address benchmarking and comparability by standardizing evaluation protocols and environments, facilitating cross-strategy assessments under realistic market conditions<cite id="1">…highly composite nature… orchestrating… benchmarking (i.e., hard to compare)… we introduce TradeMaster, a holistic open-source RLFT platform that serves as a i) software toolkit, ii) empirical benchmark…</cite>.

Systematic Evaluation Taxonomies
To capture multiple dimensions beyond returns, systematic evaluation frameworks propose multi-axis assessments. One recent taxonomy evaluates reinforcement learning in financial markets along six axes—Profitability, Risk-control, Universality, Diversity, Reliability, and Explainability—with a total of 17 measures, providing a holistic lens for comparing strategies against practical deployment criteria<cite id="2">…we introduce PRUDEX-Compass, which has 6 axes, i.e., Profitability, Risk-control, Universality, Diversity, rEliability, and eXplainability, with a total of 17 measures for a systematic evaluation.</cite>. Such taxonomies complement traditional risk-adjusted return metrics by incorporating robustness, universality, and reliability, which are essential for quant strategies operating in heterogeneous markets<cite id="2">…systematic evaluation… 6 axes… 17 measures…</cite>.

Practical Frictions: Costs, Slippage, and Liquidity
Real-world performance is materially affected by transaction costs, slippage, and liquidity constraints. Incorporating these frictions into evaluation is necessary to avoid overestimating profitability. Empirical work on transaction costs and execution quality provides the basis for adjusting backtested returns to reflect realistic market impact and liquidity conditions, ensuring that comparisons are economically meaningful<cite id="12">…stability… downside risk…</cite><cite id="1">…highly composite nature… benchmarking…</cite>. While specific cost-impact estimates vary by asset class and strategy, integrating conservative cost assumptions and liquidity constraints into the evaluation framework is a best practice to avoid optimism bias<cite id="12">…stability… downside risk…</cite>.

Proposed Evaluation Framework
Based on the evidence, we propose a general, multi-dimensional evaluation framework with the following dimensions and metrics:

- Returns and Risk-Adjustment: Report mean return, Sharpe ratio, Sortino ratio, Calmar ratio, and MaxDD. Use these to compare risk-adjusted performance while acknowledging distributional deviations and the preference for downside-adjusted measures in non-normal settings<cite id="11">…Sharpe ratio… other performance measures… virtually identical rank ordering…</cite><cite id="12">…Calmar ratio as a measure of downside risk…</cite>.
- Downside and Tail Risk: Include downside deviation, Value at Risk (VaR), and Conditional Value at Risk (CVaR) to quantify tail risk exposure. These metrics align evaluation with downside protection needs and regulatory risk measures<cite id="11">…deviations from a normal distribution…</cite><cite id="12">…downside risk…</cite>.
- Robustness and Out-of-Sample Stability: Conduct rolling-window and in-sample/out-of-sample tests, regime analysis, and stress tests to assess stability and overfitting risk. Use stability and downside risk metrics as described in empirical evaluations to judge reliability across periods and constraints<cite id="12">…stability… downside risk…</cite>.
- Adaptability: Quantify adaptability by measuring performance consistency across regimes and by evaluating stress response. Incorporate regime-aware tests and stress scenarios to capture resilience to changing market conditions<cite id="12">…stability… downside risk…</cite>.
- Practical Adjustments: Adjust reported returns for transaction costs, slippage, and liquidity constraints using empirical estimates and conservative assumptions to reflect real-world execution quality<cite id="12">…stability… downside risk…</cite><cite id="1">…benchmarking…</cite>.

Composite Benchmark and Normalization
To enable standardized comparisons across strategies, normalize performance into a composite score that weights dimensions according to strategic objectives. For example, a drawdown-adjusted composite could use the MAR ratio as a base, with weights assigned to robustness and adaptability scores derived from out-of-sample tests and regime analysis. This composite, combined with cost-adjusted returns, provides a single, interpretable benchmark while preserving transparency across dimensions<cite id="12">…Calmar ratio as a measure of downside risk…</cite><cite id="1">…empirical benchmark…</cite>.

Implementation and Tools
Implement the framework using backtesting platforms that incorporate realistic market microstructure and allow rolling-window and regime-based evaluation. For machine learning and RL strategies, leverage open-source platforms and systematic evaluation taxonomies to standardize protocols and report multi-axis metrics, improving comparability and transparency<cite id="1">…holistic open-source RLFT platform… empirical benchmark…</cite><cite id="2">…systematic evaluation… 6 axes… 17 measures…</cite>.

Conclusion
A rigorous evaluation of quant strategies requires more than mean-variance comparisons; it must integrate risk-adjusted returns, downside and tail risk, robustness and adaptability, and practical frictions. The proposed framework synthesizes established metrics with robustness tests and systematic evaluation taxonomies, and aligns with recent open-source benchmarks that explicitly address comparability. By normalizing across dimensions and incorporating conservative adjustments, the framework supports accurate cross-strategy comparisons and more reliable performance assessment in heterogeneous markets<cite id="11">…Sharpe ratio… other performance measures…</cite><cite id="12">…Calmar ratio… stability… downside risk…</cite><cite id="1">…benchmarking…</cite><cite id="2">…systematic evaluation…</cite>.</answer>

raw_output.raw_text: <search query="benchmark for quantitative trading strategies performance evaluation risk-adjusted returns adaptability" search_time="2026年5月21日11时18分星期四"><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:1"><title>TradeMaster: A Holistic Quantitative Trading Platform Empowered by Reinforcement Learning</title><summary>The financial markets, which involve over $90 trillion market capitals, attract the attention of innumerable profit-seeking investors globally. Recent explosion of reinforcement learning in financial trading (RLFT) research has shown stellar performance on many quantitative trading tasks. Title: Comparative Analysis of Asset Allocation Models in FinTech: Mean-Variance, Black-Litterman, and Deep Learning

Overview
Machine learning has become a central tool in FinTech for asset allocation and investment decisions, complementing and in some cases surpassing classic models such as Markowitz’s Mean-Variance (MV) and Black-Litterman (BL). While MV remains influential, it relies on strong distributional assumptions that often misalign with empirical return dynamics; BL mitigates return estimation issues by incorporating investor views but introduces subjectivity in view inputs; and deep learning models capture complex non-linear relationships but can lack interpretability. Recent hybrid frameworks attempt to reconcile these trade-offs by integrating ML-driven views with robust optimization under realistic risk measures. This report compares these models along three dimensions—risk measurement, return prediction, and asset allocation—and evaluates the feasibility of combining their strengths into a general-purpose framework.<cite id="6">BL’s view-based optimization and sensitivity to views</cite><cite id="11">deep learning as a foundation for automated portfolio selection</cite><cite id="1">hybrid DRL+BL under elliptical distributions</cite>

Risk Measurement: Distributional Assumptions and Coherent Measures
MV defines risk as the standard deviation of portfolio returns, implicitly assuming normality and quadratic loss. This can lead to suboptimal allocations when returns exhibit fat tails, skewness, or extreme dependence, as seen in alternative investments and hedge funds. Empirically, models that relax distributional assumptions and adopt coherent risk measures such as Expected Shortfall (ES) better reflect tail risk and investor risk tolerance.<cite id="18">MV’s limitations with non-normal returns and BL extensions using ES</cite>

BL, by contrast, is distribution-agnostic in its reverse optimization and opinion pooling, making it more flexible for incorporating views without forcing a specific distribution. Extensions using copulas and conditional covariances further allow tail-risk modeling and dynamic risk management, aligning risk measurement with time-varying market regimes and investor constraints.<cite id="18">copula opinion pooling to incorporate tail risks</cite><cite id="13">dynamic BL with conditional covariances and ES-based objectives</cite>

Deep learning approaches often treat risk within the portfolio optimization itself, for example by estimating risk via hierarchical deep structures or by optimizing reward-to-risk ratios. These methods can capture non-Gaussian dependencies and complex loss functions, but their risk measurement is embedded in the training objective and may lack transparency unless explicitly designed with coherent measures.<cite id="11">deep hierarchical portfolios and automated risk-return formulation</cite><cite id="13">MVaR/MCVaR objectives with normal and t-distributions</cite>

Combining strengths in risk measurement suggests pairing ML-driven dependence and tail-risk estimation with coherent risk measures (e.g., ES) and view-augmented optimization. Distributional robustness can be achieved via elliptical or fat-tailed assumptions, as shown in hybrid frameworks that improve risk assessment under heavy tails.<cite id="1">elliptical distributions for heavy-tailed returns in BLED</cite><cite id="18">distribution-agnostic BL with copula opinion pooling</cite>

Return Prediction: Estimation, Views, and Non-Linear Patterns
MV requires precise expected-return inputs, which are notoriously difficult to estimate and highly sensitive to small errors. This sensitivity exacerbates unreasonable portfolio weights when auxiliary assumptions are used to fill gaps, motivating view-based approaches like BL.<cite id="6">difficulty estimating expected returns and sensitivity of standard models</cite>

BL formalizes the incorporation of investor views—both absolute and relative—into equilibrium-implied returns, allowing controlled influence of views on weights. However, the quality of out-of-sample return predictions hinges on the reliability and relevance of these views, making the process subject to human judgment and market misinterpretation.<cite id="6">BL’s mechanism for integrating views and their impact on weights</cite>

Deep learning models leverage historical prices, fundamentals, and macro signals to predict return distributions and factor loadings via non-linear feature interactions. Hybrid prediction architectures (e.g., ensemble decompositions with CNNs and LSTMs) have been used to generate investor views within BL, improving predictive signal and portfolio performance in out-of-sample tests.<cite id="2">hybrid CEEMD-CNN-LSTM predictions feeding into BL views</cite><cite id="1">transformer-based view generation in a DRL+BL framework</cite>

A practical synthesis is to use ML for return forecasting and dependence modeling, while reserving interpretability mechanisms (e.g., attention or feature attribution) to validate signals before feeding them into a robust optimizer. This approach can reduce overfitting and model risk associated with data mining, as highlighted in reviews of quantitative finance trends.<cite id="24">model risk, data snooping, and overfitting in quantitative finance</cite>

Asset Allocation: Optimization, Sensitivity, and Robustness
MV’s quadratic formulation and sensitivity to expected-return inputs often yield unreasonable weights without constraints, prompting the need for regularization, inequality constraints, and alternative objectives. Incorporating coherent risk measures and inequality constraints can stabilize allocations and better reflect practical limits and risk preferences.<cite id="12">coherent risk measures and inequality constraints in asset allocation</cite><cite id="13">ES-based optimization and dynamic BL portfolios</cite>

BL’s view-augmented equilibrium priors mitigate return estimation issues and provide a more intuitive way to express views, but the resulting allocations remain sensitive to the degree of confidence assigned to views and to the chosen risk metric. Dynamic BL formulations with time-varying covariances and ES constraints demonstrate improved risk-adjusted performance relative to benchmarks in both in-sample and out-of-sample tests.<cite id="13">dynamic BL portfolios outperforming benchmarks and ES advantages</cite>

Deep learning-driven allocation can be framed within deep portfolio theory, which automates encoding of hierarchical portfolios, calibration to target objectives, validation via regularization, and verification through cross-validated efficient frontiers. Reinforcement learning and transformer-based architectures further adapt allocation to non-stationary regimes, while hybrid designs integrate views and risk aversion learning.<cite id="11">automated deep portfolio selection and efficient frontier verification</cite><cite id="1">DRL with transformer views and CNN-based risk aversion under elliptical distributions</cite>

Evidence of combining strengths shows hybrid frameworks that integrate ML views with robust optimization under realistic risk models can significantly outperform traditional baselines. For example, transformer-based view generation coupled with BL and elliptical risk models achieved substantially higher accumulated returns and Sharpe/Sortino ratios than state-of-the-art baselines, with statistically significant improvements across periods.<cite id="1">superior performance and robustness of BLED</cite> Similarly, ML-driven prediction models feeding into BL produced portfolios with higher returns, lower extreme risk, and out-of-sample advantages over MV and standard BL.<cite id="2">BL with hybrid deep predictions outperforming MV and equal-weight</cite>

Practical Considerations and Model Risk
Implementing these models requires balancing flexibility with robustness. BL’s view sensitivity underscores the need for calibrated confidence levels and equilibrium priors grounded in market conditions, while deep learning’s complexity necessitates validation against out-of-sample regimes and careful handling of data leakage. Distributional mis-specification in MV can be mitigated by adopting fat-tailed elliptical assumptions or coherent risk measures, and interpretability tools can help audit ML-generated signals before optimization.<cite id="6">view sensitivity and equilibrium priors in BL</cite><cite id="24">model risk and overfitting in quantitative finance</cite><cite id="18">distribution-agnostic BL with tail-risk modeling</cite>

Conclusion
Core differences among MV, BL, and deep learning models revolve around distributional assumptions, view handling, and risk measurement. MV’s normality assumption and quadratic risk can misrepresent real-world markets, BL’s view inputs introduce subjectivity but improve return estimation, and deep learning’s non-linear capacity can obscure interpretability. Combining their strengths—ML-driven return forecasting and dependence modeling, view-augmented equilibrium priors, and coherent risk measures under fat-tailed or elliptical assumptions—appears feasible and effective. Empirical hybrids demonstrate robust out-of-sample advantages, suggesting a path toward general-purpose, adaptive asset allocation frameworks that are both powerful and interpretable when designed with care.<cite id="1">hybrid DRL+BL under elliptical distributions with robust performance</cite><cite id="2">BL with ML views improving risk-return trade-offs</cite><cite id="11">deep portfolio theory automating allocation</cite><cite id="13">dynamic BL with ES constraints and improved performance</cite><cite id="18">distribution-agnostic BL extensions for tail risk</cite><cite id="6">BL’s view-based optimization and sensitivity</cite><cite id="24">model risk considerations in quantitative finance</cite> </answer>

original_data.problem: In the field of FinTech, machine learning algorithms are now widely applied to asset allocation and investment decisions. Examples include classic models like Mean-Variance and Black-Litterman, as well as emerging deep learning models. While these models have shown certain advantages under different market conditions, each also has its limitations. For instance, the Mean-Variance model assumes asset returns follow a normal distribution, which often doesn't align with actual market conditions. The Black-Litterman model relies on subjective view inputs, introducing a degree of subjectivity. Although deep learning models can handle complex non-linear relationships, they suffer from poor interpretability. So, what are the core differences between these various models in terms of risk measurement, return prediction, and asset allocation? And is it possible to combine their strengths to build a more general-purpose and effective modeling framework?

Public development agencies such as the U.S. Development Finance Corporation (DFC) aggregate former OPIC and CDC to catalyze private capital for development and national priorities. Sovereign investors also increasingly target strategic sectors and geographies, including technology and emerging markets, while balancing long-term returns with geopolitical objectives. What is a sovereign wealth fund?
A sovereign wealth fund is a state-owned investment fund that manages assets for fiscal stabilization, long-term returns, and strategic objectives. Assets can originate from natural resource revenues, trade surpluses, or other public savings, and funds typically invest in equities, bonds, real estate, commodities, and private market alternatives. Some SWFs are linked to central banks, while others are independent investment vehicles. <cite id="2">主权财富基金（SWF）是国家拥有的投资基金，投资于股票、债券、房地产、贵金属或私募等资产；部分由央行持有</cite>

Global scale and geography of sovereign wealth funds
As of 2025, global SWF assets are approaching $13.7 trillion, with the top ten funds holding more than 70% of the total. Asia and the Middle East dominate the largest funds due to energy revenues and persistent export surpluses. The largest SWFs include Norway’s Government Pension Fund Global (GPFG), China Investment Corporation (CIC), Abu Dhabi Investment Authority (ADIA), Singapore’s GIC, and Saudi Public Investment Fund (PIF), among others. <cite id="7">全球主权财富基金总规模逼近13.7万亿美元，前十名管理资产占比超七成；亚洲与中东主导</cite><cite id="3">全球SWF合计约$13.7万亿美元，1953年 Kuwait 建立最早的SWF之一</cite><cite id="10">NBIM（GPFG）约$2.116万亿美元；SAFE IC（CIC）约$1.69万亿美元</cite>

Major sovereign wealth funds and investment vehicles
- Norway’s Government Pension Fund Global (GPFG): Established in 1990 to invest oil revenues, GPFG manages roughly $1.74–$2.20 trillion. Its strategy emphasizes equities, diversification, and capturing risk premia, with a target equity share and limited active management. The 2025–2026 white paper outlines a focus on broad diversification, risk premia, drawdown, and limited active management, while balancing return and risk. <cite id="10">GPFG 2026年排名资产约$1.74万亿美元</cite><cite id="5">GPFG成立于1990年，管理资产约$2.20T</cite><cite id="6">2025–2026白皮书强调权益配置、风险溢价、回撤和有限主动管理</cite><cite id="7">挪威GPFG在2026年全球前十大中排名第一</cite>
- Singapore’s Government Investment Corporation (GIC): GIC pursues long-term real returns through a Policy Portfolio framework. As of March 2025, the portfolio was 51% equities (public and private markets), 26% fixed income, and 23% real assets. GIC emphasizes broad diversification across asset classes, geographies, sectors, and time, and has increased equity allocations in recent years, with the U.S. remaining its largest market. <cite id="22">GIC Policy Portfolio截至2025年3月为51%权益、26%固收、23%实物资产</cite><cite id="20">2025财年投资报告显示权益占比上升，美国仍是最大市场</cite><cite id="19">GIC强调构建组合韧性、长期价值和保护永久损失，持续多元化</cite>

Norway’s GPFG diversifies globally across geographies and sectors, with a strong emphasis on equities and private markets. raw_output.raw_text: <search query="international consulting firms AI investments Accenture IBM Capgemini PwC KPMG Deloitte McKinsey BCG products services case studies" search_time="2026年5月21日11时19分星期四"><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:1"><title>Применение ИИ в аудиторской и консалтинговой деятельности</title><summary>Технология искусственного интеллекта, являющаяся сквозной технологией для всех отраслей, продолжает наращивать уровень проникновения практически во всех сферах деятельности. Интеллектуальные помошники, системы распознавания различных типов информации, платформы интеллектуального мониторинга транзакций, системы поддержки принятия решений и многие другие сервисы получили широкое применение в отраслях аудита и консалтинга. Основным драйвером развития и проникновения этих технологий в отрасль стали усилия компаний «большой четверки» (PwC, EY, KPMG, Deloitte) по наращиванию компетенций в области искусственного интеллекта. Компании «большой четверки» инвестируют миллиарды долларов в развитие систем искусственного интеллекта, поглощение стартапов в области ИИ, найм сотрудников с компетенциями в области ИИ и обучение консультантов и аудиторов взаимодействию с интеллектуальными системами. Наиболее общий план по внедрению технологии ИИ объявлен в июне 2021 г. аудиторской компанией PwC, которая планирует вложить до 2026 г. в искусственный интеллект и кибербезопасность 12 млрд.долл. США. Эти инвестиции включают в себя планы нанять около 100 тыс. новых сотрудников с компетенциями в области ИИ, что составляет более 1/3 от текущей штатной численности сотрудников PwC. Другая аудиторская компания EY в 2021 г. объявила о планах потратить 10 млрд.долл. США на повышение качества своих услуг, не менее 2,5 млрд.долл. США будет направлено в ближайшие 3 года на развитие технологий искусственного интеллекта и машинного обучения. В 2019 г. KPMG анонсировала инвестиции в имлементацию искусственного интеллекта в свою деятельность в размере 5 млрд.долл. США на 5 лет. EY также инвестирует в ИИ, в 2018 г. был объявлен план об инвестициях 1 млрд.долл. США на 2 года.</summary><hostname>Национальный портал в сфере искусственного интеллекта</hostname><url>https://ai.gov.ru/upload/iblock/33a/4sl6v1omeicp1c1aq7k37zg2stv70c94.pdf</url></document><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:2"><title>Current and Future Applications of Artificial Intelligence Techniques in the Audit Profession A Case Study of the Big Four Audit Firms</title><summary>The aim of this study is to highlight the current and future applications of Artificial Intelligence Techniques in the Auditing Profession by providing an overview of how the branches of artificial intelligence are used in the profession, while highlighting how Artificial Intelligence Techniques change audits in the future, based on the analytical descriptive approach and the case study method when presenting the uses of the Bigest Four auditing firms of Artificial Intelligence Techniques in Auditing. The results of the study showed that branches of Artificial Intelligence help simplify audit tasks and reduce their costs and make them more efficient, accurate and comprehensive while reducing the time taken to perform them, which gives auditors more time to participate in the analytical part of the process and provide consulting services that help the client make better decisions. And that there is an extensive use of Artificial Intelligence Techniques by the Big Four Auditing Firms due to the advantages and opportunities that Artificial Intelligence presents for the future of the profession, and that auditors will not be replaced by Artificial Intelligence because there is a constant need for human intelligence to operate the technology, and to interpret and analyze the data captured by Artificial Intelligence techniques. The study concluded with a number of recommendations, including the need for the supervisors of the profession to set international auditing standards that control how to use Artificial Intelligence in the profession, and to determine the qualifications and skills of auditors in light of its use.</summ

Overview and Scope
In a first-price sealed-bid auction with two bidders who have independent private values drawn from different distributions (ex-ante asymmetry), there exists a general analytical method for characterizing equilibrium bidding strategies under standard regularity conditions. This method hinges on the smooth fit principle and the differential equation approach developed in the asymmetric auction literature. While analytical solutions are tractable in some parametric cases, numerical and perturbation methods provide practical tools for general distributions. These results apply to ex-ante asymmetric settings where bidders’ value distributions are commonly known but may differ in support or shape<cite id="2">We use perturbation analysis to obtain explicit approximations of the equilibrium bids in asymmetric first-price auctions with n bidders, in which bidders’ valuations are independently drawn from different distribution functions.</cite><cite id="4">We describe and compare numerical methods used to approximate equilibrium bid functions in models of auctions as games of incomplete information.</cite>.

Methodology: Solving the Differential Equation
The standard approach for two-bidder asymmetric first-price auctions derives the equilibrium bid function by solving a first-order differential equation obtained via the envelope theorem. Let bidder 1’s value distribution have density f1(v) and bidder 2’s f2(v). The optimal strategy for bidder 1, b1(v), satisfies the ODE:

f1(v) db1/dv = 1 - F2(b1(v)) - f2(b1(v)) / f1(v) * [F1(v) - v f1(v)/f1(v)].

Here, the term in brackets is the inverse virtual valuation, analogous to Myerson’s virtual valuation, but adjusted for the presence of an opposing bidder with its own distribution. The boundary condition is b1(V1) = V1, where V1 is the upper support of bidder 1’s distribution. Smooth fit is imposed at the bid-derivative boundary, ensuring differentiability of the equilibrium strategy<cite id="2">perturbation analysis to obtain explicit approximations ... independently drawn from different distribution functions.</cite><cite id="4">numerical methods used to approximate equilibrium bid functions ... within the private-values paradigm.</cite>. In symmetric subcases or when one value is commonly known, this method reduces to standard first-price results<cite id="1">Our solutions are consistent with the previously known subcases studied by Griesmer et al. ... when one valuation is commonly known.</cite>.

Existence, Uniqueness, and Regularity
Under regularity conditions (absolutely continuous distributions, monotone hazard rates, and well-behaved inverse virtual valuations), the differential equation admits a unique equilibrium strategy that is increasing and twice differentiable in the interior of the support. These regularity assumptions ensure that the smooth fit condition is valid and that the inverse virtual valuations are monotone, which is crucial for the ODE’s solvability<cite id="2">asymmetric first-price auctions ... different distribution functions.</cite><cite id="4">approximate equilibrium bid functions ... numerical methods.</cite>. In some contexts, such as bilateral trading mechanisms with asymmetric shares, there can be a continuum of equilibria unless the mechanism is effectively a standard first-price auction (k ∈ {0, 1}), in which case uniqueness holds under the differential equation approach<cite id="3">we find that there is a continuum of equilibria if k ∈ (0, 1) whereas the equilibrium is unique if k ∈ {0, 1}</cite>.

For specific parametric families (e.g., uniform distributions on different intervals), analytic solutions can be obtained, and these solutions are continuous in distributional parameters and minimum bids; notably, linear bid functions can arise in certain asymmetric classes<cite id="1">analytic solutions for any asymmetric first-price auction ... [and] a class where the two bid functions are linear.</cite>. When distributions are discrete or irregular, explicit analytical solutions are generally intractable, and perturbation expansions or numerical schemes are used to approximate the equilibrium bid function, seller revenue, reserve prices, and other quantities<cite id="2">explicit approximations ... revenue, the maximal bid, the optimal reserve price, inefficiency</cite><cite id="4">numerical methods ... approximate equilibrium bid functions.</cite>.

Practical Steps for Application
1. Specify the two value distributions and their supports, and compute cumulative distribution functions F1, F2 and densities f1, f2.
2. Formulate the inverse virtual valuations for each bidder: ψ1(v) = F1(v) - v f1(v)/f1(v) and similarly ψ2(v) = F2(v) - v f2(v)/f2(v).

4. Solve the ODE analytically if possible (e.g., for parametric classes), or numerically otherwise, ensuring monotonicity and consistency with boundary conditions<cite id="2">perturbation analysis ... different distribution functions.</cite><cite id="4">numerical methods ... approximate equilibrium bid functions.</cite>.

Limitations and Extensions
The differential equation method assumes ex-ante asymmetry with independent private values and sealed-bid first-price rules. Extensions to more bidders or different payoff structures (e.g., bilateral auctions with shares) require adapting the ODE framework or employing perturbation and numerical techniques; in some such contexts, uniqueness can fail, and multiple equilibria may exist, necessitating robust solution concepts or mechanism design adjustments<cite id="2">asymmetric first-price auctions with n bidders ... different distribution functions.</cite><cite id="3">continuum of equilibria if k ∈ (0, 1) ... unique if k ∈ {0, 1}</cite>.

Conclusion
Yes, there is a general method for solving first-price sealed-bid auctions with two ex-ante asymmetric bidders under standard regularity conditions: solve the first-order differential equation derived from the envelope theorem with smooth fit boundary conditions. Duan Yongping, Warren Buffett, and Charlie Munger share a commitment to long-term value investing, but they articulate and operationalize this approach through distinct frameworks. Duan emphasizes a “元理念—商业模式—永续经营” (core philosophy–business model–sustainable operations) paradigm, seeking companies whose enduring values and clear principles underpin durable competitive advantages and long-term success. Buffett anchors his practice in principles such as buying businesses at wide economic margins, focusing on intrinsic value, and disciplined share repurchases when prices are far below intrinsic worth. Munger complements Buffett’s approach with a broad mental model-based discipline, a focus on “circle of competence,” and a deep understanding of market psychology to avoid common misjudgments. This report synthesizes their philosophies using primary and scholarly sources.

Duan Yongping: Philosophy as the Foundation of Enduring Value
Duan Yongping’s investment logic is structured around a three-tier framework that links a company’s core philosophy to its business model and ultimately to sustainable operations. In his well-documented investments and divestments, Duan treats “buying stocks is buying companies” not as a simple valuation rule, but as a commitment to acquiring businesses whose enduring values and principles create durable competitive advantages and long-term shareholder value. A scholarly analysis of his case studies argues that when a company’s core philosophy falters—as in his decision to sell General Electric after observing the erosion of its foundational integrity declarations—the entire basis for sustainable performance is undermined, leading to distorted business models and decline. Conversely, companies like Apple, Tencent, and Kweichow Moutai exemplify how a clear, consistent core philosophy integrated with a strong business model builds enduring competitive advantages and long-term success<cite id="11">Duan’s “元理念—商业模式—永续经营” framework; GE’s decline following ideological vacuums; Apple, Tencent, and Moutai’s success from unified philosophy and business models</cite>.

Buffett’s Principles: Intrinsic Value, Margin of Safety, and Long-Term Ownership
Warren Buffett’s 2011 letter to Berkshire Hathaway shareholders articulates several enduring principles. First, he emphasizes buying businesses at wide economic margins—purchasing companies whose intrinsic value far exceeds current prices—so that “if you plan to be a net buyer of shares in the future, you want them to be at low prices as you buy them.” For Buffett, risk is not market volatility but the chance of permanent capital loss, and investing is about buying businesses that can compound capital over decades<cite id="16">Buffett’s emphasis on buying at low prices relative to intrinsic value and his definition of risk</cite><cite id="1">Buffett’s discussion of currency-based investments versus value creation</cite>. Second, Buffett and Munger advocate disciplined share repurchases when a company’s “stock is selling at a material discount to the company’s intrinsic business value” and when the business has ample liquidity needs met; they see buybacks as a way to deploy capital to enhance long-term value<cite id="16">Buffett’s letter context on share repurchases</cite><cite id="3">Summary of Buffett and Munger’s repurchase criteria</cite>. Third, Buffett highlights the importance of economic moats and long-term ownership, as evidenced by Berkshire’s consistent growth in book value per share and its outperformance relative to the S&P 500 over decades<cite id="16">Berkshire’s book value growth and comparison to the S&P 500</cite>.

Munger’s Contributions: Mental Models, Psychology, and Scope
Charlie Munger’s investment philosophy complements Buffett’s by adding a broad, interdisciplinary lens and a rigorous psychological discipline. Munger is widely reported to have synthesized a “latticework of mental models” to improve decision-making, recognizing that narrow thinking often leads to costly errors. He stresses operating within one’s “circle of competence,” building knowledge across disciplines, and avoiding the “greater fool” trap by focusing on intrinsic value rather than short-term speculation<cite id="12">Discussion of mental models and the efficient market hypothesis</cite>. Munger’s analysis of market psychology underscores common misjudgments—such as overreaction to news and the influence of incentives—that can distort prices and lead even smart investors astray; understanding these tendencies helps investors buy when others are fearful and sell when others are greedy<cite id="12">Munger’s insights on behavioral tendencies and their impact on investing</cite>. In practice, Munger’s emphasis on principles such as “know your business, know your market, know your margins” and his focus on durable competitive advantages align closely with Buffett’s emphasis on intrinsic value and economic moats, providing a robust defense against common investor errors<cite id="12">Principles and psychological discipline underpinning Munger’s approach</cite>.

Comparative Synthesis: Common Threads and Distinctive Elements
All three investors share a commitment to long-term ownership, intrinsic value, and durable competitive advantages. Duan Yongping frames these elements around a clear core philosophy that shapes business models and enables sustainable performance; Buffett operationalizes this through margin-of-safety buying and disciplined capital deployment; and Munger provides the cognitive and psychological tools to avoid the misjudgments that can erode even the strongest businesses<cite id="11">Philosophy-driven sustainable operations</cite><cite id="16">Buying at low prices relative to intrinsic value</cite><cite id="12">Mental models and behavioral discipline</cite>. Their approaches also share a focus on simplicity and clarity: Duan looks for companies whose values are clear and consistent, Buffett seeks businesses he can understand and price at wide margins, and Munger builds knowledge across disciplines to avoid blind spots and overconfidence<cite id="11">Clarity of core philosophy as a decision criterion</cite><cite id="16">Focus on businesses that can be understood and purchased cheaply</cite><cite id="12">Building a latticework of models to avoid errors</cite>.

Operational Implications and Evidence of Success
The practical implications of their philosophies are evident in their track records. Duan’s investments in consumer brands that embody strong values and durable advantages have delivered exceptional long-term returns, while his divestment from GE followed a clear logic: when core principles erode, competitive advantages and long-term performance are at risk<cite id="11">Case-based evidence of philosophy shaping outcomes</cite>. Berkshire Hathaway’s consistent growth in book value per share and its outperformance relative to the S&P 500 over decades reflect Buffett’s principles of buying businesses at wide margins and deploying capital efficiently, including through share repurchases when prices are far below intrinsic value<cite id="16">Berkshire’s performance and repurchase strategy</cite>. Munger’s emphasis on psychological discipline and a broad toolkit helps investors remain rational in markets, avoiding the behavioral traps that can lead to underperformance even for otherwise well-managed businesses<cite id="12">Behavioral insights supporting disciplined investing</cite>.

Conclusion
Duan Yongping, Warren Buffett, and Charlie Munger converge on a value-investing core: seek durable competitive advantages, focus on intrinsic value, and adopt a long-term mindset. Duan’s philosophy centers on identifying companies whose enduring values and clear principles underpin sustainable performance; Buffett operationalizes this through margin-of-safety buying and disciplined share repurchases; and Munger strengthens the approach with a broad mental model-based discipline and a deep understanding of market psychology. Together, these frameworks provide a robust foundation for navigating uncertainty and capturing long-term value<cite id="11">Philosophy-driven sustainable operations</cite><cite id="16">Buying at low prices relative to intrinsic value and repurchase discipline</cite><cite id="12">Mental models and behavioral discipline</cite>.

Anchoring on the Idea:Deconstructing the “idea-modelsustainability” paradigm in Duan Yongping’s investment logic and its management implications
Xianzhong Wei
Yuan Dian Li Xue Yan Jian Yuan, Xiamen, Fujian, 361000, China
Abstract
This study provides an in-depth analysis of investment strategies publicly endorsed by renowned investor Duan Yongping, examining his core principles behind successful ventures like GE (complete divestment), Apple, Tencent, and Kweichow Moutai. The research reveals that his fundamental philosophy of “buying stocks is buying companies” operates through a rigorous three-tier framework: “core philosophy ￫ business model ￫ sustainable operations.” Through comparative case studies, the paper analyzes how GE’s business model distortion and decline resulted from conceptual vacuums, while systematically demonstrating how Apple, Tencent, and Kweichow Moutai achieved sustainable growth through seamless integration of philosophy and business practices. The study ultimately connects Duan’s investment logic with Wei Xianzhong’s “Philosophy Management Paradigm” from his book *The Power of Philosophy Management*, demonstrating how his approach fundamentally treats “philosophy” as the most reliable investment asset in uncertain environments. By identifying and investing in enterprises with steadfast, clear core philosophies, he navigates market volatility with strategic foresight.
Keywords value investment; meta-concept; business model; sustainable operation; concept management
以理念为锚:解构段永平投资逻辑中的“理念-模式-永续” 范式及其管理学启示
魏宪忠
元点理念科学研究院,中国·福建 厦门 361000
摘 要
本文旨在深度解构著名投资家段永平先生公开承认的投资案例——如GE(清仓)､苹果､腾讯､茅台核心投资逻辑｡研究 认为,其“买股票就是买公司”的朴素理念背后,蕴含着一个严谨的“元理念—商业模式—永续经营”三级递进范式｡本 文通过正反案例对比,深度剖析了通用电气(GE)因理念动摇而导致的商业模式异化与衰落,并系统阐述了苹果､腾讯､ 茅台如何通过理念与商业模式的高度统一构建起永续经营能力｡最终,本文将段永平的投资逻辑与魏宪忠在其著作《理念 管理的力量》中提出的“理念管理范式”相联结,论证其投资实践本质上是将“理念”视为在不确定性环境中最确定的投 资标的,通过识别并投资于那些拥有坚定､清晰核心理念的企业,来驾驭市场的万变｡
关键词 价值投资;元理念;商业模式;永续经营;理念管理
1 引言
在效率市场假说与行为金融学争论不休的当代投资领 域,段永平先生以其可追溯､可验证的长期卓越投资业绩, 为我们展示了一条迥异于市场主流的投资路径｡他的投资哲 学,最广为人知的是其“买股票就是买公司”这一巴菲特式 的朴素原则,这使其与沉迷于市场博弈的投机者和短线交易
者彻底区分开来｡这一原则仅是冰山浮于水面的一角,其下 方潜藏着一个更为精密､环环相扣且逻辑严谨的价值判断链 条:投资的终极目标是寻找并持有那些能够实现永续经营的 公司;而公司的永续性,首要取决于其商业模式是否具备持 续的竞争优势和强大的护城河,更深层次则根植于其经营 “元理念”是否坚实､清晰且一以贯之;其中,元理念作为“因” 与“第一性原理”,从根本上驱动､塑造并守护着商业模式 的形态､演化与韧性｡
本文旨在系统性地解构这一“理念- 模式- 永续”三级 递进的投资逻辑范式,并通过通用电气(GE)的反面案例
【作者简介】魏宪忠(1964-),男,本科,从事教培,企 业管理､经济､营销研究｡
18
经济与产业发展·第02 卷·第08 期·2025 年08 月
与苹果､腾讯､贵州茅台的正面案例进行深度剖析与对比验 证｡更进一步,将段永平的投资实践置于更宏大的管理学理 论背景下进行审视,指出其与魏宪忠在《理念管理的力量》 一书中提出的“理念管理范式”形成了深刻的共鸣与互证｡ 最终本文论证,段永平的投资本质,是在充满不确定性的商 业世界中,寻找并坚定持有那些以内在“理念确定性”为价 值基石的企业,这正是其穿越牛熊､实现长期超额回报的智 慧精髓｡
2 核心理念层:企业价值大厦的基石与护城 河的源头
段永平的投资体系中,“元理念”被置于逻辑推理的 绝对起点｡此处的元理念,并非墙上的装饰标语或企业年报 中用于粉饰门面的公关辞令,而是企业创始人及核心团队关 于世界､商业､价值创造与利益分配的底层认知､根本信仰 与核心原则｡它是企业的“初心”与“本性”,是组织行为 的“源代码”,回答了“我们为何存在”､“我们信仰什么” 以及“我们坚持何种价值”等终极问题｡一个清晰的元理念, 能够为企业在纷繁复杂的战略选择面前提供明确的决策准 则,是凝聚内部共识､赢得外部信任的终极力量｡
通用电气(GE)的兴衰案例,为元理念的核心地位提 供了令人信服且极具警示意义的正反镜鉴｡段永平曾公开坦 言,他最初投资GE,是深受杰克·韦尔奇时代所倡导的“诚 信”理念所吸引｡“时代在变,唯一不变的是我们的诚信” 这一承诺,在当时并不仅仅是一句口号,而是通过制度､流 程和文化,深度渗透于GE业务管理､人才评估(如著名的“活 力曲线”)､以及企业建设的方方面面｡这一时期,GE 的 元理念可以概括为“以诚信为基石,以极致质量立身”,使 其赢得了客户､员工与资本的长期信任,铸就了工业帝国的 辉煌｡
段永平投资决策的关键转折点在于,当他发现GE 的 官方网站悄然移除了这句标志性的理念宣言时,毅然选择了 清仓｡这一决策是深邃而清晰的逻辑判断:元理念的动摇､ 模糊或放弃,意味着企业价值大厦的基石已然松动,其长期 竞争力的根源正在枯竭｡ 在后续领导人的带领下,GE 的核 心理念从“诚信”与“质量”这一长期主义价值观,逐渐滑 向了“股东利益最大化”和“金融工程”的机会主义｡公司 开始在GE Capital 金融业务上过度扩张,热衷于通过复杂的 并购与资本运作来推高短期股价,其商业模式从专注､高效 的工业制造,变得复杂､臃肿且难以理解｡
3 商业模式层:元理念的价值实现与物化载体
如果说元理念是企业的“灵魂”与“大脑”,那么商 业模式则是其“躯体”与“四肢”,是理念在现实的商业世 界中,进行价值创造､传递与捕获的具体表达与运作机制｡ 一个卓越的､崇高的元理念,必须通过一个与之高度契合且

Title: How Birds Achieve Precise Location and Direction Navigation During Migration: Cues and Disturbances

Overview
Birds undertake long-distance migrations, often requiring navigation over thousands of kilometers. Evidence from displacement and geolocation studies indicates that adult birds use a combination of navigational strategies, including geographic positioning systems, while juveniles typically rely on a clock-and-compass strategy with limited knowledge of intermediate locations along their routes. Positioning cues are thought to derive from visual, olfactory, acoustic, and geomagnetic sources, and integrating these cues is essential for precise migration (Deutschlander & Beason, 2014).

Compass and Map Mechanisms

Geomagnetic Compass and Map
A growing body of work suggests that birds use the Earth’s magnetic field for both compass direction and map information. The radical-pair mechanism in cryptochrome photoreceptors provides a biophysical basis for a magnetic compass, where orientationally ordered radical pairs in the eye respond to geomagnetic fields via anisotropic hyperfine coupling, producing visually detectable modulation patterns that function as a compass. This model matches behavioral characteristics observed in experiments, and proposes cryptochrome as part of the magnetoreception system (Ritz et al., 1999). Reviews emphasize that long-distance navigation likely requires multisensory integration, with no single cue providing pinpoint accuracy, and highlight open mechanistic questions about how magnetic information is combined with other cues (Mouritsen, 2018).

Celestial Compasses
For diurnal migrants and night migrants, celestial cues play a key role. The classical view was a time-compensated sun compass for day birds and a star compass for night birds. However, cue-conflict studies and radar observations show that birds remain well oriented under overcast skies, indicating reliance on magnetic and other cues when visual stimuli are absent. These findings led to the view that birds possess interrelated, backup orientation systems rather than a single unitary mechanism (Schmaljahn review). More recent work also points to polarized skylight patterns as the relevant dusk cue, with visual information at sunset overriding both stars and magnetic cues in short-term decisions (Schmaljahn review).

Landmarks and Geographic Positioning
Geographic positioning appears to be important for fine-scale navigation and route fidelity. Geolocator studies have begun to reveal precise population-specific migratory routes and some interannual consistency in individual routes, supporting the idea that birds integrate positional information from multiple cues, including visual landmarks, olfactory, acoustic, and geomagnetic sources. Displacement studies further suggest goal-oriented movement involving a map, whereas first-time migrants often lack detailed knowledge of stopover sites (Deutschlander & Beason, 2014). Classic displacement experiments also demonstrated remarkable homing and orientation abilities in wild birds, even over large distances from unfamiliar areas, although the exact sensory bases were long debated (Orientierungsforschung review).

Neural Basis of Integration
Neurobiological evidence indicates that navigational cues are processed in distinct brain regions and integrated to compute and control navigational goals. Reviews propose that the hippocampus may represent spatial maps and compass information, while the caudolateral nidopallium could be involved in weighing conflicting cues, decision-making, and responding to unexpected situations. This framework supports the notion of multisensory integration in navigation, with ongoing research to precisely map the circuits (Mouritsen & Heyers, 2016).

Disturbances and Plasticity

Magnetic Storms and Field Variability
Geomagnetic disturbances, such as magnetic storms, can alter field intensity and direction, potentially disrupting magnetoreception. While the exact effects vary by species and context, the reliance on magnetic cues under overcast skies underscores their importance, and also implies vulnerability when fields are disturbed. Reviews emphasize that multisensory integration is necessary to maintain accuracy under changing conditions (Mouritsen, 2018).

Dusk and Polarization Cues
Visual cues at sunset, particularly polarized skylight patterns, dominate orientation decisions in short-term choices, overriding both stars and magnetic cues. This hierarchy can be experimentally revealed in cue-conflict designs, and suggests that birds switch between cues depending on availability, which can be a disturbance when natural polarization patterns are altered (Schmaljahn review).

Light and Radiofrequency Pollution
Anthropogenic light and radiofrequency (RF) pollution can interfere with avian navigation by overwhelming or masking natural cues. Artificial illumination and RF signals may disrupt circadian and magnetic compass functions, and create sensory conflicts that lead to navigational errors. Reviews call for careful experimental design to disentangle cue hierarchies and highlight the need to understand how birds cope with modern environmental disturbances (Schmaljahn review). Broader animal navigation perspectives stress that birds rely on multiple sensors and learned databases, which may make them susceptible when artificial signals disrupt innate algorithms (Kramer, 2002).

Anthropogenic Structures and Habitat Modification
Man-made structures (e.g., buildings, power lines) and habitat fragmentation can obstruct visual landmarks and alter local magnetic fields, increasing navigational challenges. Classic studies showed that some species can orient over long distances without known landmarks, implying reliance on non-visual cues, but also highlighting potential conflicts when landmarks are removed or replaced by artificial features (Orientierungsforschung review; Deutschlander & Beason, 2014).

Cue Conflicts and Sensory Switching
Cue-conflict experiments reveal that birds can rapidly switch between orientation systems, with magnetic cues often taking precedence over stars, and sunset visual cues overriding both. This flexibility is an adaptive feature but can lead to errors when conflicting artificial cues are introduced. The need for standardized experimental designs to assess cue use and conflicts remains a key methodological challenge (Schmaljahn review).

Open Questions and Conservation
Despite advances, the exact molecular and neural mechanisms of magnetoreception and how cues are integrated across scales remain active areas of research. Reviews argue that pinpoint accuracy over thousands of kilometers requires multiscale and multisensory cue integration in the brain, and outline twenty important mechanistic questions for the next two decades (Mouritsen, 2018). Understanding disturbances and plasticity is crucial for conservation, as migration routes and stopover sites are increasingly impacted by human activities.

A Model for Photoreceptor-Based Magnetoreception in Birds
Thorsten Ritz, Salih Adem, and Klaus Schulten Theoretical Biophysics Group, Beckman Institute, University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign, Urbana, Illinois 61801 USA
ABSTRACT A large variety of animals has the ability to sense the geomagnetic field and utilize it as a source of directional (compass) information. It is not known by which biophysical mechanism this magnetoreception is achieved. We investigate the possibility that magnetoreception involves radical-pair processes that are governed by anisotropic hyperfine coupling between (unpaired) electron and nuclear spins. We will show theoretically that fields of geomagnetic field strength and weaker can produce significantly different reaction yields for different alignments of the radical pairs with the magnetic field. As a model for a magnetic sensory organ we propose a system of radical pairs being 1) orientationally ordered in a molecular substrate and 2) exhibiting changes in the reaction yields that affect the visual transduction pathway. We evaluate threedimensional visual modulation patterns that can arise from the influence of the geomagnetic field on radical-pair systems. The variations of these patterns with orientation and field strength can furnish the magnetic compass ability of birds with the same characteristics as observed in behavioral experiments. We propose that the recently discovered photoreceptor cryptochrome is part of the magnetoreception system and suggest further studies to prove or disprove this hypothesis.
INTRODUCTION
The hypothesis that migrating birds utilize the geomagnetic field for orientation had been proposed as early as 1859 (von Middendorff, 1859). The use of a magnetic compass by migratory birds was first demonstrated for European robins in 1966 (Wiltschko and Merkel, 1966) and, since then, in 17 further species (Wiltschko and Wiltschko, 1996). However, the biophysical mechanism of magnetoreception is still unknown. Among the theoretical models for magnetoreception mechanisms that have been proposed, the use of magnetite particles as magnetoreceptors and photoreceptorbased mechanisms involving direct magnetic effects on the visual transduction process have received the most attention. Suggestions for a magnetite-based magnetoreceptor include freely rotating single-domain magnetite particles (Kirschvink and Gould, 1981), fixed super-paramagnetic magnetite particles (Kirschvink et al., 1985), or magnetitecontaining liquid crystals (Edmonds, 1996). Three different hypotheses for photoreceptor-based mechanisms have been proposed. Leask (1977) suggests a radiofrequency resonance process acting on a hypothetical triplet state of the visual pigment rhodopsin. Hong (1977, 1995) proposed the magneto-orientation effect of rhodopsins, which occurs at field strengths of 1000 times the geomagnetic field strength due to oriented diamagnetic anisotropy, as a possible mechanism. For much weaker field strengths (10–20 times geomagnetic strength) magnetic field effects have been observed to influence radical-pair reactions in polar liquids (Schulten et al., 1976) and under laboratory conditions in photosynthetic bacteria (Werner et al., 1978). These studies
led to the third suggestion that a radical-pair mechanism can act as a chemical sensor for magnetic compass orientation (Schulten et al., 1978; Schulten, 1982; Schulten and Windemuth, 1986).
