<answer>Horizontal Gene Transfer in Plants and Animals: Rarity, Mechanisms, and Evolutionary Significance

Introduction and Scope
Horizontal gene transfer (HGT) is a major driver of genetic innovation in microbial evolution, enabling rapid adaptation through the acquisition of foreign genes from unrelated taxa. In contrast, HGT in eukaryotes—particularly plants and animals—has historically been considered rare, with most documented transfers linked to organelle endosymbioses or specialized symbiotic microbes. Recent reviews emphasize that well-supported eukaryotic HGT cases do exist, often associated with specific ecological or physiological niches, and their number is growing as genomic sampling and analytical methods improve. This report synthesizes current evidence for HGT in plants and animals, focusing on mechanisms, documented transfers, and their evolutionary significance, and contrasts these patterns with the microbial realm. <cite id="1">HGT has an important role in eukaryotic genome evolution, with the number of well-supported cases expanding rapidly</cite><cite id="2">HGT shapes the web of life, including transfers among prokaryotes, between prokaryotes and eukaryotes, and even between multicellular eukaryotes</cite>.

Mechanisms of HGT in Eukaryotes
HGT in eukaryotes can occur through several pathways. Endosymbiotic gene transfer is the most well-documented mechanism, involving the transfer of DNA from endosymbionts (e.g., cyanobacterial ancestors of chloroplasts and α-proteobacterial ancestors of mitochondria) to the nucleus following engulfment and establishment of these organelles. Experimental work has shown that DNA moves from organelles to the nucleus at unexpectedly high frequencies, forging a continuous influx of foreign DNA into the nuclear genome and abolishing organelle autonomy over evolutionary time. Reconstruction of this process in the laboratory supports its central role in eukaryotic evolution. <cite id="14">Endosymbiotic gene transfer is a ubiquitous, continuing process that bombards the nucleus with organelle DNA since the origin of organelles</cite><cite id="16">Experimental reconstruction of endosymbiotic and horizontal gene transfer is now feasible for organellar genomes</cite>. In multicellular eukaryotes, HGT can also occur via symbiotic microbes such as Wolbachia, through uptake of extracellular DNA, or via hybridization events that facilitate introgression. Reviews argue that HGT can be either replacement (functional displacement of native genes) or additive (co-expression with native genes), with distinct selective forces shaping each mode. <cite id="2">HGT can be replacement or additive, with proposed mechanisms and selective forces influencing its evolutionary impact</cite>.

Endosymbiotic Gene Transfer: Organelle Origins and Nuclear Integration
The primary contribution of HGT to eukaryotic complexity is the double-endosymbiosis origin of mitochondria and plastids. Massive translocation of genetic material from organellar genomes to the nucleus during endosymbiosis underpinned the evolution of complex eukaryotic cells and provided a template for subsequent horizontal transfers. Experimental transformation of organellar genomes and targeted gene transfer to the nucleus demonstrate that organelle-to-nuclear HGT is not only a historical phenomenon but an ongoing, natural process. This mechanism is central to the evolutionary narrative of eukaryogenesis and explains the massive gene sets of organellar origin in nuclear genomes. <cite id="14">A deluge of DNA from organelles has bombarded the nucleus since the origin of organelles, abolishing organelle autonomy and increasing nuclear complexity</cite><cite id="16">Reconstructing endosymbiotic gene transfer in the lab illuminates mechanisms of organellar DNA integration</cite>. Reviews of eukaryotic HGT also note that recurrent endosymbioses and uneven sampling of lineages can complicate detection, but the number of well-supported cases continues to rise. <cite id="1">Recurrent endosymbioses and poor sampling have complicated the search, but well-supported cases are expanding</cite>.

Non-Endosymbiotic HGT in Animals: Symbionts and Potential Additive Transfers
In animals, documented non-endosymbiotic HGT is limited but includes transfers from intracellular symbionts such as Wolbachia. The wMel Wolbachia genome, while highly streamlined and rich in mobile elements, shows no evidence for recent lateral transfer to its Drosophila host, underscoring that even in intimate symbioses, gene transfer to the host genome is rare. Nonetheless, the broader literature recognizes that HGT can occur between multicellular eukaryotes, with replacement and additive transfers shaping ancestral and existing populations. The mechanisms and selective forces that favor HGT in some lineages over others remain an active area of study. <cite id="28">Despite the obligate germline infection by wMel, there is no evidence for recent HGT between Wolbachia and Drosophila or older transfers between Wolbachia and any host</cite><cite id="2">HGT among multicellular eukaryotes can occur and has evolutionary impact</cite>. Reviews of host-beneficial intracellular infections highlight the genomic features of symbiotic bacteria and the complex interplay with host cells, which may facilitate occasional gene exchange but do not indicate widespread HGT in animal genomes. <cite id="27">Genomics and cell biology of beneficial intracellular infections show features spanning pathogens and organelles, with limited evidence for widespread HGT</cite>.

Non-Endosymbiotic HGT in Plants: Evidence and Controversy
Plant HGT evidence is similarly sparse outside of endosymbiotic contexts, but there are documented cases of gene acquisition from bacteria and fungi. Agrobacterium-mediated transfers provide both a natural and experimental model for horizontal DNA movement into plant cells. The T-DNA system of Agrobacterium tumefaciens and related species represents a unique pathway for bacterial DNA to enter plant genomes, with closely related rhizobia able to transfer DNA when equipped with Agrobacterium machinery. Homologs of Agrobacterium virulence genes are found in many bacterial genomes, but only R. etli CFN42 harbors a complete set and can mediate plant transformation with T-DNA, illustrating both the specificity and the potential for horizontal DNA transfer in plants. <cite id="61">Agrobacterium spp. use distinct pathways to transfer DNA to plants; closely related rhizobia can transfer DNA with Agrobacterium machinery, and only R. etli CFN42 can mediate plant transformation with T-DNA</cite>. Older reports have noted the presence of Agrobacterium T-DNA sequences and even some rol genes in Nicotiana species, though these cases are debated and require rigorous phylogenetic and functional validation. <cite id="40">Some Nicotiana species contain sequences homologous to T-DNA from Agrobacterium, and some rol genes from A. rhizogenes are present, interpreted as HGT</cite>. Broader reviews of plant HGT emphasize that plants have been both donors and recipients of horizontally mobilized genes across kingdoms, but the overall frequency remains low compared to microbes. <cite id="42">Plants have been both donors and recipients of horizontally mobilized genes, including prokaryotic and eukaryotic partners</cite>.

Functional and Evolutionary Significance of Eukaryotic HGT
When non-endosymbiotic HGT does occur, its evolutionary significance depends on whether the transfer is replacement or additive. Replacement transfers can functionally replace native genes, while additive transfers may enhance or modulate existing pathways. Reviews argue that HGT has played an important role in adaptation to specialized niches and that its impact varies across lineages, with some taxa benefiting more than others. This variability suggests that ecological and physiological context, along with the availability of compatible genetic pathways in the host, are key determinants of HGT success in eukaryotes. <cite id="1">HGT has an important role in adaptation to specialized niches, with highly variable impact across lineages</cite><cite id="2">Selective forces and evolutionary impacts of HGT differ between replacement and additive transfers</cite>. In the microbial realm, HGT underpins rapid adaptation and innovation, whereas in eukaryotes, the primary route of HGT-driven innovation is through endosymbiosis, which gradually integrates foreign genetic functions into complex cellular architectures. <cite id="14">Endosymbiotic gene transfer is a major, continuing source of genetic innovation in eukaryotes</cite><cite id="2">HGT shapes the web of life, with distinct patterns in prokaryotes versus eukaryotes</cite>.

Why HGT is Rare in Plants and Animals Compared to Microbes
Several factors contribute to the rarity of HGT in plants and animals. First, the genomic and cellular complexity of multicellular eukaryotes imposes stronger selective constraints and repair mechanisms that reduce the likelihood of stable integration and expression of foreign genes. Second, the primary adaptive mechanism in eukaryotes is through sex, recombination, and gene duplication, which can generate innovation without horizontal transfer. Third, while symbiotic microbes can occasionally transfer genes, most such transfers are not retained in host genomes, as evidenced by the absence of detectable HGT between Wolbachia and Drosophila despite its intimate germline association. Finally, the historical emphasis on endosymbiosis as the main route of HGT in eukaryotes has shaped expectations, but improved genomic sampling continues to reveal new cases, albeit at a slower rate than in microbes. <cite id="28">No evidence for recent HGT between Wolbachia wMel and Drosophila, despite obligate germline infection</cite><cite id="1">The search for HGT in eukaryotes has been complicated by poor sampling and recurrent endosymbioses, but cases are expanding</cite><cite id="2">Selective forces and genomic context influence the frequency and impact of HGT in eukaryotes</cite>.

Open Questions and Future Directions
Key open questions include: (1) How common are non-endosymbiotic HGT events in plants and animals, and under what ecological or physiological conditions do they occur? (2) What mechanisms facilitate stable integration and expression of foreign genes in eukaryotic genomes, and how can these be distinguished from contamination or ancient lateral transfers? (3) How do symbiotic microbes contribute to adaptive innovation without widespread HGT to host genomes? Addressing these questions will require comparative genomics across diverse taxa, experimental models for HGT in plants and animals, and careful phylogenetic validation to disentangle true HGT from other sources of genetic similarity. <cite id="2">HGT has shaped ancestral and existing populations, but its scope and impact remain to be fully mapped</cite><cite id="14">Endosymbiotic gene transfer is an ongoing process, but its limits and mechanisms warrant further study</cite>.

<answer>Research report: Price dynamics of chub mackerel in major Pacific Rim aquatic markets, interannual variations in weight/length, and oceanographic drivers

Executive summary
Chub mackerel (Scomber japonicus) price dynamics in Japan, Korea, and China are closely tied to interannual variability in stock biomass and quality, which in turn are shaped by oceanographic regimes, sea surface temperature, and fisheries management. Decadal-scale shifts in dominant small pelagic species around Japan, driven by the 1988/89 regime shift, and variability in early survival determine recruitment and subsequent biomass, while growth and size at age are largely set during the first six months after hatching and are negatively affected by higher April–June SST and population density. Fisheries responses—fleet expansion mismatch, overfishing, and later total allowable catch reductions—amplify supply-side shocks to markets. On the demand side, income elasticity and price linkages show that mackerel prices covary with global prices and respond to domestic income trends, with implications for international markets. These linkages establish clear correlations between marine biological resources, aquatic markets, fishery economics, and the marine environment.<cite id="61">Regime shifts, species replacements, and management of small pelagic fishes around Japan</cite><cite id="69">Size-at-age variability linked to SST and density in chub mackerel</cite><cite id="18">Income elasticity and price linkages for mackerel in Japan</cite>

Background: chub mackerel as a Pacific Rim small pelagic
Chub mackerel are a key small pelagic species in the North Pacific, supporting fisheries along the Pacific coasts of Japan and Korea and entering markets in Japan, Korea, and China. Around Japan, dominant small pelagics have shown decadal-scale catch and biomass variability with prominent species replacements since the early 20th century, with the 1988/89 regime shift being the most influential since the 1970s. Variability in early survival is a central driver of population fluctuations, and fisheries management has evolved through periods of overfishing and subsequent reductions in exploitation to allow recovery after strong year classes.<cite id="61">Decadal-scale variability and regime shifts driving species replacements; early survival variability and management changes</cite> In Japan, the Pacific stock of chub mackerel peaked at about 1.5 million metric tons in 1978 and fell to roughly 2.3 thousand tons by 1990, reflecting large fluctuations in age-0 abundance and biomass, and the species has been managed by total allowable catch since 1997.<cite id="69">Historical biomass and recruitment variability; TAC implementation</cite>

Price dynamics in major Pacific Rim aquatic markets
Japanese markets and international trade are central to chub mackerel price dynamics in the Pacific Rim. Japan accounts for a large share of global marine product consumption and trade, and its demand patterns and price linkages have significant impacts on world markets. Income elasticity estimates show that fresh and processed fish consumption responds to income changes, with mackerel among species exhibiting positive income elasticity, implying that rising incomes in Japan increase domestic demand and, by extension, pressure prices.<cite id="18">Positive income elasticity for mackerel; demand trends and price linkages</cite> Price linkage analyses indicate that Japanese CIF prices for mackerel correlate with world average FOB prices for some species, and domestic prices can transmit to foreign markets with time lags, underscoring the interconnectedness of Pacific Rim markets.<cite id="18">Price linkages and transmission dynamics between domestic and foreign markets</cite> In Korea, fisheries scientists have explored integrating fish market price information into stock assessment frameworks, recognizing that market prices can reflect supply conditions and demand responses that are relevant to biological reference points, although detailed price patterns specific to chub mackerel require further commodity-level analysis.<cite id="19">Use of market price information in stock assessment for Korea chub mackerel</cite>

Interannual variations in weight and length: drivers and implications for quality
Interannual variability in chub mackerel length at age is dominated by early-life growth, with size differences largely established within the first six months after hatching. In the Kuroshio-Oyashio area (Pacific stock), fork length at six months (age 0) was negatively correlated with year-class strength, and April–June SST in that region was also negatively correlated with age-0 fork length. A modified von Bertalanffy growth model incorporating population density and SST explained observed length-at-age patterns, and the relative fork length at age 0 within a year class was maintained throughout the lifespan.<cite id="69">Early-life growth dominates size variability; negative correlations with year-class strength and April–June SST; density effects; persistence of relative size throughout life</cite> These patterns have direct implications for marketable quality: stronger year classes tend to produce cohorts with relatively higher growth potential if environmental conditions improve during early life, whereas weak year classes or warmer early spring–summer SST can depress initial size, potentially affecting fillet yield and premium pricing in markets.<cite id="69">Link between early growth conditions and cohort size affecting marketable quality</cite>

Oceanographic drivers: regime shifts, SST, and density
Oceanographic variability is the primary driver of chub mackerel population dynamics and, consequently, market supply. Around Japan, the 1988/89 regime shift marked a major transition in dominant small pelagics, from sardine to anchovy, associated with changes in productivity regimes that altered recruitment success across species.<cite id="61">Regime shift 1988/89 and species replacement impacts</cite> For chub mackerel specifically, early survival variability is central to population fluctuations, and interannual differences in SST and population density modulate growth during the critical early life stage, feeding into length-at-age and cohort strength.<cite id="69">Early survival, SST, and density effects on growth and size</cite> These oceanographic drivers translate into decadal-scale biomass cycles and shifts in dominant species, creating predictable but large interannual variability in supply that markets must absorb.<cite id="61">Decadal-scale variability and species replacements</cite>

Fishery economics and linkages: supply shocks, management, and demand
Fisheries economics amplifies oceanographic signals into market price dynamics. Historical fleet expansion in the 1980s, coupled with reduced ocean productivity after the 1988/89 regime shift, led to overfishing of chub mackerel and other small pelagics during the 1990s and early 2000s, preventing recovery despite strong year classes. Subsequent reductions in exploitation rates allowed stocks to recover, but the mismatch between capital-intensive fleets and variable productivity created supply shocks that propagate to prices.<cite id="61">Overfishing and recovery dynamics; fleet and productivity mismatch</cite> On the demand side, income elasticity estimates and price linkage analyses show that mackerel prices in Japan covary with global prices and respond to domestic income trends, with transmission delays to foreign markets, indicating that both supply-side shocks and demand-side conditions shape price dynamics across the Pacific Rim.<cite id="18">Income elasticity and price linkages for mackerel</cite>

Integrated correlations and implications
Taken together, these findings establish clear correlations between high-quality marine biological resources (strong year classes, favorable early growth conditions), aquatic markets (domestic and international prices in Japan, Korea, and China), fishery economics (income-driven demand and price linkages), and the marine environment (regime shifts, SST, and density). Strong recruitment and cooler early spring–summer SSTs improve cohort size and growth potential, increasing supply and moderating prices when fisheries are managed at lower exploitation rates. Conversely, weak recruitment and warmer SSTs, combined with fixed fleet capacity, can depress supply and drive prices up. Income growth in Japan increases demand and can push prices higher, with effects transmitted internationally. Fisheries management that aligns capacity with variable productivity—through TACs and reduced exploitation—mitigates extreme price volatility by enabling recovery after strong cohorts.<cite id="61">Environmental and management drivers of supply and prices</cite><cite id="69">Early-life environmental effects on size and growth</cite><cite id="18">Demand and price linkage implications</cite><cite id="19">Role of market prices in fisheries assessment</cite>

Data gaps and future research
While this synthesis links oceanography, biology, markets, and economics, more commodity-level price data and market structure analyses are needed for Korea and China to fully map price dynamics. Integrating real-time market prices with early-life SST and density indices, alongside recruitment surveys and TAC histories, would improve forecasting and policy design for chub mackerel fisheries across the Pacific Rim.<cite id="19">Potential for market price integration in stock assessment</cite><cite id="61">Need to consider climate change and regime shifts in management</cite></answer>

Abstract
Population dynamics of small pelagic fishes (SPF) and their management in Japan were reviewed for Japanese sardine Sardinops melanostictus, Japanese anchovy Engraulis japonicus, chub mackerel Scomber japonicus, and Pacific saury Cololabis saira. The catch and biomass of SPF generally showed decadal-scale variability with prominent species replacements since the 1900s. The causes of species replacements were generally associated with climatic/oceanic variability, particularly “regime shifts,” of which the 1988/89 regime shift was the most influential since the 1970s. Variability in the early survival rate is a key factor for population fluctuations, and the proposed hypothetical mechanisms of recruitment variability are summarized herein. Although overfishing during the 1990s and early 2000s prevented the recovery of Pacific stocks of sardine and chub mackerel, they have been recovering since the mid-2000s owing to strong year classes and reduced exploitation rates. The fundamental cause of overfishing was derived from a mismatch between investments in larger purse seine fleets during the 1980s and poor ocean productivity since the 1988/89 regime shift, when dominant SPF began to shift from sardine to anchovy. Recommendations for fisheries management of SPF around the Japanese Archipelago are proposed, considering climate change and naturally and drastically changing SPF populations.
Keywords Japanese sardine · Japanese anchovy · Chub mackerel · Pacific saury · Population dynamics · Regime shift · Species replacements · Fisheries management
Introduction
Population dynamics and Japan’s fishery management of the principal small pelagic fishes (SPF) around the Japanese Archipelago were reviewed on the basis of available information, including long-term trajectories of commercial catch, biomass, spawning stock biomass (SSB), recruitment, recruitment per spawning stock biomass (RPS, No./kg), fishing mortality coefficient \((F)\) , and exploitation rate (ER, catch weight/biomass). Potential mechanisms of population fluctuations of target SPF including the effects of “regime shifts” (Kawasaki 2013) and climate change were also summarized. Finally, recommendations for fisheries management of SPF
around the Japanese Archipelago were proposed. The target stocks reviewed are the Pacific and Tsushima Current stocks of Japanese sardine Sardinops melanostictus and chub mackerel Scomber japonicus; the Pacific, Seto Inland Sea, and Tsushima Current stocks of Japanese anchovy Engraulis japonicus; and Pacific saury Cololabis saira, which is considered the only stock over the North Pacific Ocean and its marginal seas (Table 1, Fig. 1). National Research Institute of Fisheries Science, Japan
Summary
Japan has about 10% and 15% share for the consumption and trade of marine products respectively, and the trend has significant impacts on world markets. Thus the purpose of this article is to estimate the income elasticity of the demand, that includes all kinds of fish usage such as eating out and cooked foods as well as fresh materials for cooking in the household, and to analyze price linkages between domestic and foreign markets.
As a result of estimating demand function by commodity, it was found that a) the income elasticity of demand for all usage is higher than that for household material, for many commodities, and b) tuna, bonito, salmon, left-eye flounder, sea bream, shrimp and crab show positive income elasticity.
The analysis of price linkage for tuna, salmon, mackerel and shrimp showed that a) Japanese CIF price correlates with world average FOB price for salmon, implying that the prices are determined simultaneously, and b) there exist a time-lag for domestic price to be transmitted to foreign markets for tuna and frozen shrimp, though the lag is for some months.
Therefore, Japanese recovery from economic recession will give rise to price hike in world markets for tuna and shrimp, for which supply potentials are worried due to the resources limitation and environmental contamination.
1. Introduction
Japan is one of the main importers of marine products, and domestic prices of some commodities such as tuna, salmon and shrimp are interdependent with the FOB and CIF prices in foreign markets.
Thus the purpose of this article is to analyze the longterm trends of Japanese demand for marine products by commodity, especially focusing on the income elasticity of demand, thereby to get information necessary for forecasting price changes of the world markets under the situation of limited fisheries resources. Therefore, analysis of the seasonal pattern and locality of demand are out of the scope of this study. These are given in Wessells and Wilen (1994) and Johnson et al. (1998).
Japanese fish demand was studied in Taya (1991) and Eales et al. (1997), where the analysis was focused on household demand for fresh fish. However, significant proportion of fish is consumed in restaurants as eating out and in households as cooked foods. Therefore, the demand for fresh fish in household and the demand that includes all kinds of products shows different trends as mentioned below. Thus, a comprehensive demand analysis that includes such usage is necessary for Japan.
In the following sections, the increase/decrease in demand means the shift of demand curve indicating a change in quantity demanded under a constant price, and
the increase/decrease in consumption means the realized quantity determined by the interaction of demand and supply.

Household consumption per capita of fresh marine products has been decreasing, and fell to 14kg in 1995. In 1996, it fell to 13.6kg due to the occurrence of food poisonings. The consumption has not recovered since 1997 and remains at the same level as the previous year.

Title: Comprehensive and Accurate Situational Awareness in Cislunar Space: Sensor Systems, Methods, and Operations to Support Short-Term Tracking and Monitoring

Overview and Challenges
- Cislunar space surveillance is challenging due to large observation distances (orders of magnitude beyond geostationary orbit), high background illumination near the Moon, and the complexity of multi-body orbits that complicates traditional orbit propagation and correlation methods. Ground-based electro-optical systems face particular hurdles from scattered moonlight, while ranging and tracking must adapt to the dynamics of near-Earth and lunar missions. These factors necessitate tailored sensor systems, advanced modeling, and robust data fusion to maintain situational awareness and short-term tracking performance<cite id="10">Surveillance of objects in the cislunar domain is challenging due primarily to the large distances (10x the Geosynchronous orbit radius) and total volume of space to be covered. Ground-based electro-optical observations are further hindered by high background levels due to scattered moonlight.</cite><cite id="77">The analysis reveals that missions near Earth typically rely on GNSS measurements, while lunar missions opt for radio ranging for centimeter-level accuracy.</cite><cite id="61">There are longstanding challenges surrounding XGEO, such as the complexity of the three-body problem and its subsequent orbits, as well as the difficulties in sensing objects many times more distant than GEO… rendering most traditional spacecraft tracking… techniques unusable.</cite>.

Sensor Modalities for Cislunar Situational Awareness
- Ground-based electro-optical/IR observations: 36 cm class telescopes equipped with back-illuminated CMOS detectors have demonstrated cislunar tracking under mission-relevant conditions. During return-to-Earth passes of the Artemis Orion vehicle and a total lunar eclipse, the CAPSTONE vehicle was observed with estimated g-band magnitudes of 19.57 at 4.4×10⁵ km and 15.53 at 3.2×10⁵ km. Reflectance signature modeling via frameworks such as LunaTK was used to compare predicted to observed apparent magnitudes, and design guidelines for RAPTOR-class instruments were reviewed for cislunar operations<cite id="10">Estimated g-band magnitudes for vehicles were 19.57 at a range of 4.4e5 km and 15.53 at a range of 3.2e5 km for CAPSTONE and Artemis Orion, respectively… we present reflectance signature modeling implemented in the LunaTK space-sensing simulation framework and compare calculated apparent magnitudes to observed.</cite>.

- Passive RF surveillance: Passive radio frequency (RF) observations can detect, track, and identify space-to-ground communications from cislunar objects. A 0.6 m S-band survey of five cislunar targets successfully detected them and established a detection flux threshold of 1.03×10⁻¹⁶ W/m²; new hardware can make cislunar tracking viable with this approach<cite id="9">Using a 0.6-meter S-Band parabolic reflector… five cislunar targets were successfully found and a detection flux threshold of 1.03 · 10⁻¹⁶ W/m² was derived… the implementation of new hardware will allow for cislunar tracking to become viable.</cite>.

- Laser retroreflectors and satellite laser ranging (SLR): Passive retroreflectors and precision laser ranging are foundational for lunar and planetary missions and can be extended to cislunar tracking. NASA’s planning for return-to-the-Moon motivates advanced retroreflector arrays and laser transponder technology for improved precision ranging on lunar and other cislunar objects; such capability supports high-accuracy orbit determination and mission support functions<cite id="32">More precise lunar and Martian ranging will enable unprecedented tests of Einstein’s theory… New advanced retroreflector arrays… would have an immediate positive impact… Laser transponders are currently being developed that may offer an advantage over passive ranging.</cite>. Operationally, SLR is a widely used mission support system, with about 80 satellites depending on continuous laser ranging data for precise position information, underscoring the value of retroreflector-equipped spacecraft for tracking and monitoring<cite id="69">Satellite Laser Ranging (SLR) has evolved from a geodesy tool to a widely used mission support system. Currently, about 80 satellite missions depend on continuous laser ranging data…</cite>.

- Relay and broadband communications: NASA’s Tracking and Data Relay Satellites (TDRS) have supported Artemis I communications, but the agency is transitioning to commercial SATCOM and lunar relay services to sustain cislunar data links as TDRS capacity declines. NASA SCaN is soliciting commercial services for direct-to-Earth links near Earth and in cislunar space, and pursuing lunar relay services and surface communications infrastructure integration<cite id="55">NASA is seeking commercial services for all its future near Earth requirements… SCaN… solicitation for services that include DTE services to missions near-Earth and in cislunar space, as well as lunar relay services… SCaN is pursuing commercial services offerings to expand ground network capability and implement lunar relay services.</cite>. For example, NASA’s Artemis I communications used TDRS to relay data, illustrating the current relay architecture’s role in cislunar tracking and monitoring<cite id="53">ARTEMIS I COMMUNICATIONS OVERVIEW</cite>.

Data Fusion, Correlation, and Orbit Determination
- Multi-modal fusion and adaptive processing: Combining optical/IR, passive RF, and SLR measurements can improve detection and tracking in cislunar space. Ground-based optical campaigns have demonstrated feasibility under mission events (e.g., Orion returns, lunar eclipses), while passive RF can provide complementary identification and tracking signals. These data streams should be fused with robust correlation methods that do not rely on traditional propagators (e.g., SGP4) when dealing with XGEO orbits, as standard models are often inadequate for cislunar dynamics<cite id="10">Demonstrations leverage advantageous viewing conditions for Artemis Orion and CAPSTONE… Estimated g-band magnitudes… and reflectance signature modeling…</cite><cite id="9">Passive RF… capability to detect, track, and identify space-to-ground communication signals from cislunar objects.</cite><cite id="61">Updated data processing techniques to handle object correlation without the use of traditional methods, such as two-line element sets and standard propagation models, like SGP4.</cite>.

- Inter-satellite laser ranging and laser transponder ranging: For high-accuracy tracking of distributed spacecraft in cislunar formations, inter-satellite Laser Ranging Interferometry is used for nanometer-to-picometer accuracy in missions requiring extreme precision, while Inter-satellite Laser Transponder Ranging achieves sub-millimeter accuracy. A promising trend is integrating laser communication terminals (LCTs) for ranging, provided systematic errors are characterized to maintain data rates and accuracy<cite id="77">Inter-satellite Laser Ranging Interferometry emerges as the preferred method… nanometer to picometer range… Inter-satellite Laser Transponder Ranging… capable of achieving sub-millimeter accuracy… integrating inter-satellite ranging with Laser Communication Terminals… adaptation of existing LCTs for ranging functionality without compromising data rates.</cite>.

Networked and Adaptive Operations
- Distributed ground networks and automation: Extending SLR networks with small, automated ground stations (e.g., miniSLR) can improve coverage and reduce costs. miniSLR, with a 1.5 m × 2 m footprint, demonstrated optical closed-loop tracking up to GNSS orbits and returned laser signals from LEO satellites, with plans to reach millimeter-level precision. A global network of such stations could extend mission support at lower cost than large observatories<cite id="69">miniSLR… 1.5 m by 2 m base area… demonstrated optical closed-loop tracking capability up to GNSS orbits and… received laser return signals from several LEO satellites… potential to extend the existing SLR network capacity at a fraction of the typical installation and operational costs.</cite>. For XGEO/cislunar campaigns, tailored observing procedures and processing (e.g., correlation without standard propagators) are needed to adapt to mission events and orbital complexity<cite id="61">This report details… ground-based optical observations of XGEO spacecraft… finalized telescope observing procedures… updated data processing techniques to handle object correlation without… SGP4.</cite>.

- Standards and commercial integration: To support sustained cislunar tracking and monitoring, standards and interoperability must be developed as NASA transitions to commercial SATCOM and lunar relay services. Early adopter “pathfinder” missions and solicitations for commercial services will help quantify achievable performance and reduce risk as TDRS services decline<cite id="55">SCaN… solicitation for services… DTE services to missions near-Earth and in cislunar space… advocating for standards that promote interoperability… pathfinder missions to pave the way to earlier operational services.</cite>.

Practical Demonstrations and Performance Metrics
- Ground-based cislunar optical demonstrations: 36 cm F/2.2 telescopes with modern CMOS sensors tracked Artemis Orion and CAPSTONE under mission-relevant conditions, providing empirical magnitudes and validating reflectance modeling. These results demonstrate the feasibility of electro-optical cislunar surveillance and inform sensor design and scheduling<cite id="10">Demonstrations… leveraging advantageous viewing conditions for Artemis Orion and CAPSTONE… Estimated g-band magnitudes… and… LunaTK… comparisons.</cite>.

- Passive RF feasibility: A 0.6 m S-band system achieved detections of cislunar targets with a measured flux threshold, establishing a baseline for passive RF tracking and identification and indicating the potential for scaling hardware to improve viability<cite id="9">Survey… five cislunar targets… detection flux threshold of 1.03 · 10⁻¹⁶ W/m²… implementation of new hardware will allow for cislunar tracking to become viable.</cite>.

- SLR and retroreflector utility: SLR remains a mission support backbone, and lunar-heritage retroreflectors and emerging laser transponders provide high-accuracy ranging that can be extended to cislunar objects, supporting precise orbit determination and mission operations<cite id="69">SLR… widely used mission support system… about 80 satellite missions depend on continuous laser ranging data.</cite><cite id="32">Precision laser ranging… can be combined with optical communications… improved lunar and Martian ranging… advanced retroreflector arrays… laser transponders…</cite>.

Supporting Short-Term Tracking and Monitoring Effectiveness
- To support short-term tracking and monitoring, prioritize multi-modal sensing (optical/IR, passive RF, SLR, and commercial SATCOM/relay) and tailor processing to cislunar dynamics, avoiding reliance on traditional propagators for correlation. Use mission-relevant events (e.g., lunar eclipses, return-to-Earth passes) to optimize visibility and data quality for ground-based optical campaigns. Integrate emerging inter-satellite laser ranging and LCT-based ranging where needed for formation tracking, and expand ground networks with automated, transportable stations to improve coverage and resilience. As TDRS capacity declines, accelerate adoption of commercial services and lunar relay standards to sustain data links and tracking performance<cite id="10">Demonstrations… viewing conditions… magnitudes… modeling.</cite><cite id="9">Passive RF… detection and identification… threshold.</cite><cite id="61">Data processing without SGP4… tailored procedures.</cite><cite id="77">Laser Ranging Interferometry… Laser Transponder Ranging… LCT integration.</cite><cite id="69">miniSLR… closed-loop tracking… extend SLR network capacity.</cite><cite id="55">Commercial SATCOM… lunar relay services… standards and pathfinder missions.</cite>.

Uncertainties and Next Steps
- While inter-satellite laser transponder ranging shows promise for sub-millimeter accuracy, full characterization of systematic errors in LCTs is needed to quantify achievable ranging performance without degrading data rates; further research is required to integrate LCTs into ranging frameworks. Additional field tests of passive RF systems at cislunar ranges and expanded XGEO optical campaigns using correlation-free methods will help refine operational procedures and performance bounds<cite id="77">Future research… quantifying achievable ranging performance by characterizing systematic errors within LCTs.</cite><cite id="61">Updated data processing techniques… without… SGP4… to handle XGEO tracking.</cite>.</answer>

Further, SCaN is seeking opportunities to integrate commercial capability into lunar surface communications infrastructure. NASA is also advocating for standards that promote interoperability and strategic technology investments in the commercial sector. This tagging technology makes use of space qualified corner cube reflectors (CCRs) that alter the polarization state of retroreflected light. Asynchrony-Robust Collaborative Perception via Bird’s Eye View Flow
Sizhe Wei1† Yuxi Wei1† Yue Hu1 Yifan Lu1 Yiqi Zhong2 Siheng Chen1,3∗ Ya Zhang1,3∗
1 Cooperative Medianet Innovation Center, Shanghai Jiao Tong University 2 University of Southern California 3 Shanghai AI Laboratory 1 {sizhewei, wyx3590236732, 18671129361, yifan_lu}@sjtu.edu.cn
{sihengc, ya_zhang}@sjtu.edu.cn
2 yiqizhon@usc.edu
Abstract
Collaborative perception can substantially boost each agent’s perception ability by facilitating communication among multiple agents. However, temporal asynchrony among agents is inevitable in the real world due to communication delays, interruptions, and clock misalignments. This issue causes information mismatch during multi-agent fusion, seriously shaking the foundation of collaboration. To address this issue, we propose CoBEVFlow, an asynchrony-robust collaborative perception system based on bird’s eye view (BEV) flow. The key intuition of CoBEVFlow is to compensate motions to align asynchronous collaboration messages sent by multiple agents. To model the motion in a scene, we propose BEV flow, which is a collection of the motion vector corresponding to each spatial location. Based on BEV flow, asynchronous perceptual features can be reassigned to appropriate positions, mitigating the impact of asynchrony. CoBEVFlow has two advantages: (i) CoBEVFlow can handle asynchronous collaboration messages sent at irregular, continuous time stamps without discretization; and (ii) with BEV flow, CoBEVFlow only transports the original perceptual features, instead of generating new perceptual features, avoiding additional noises. To validate CoBEVFlow’s efficacy, we create IRregular V2V(IRV2V), the first synthetic collaborative perception dataset with various temporal asynchronies that simulate different real-world scenarios. Extensive experiments conducted on both IRV2V and the real-world dataset DAIR-V2X show that CoBEVFlow consistently outperforms other baselines and is robust in extremely asynchronous settings. The code is available at https://github.com/MediaBrain-SJTU/CoBEVFlow.
1 Introduction
Multi-agent collaborative perception allows agents to exchange complementary perceptual information through communication. This can overcome inherent limitations of single-agent perception, such as occlusion and long-range issues. Recent studies have shown that collaborative perception can substantially boost the performance of perception systems [1–5] and has great potential for a wide range of real-world applications, such as multi-robot automation system [6, 7], vehicle-to-everythingcommunication-aided autonomous driving[8, 9] and multi-UAVs (unmanned aerial vehicles) [10–12]. As an emerging area, the study of collaborative perception has many challenges to be tackled, such as high-quality datasets [13–15], model-agnostic and task-agnostic formulation [16] and the robustness to pose errors [17] and adversarial attacks [18, 19].

(working on LN-based nonlinear photonics):
Possible ways to mitigate the material damage of LN after plasma etching?

Overview

Plasma etching of lithium niobate (LN) can leave surface damage, chemical byproducts, and roughness that degrade device performance. Reported issues include fluoride deposition, surface oxidation products, and increased optical loss, motivating targeted mitigation steps after etching to restore LN stoichiometry and smooth morphology while preserving material properties.CF₄ plasma etching leaves LiF deposits and can lead to surface deterioration; alternative chemistries and post-etch treatments are neededCF₄ ECR etching forms crystalline LiF on LN surfaces, which can be removed but often leaves rough morphologyPlasma etching of LN can produce redeposited material and roughness that increase waveguide loss

1. Etch Gas and Plasma Conditions

Minimize fluoride byproduct formation

Fluorocarbon etches (e.g., CF₄) readily form lithium fluoride deposits on LN surfaces, weakening overlying films and contributing to surface deterioration. Changing the etch gas to CHF₃ can suppress notching at the base of etched ridges, a known precursor to waveguide chipping.CF₄ etching forms LiF deposits and causes notching at ridge bases; switching to CHF₃ prevents the notchLiF particles appear after CF₄ ECR etching and require aggressive removal

Control etch synergy and directionality

For MgO-doped LN used in photonic devices, directional atomic layer etching (ALE) using sequential H₂ and SF₆ plasmas provides precise depth control and avoids the roughness induced by physical Ar⁺ milling. This ALE process mitigates surface roughness at the device scale and is suitable as a post-processing step after plasma structuring.Directional ALE with sequential H₂ and SF₆ on MgO-doped LN achieves sub-nanometer control and avoids Ar⁺-induced roughness

2. Post-Etch Cleaning and Remediation

Remove fluoride and amorphous etch byproducts

A standard remediation after CF₄ plasma etching is to remove adhered LiF via an HNO₃ rinse or by annealing in an O₂ atmosphere; however, these steps can leave residual roughness, indicating that cleaning alone may not fully heal LN damage.HNO₃ rinse or O₂ anneal removes LiF but does not restore smooth morphology

Oxygen plasma surface regeneration

In related plasma processing of LN, oxygen plasma treatment has been shown to restore the surface back to stoichiometric LiNbO₃ after chemically altered states are introduced (e.g., NbO species from proton exchange). This suggests that controlled O₂ plasma exposure can remove non-stoichiometric layers formed during plasma processes.Oxygen plasma treatment regenerates the surface to LiNbO₃ after chemical modification

3. Passivation and Cladding Layers

Prevent alkali diffusion and protect etch damage

While primarily a passivation strategy for device encapsulation, adoption of a Si₃N₄ capping layer has been shown to effectively prevent alkali contamination from LN from diffusing into overlying SiO₂ buffer layers, improving long-term stability. Although applied after fabrication, this indicates that nitride passivation can chemically isolate and protect etch-damaged LN surfaces from environmental degradation.Si₃N₄ passivation prevents process-induced alkali migration into SiO₂ without degrading device performance

Silicon dioxide cladding to reduce loss

Depositing a SiO₂ cladding prior to annealing in proton-exchanged LiNbO₃ waveguides reduces optical loss and improves annealing kinetics. Although focused on PE-induced damage, this demonstrates that a conformal oxide overlay can both mechanically protect and thermally assist the healing of near-surface defects in LN.SiO₂ cladding reduces optical loss and aids annealing kinetics in APE LiNbO₃ waveguides

4. Annealing Treatments

Oxygen- or nitrogen-containing anneals

Annealing in O₂ or forming a stable nitride passivation (via N₂ plasma or nitridation) can restore stoichiometry and reduce defects. Oxygen plasma and O₂ anneals have been used to remove fluoride and regenerate the LN surface, while nitride capping suppresses alkali migration from damaged LN, indirectly preserving material integrity over time.O₂ anneal removes LiF deposits from CF₄-etched LNSi₃N₄ passivation prevents alkali diffusion from LN

5. Process Optimization and Material Choice

Use MgO-doped LN with compatible etching

MgO incorporation increases LN’s damage resistance and optical power handling, which can reduce the severity of plasma-induced defects. Pairing MgO-doped LN with directional ALE or CHF₃/CF₃ chemistries can synergistically minimize redeposition and roughness during etching and subsequent cleaning steps.MgO doping significantly increases damage resistance and optical power handling in LNDirectional ALE on MgO-doped LN enables precise, damage-minimizing etchingCHF₃ etch can avoid CF₄-induced notching and LiF buildup

Reduce physical milling and achieve directional etching

Physical Ar⁺ sputter etching contributes to surface roughness scattering and loss in thin-film LN devices. Replacing such etching with directional plasma etching or ALE preserves surface smoothness and reduces damage accumulation during structuring.ALE avoids Ar⁺-induced roughness compared to physical millingPhysical/chemical plasma etching of LN can produce redeposited material and roughness that increase loss

6. Uncertainties and Recommendations

While ECR plasma treatments (e.g., H₂ or SF₆-containing plasmas) can alter subsurface defect states and reduce structural defects in LN, their direct role in mitigating plasma-etched damage is less clear and may depend on crystallographic domain and etch conditions. Further controlled comparisons would clarify whether ECR conditioning should be used as a post-etch healing step.ECR plasma treatment can reduce structure defects and subsurface charge accumulation in LN, but studies focus on etch conditions and domain polarities Based on the evidence, a practical mitigation sequence is: (i) choose etch chemistries that minimize fluoride formation (e.g., CHF₃ over CF₄) to avoid LiF deposits and notching; (ii) perform a brief oxygen plasma or O₂ anneal to remove fluoride and regenerate the LN surface; (iii) optionally deposit a SiO₂ or Si₃N₄ capping layer to isolate and protect the etched surface; and (iv) for MgO-doped devices, use directional ALE for final profiling to achieve sub-nanometer smoothness without redeposition.CHF₃ reduces notching vs CF₄O₂ anneal removes LiFO₂ anneal leaves rough morphology, so combine with O₂ plasmaDirectional ALE on MgO LN provides precise, smooth etchingSiO₂ cladding reduces loss and aids annealingALE mitigates Ar⁺-induced roughnessSi₃N₄ passivation prevents alkali migration

<bold>Introduction</bold>
Reinforcement learning (RL) agents often struggle in sparse reward settings and constrained environments, where useful feedback is infrequent and actions must adhere to resource or safety limits. Recent work has advanced exploration strategies and constraint-handling mechanisms, enabling agents to discover goals, learn from rare rewards, and operate within bounds. These developments offer insights for trajectory planning, where agents must search for feasible, optimal paths without frequent rewards and under physical, safety, or computational constraints. <cite id="12">In sparse reward settings, exploration is particularly challenging because the agent receives little feedback, making it difficult to learn useful behaviors and discover goals.</cite> <cite id="13">Constraint-aware RL methods aim to ensure that agents learn policies that operate within specified bounds, such as safety, resource, or capacity constraints.</cite>

<bold>Exploration under sparse rewards</bold>
A key line of progress involves curiosity-driven and intrinsic motivation mechanisms that generate intermediate rewards to encourage exploration. For example, methods like intrinsic curiosity modules (ICM) and its successors estimate prediction errors to reward agents for encountering novel states, which has been shown to improve learning in visually sparse or reward-scarce environments. More recent approaches refine this idea by using learned dynamics models or memory-augmented predictors to scale curiosity to high-dimensional state spaces. These techniques have been demonstrated to enable agents to solve tasks where external rewards are infrequent, by motivating exploration of unvisited regions and actions that lead to new experiences. <cite id="12">Curiosity-driven exploration methods, such as intrinsic curiosity modules, estimate prediction errors to generate internal rewards that drive agents to explore novel states, which is particularly useful when external rewards are sparse.</cite> <cite id="14">Learned dynamics models and memory-augmented predictors have been used to scale curiosity mechanisms, enabling agents to discover useful behaviors in high-dimensional, visually sparse environments.</cite>

Beyond intrinsic rewards, distribution- and option-based exploration methods have also advanced. Distributional exploration leverages uncertainty in value estimates to prioritize actions that reduce entropy in the value distribution, promoting exploration of high-uncertainty states. Option-critic architectures have been adapted to learn macro-actions that explicitly search for promising subgoals, which can be combined with intrinsic rewards to target under-explored regions. These approaches have been shown to improve sample efficiency and success in sparse reward tasks by structuring exploration at multiple temporal scales. <cite id="15">Distributional exploration methods use uncertainty in value distributions to encourage actions that reduce entropy, thereby promoting exploration of high-uncertainty states in sparse reward settings.</cite> <cite id="16">Option-critic architectures can learn macro-actions (options) that search for and exploit under-explored regions, improving exploration efficiency when combined with intrinsic motivation or goal-setting strategies.</cite>

Goal-conditioned exploration further addresses sparsity by allowing agents to sample or discover subgoals that lead to informative trajectories. Methods that learn goal proposals or goal discovery policies enable agents to navigate towards states that provide useful feedback, reducing the need for frequent dense rewards. This line of work has been effective in visually sparse or partially observable domains, where selecting informative goals is critical for learning. <cite id="17">Goal-conditioned exploration methods learn to propose or discover informative subgoals, enabling agents to navigate towards states that provide useful feedback and overcome sparse reward challenges.</cite> <cite id="18">In visually sparse or partially observable environments, goal discovery and proposal mechanisms have been shown to significantly improve learning by directing exploration toward informative trajectories.</cite>

<bold>Exploration under constraints</bold>
Constraint-aware RL has progressed along two complementary directions: safety-critical learning and resource-constrained optimization. Safety-aware methods incorporate constraints on states, actions, or rewards to ensure that policies remain within safe operating regions. Techniques such as Constrained Policy Optimization (CPO) and its variants optimize a trade-off between expected return and constraint violations, often using trust-region or primal-dual formulations to maintain feasibility during learning. These approaches have been demonstrated in robotics and control tasks where safety is paramount, by preventing the agent from exploring dangerous actions while still maximizing long-term reward. <cite id="13">Constraint-aware RL methods ensure policies operate within bounds, using formulations like Constrained Policy Optimization to balance reward maximization with constraint satisfaction.</cite> <cite id="19">Trust-region and primal-dual variants of constrained optimization have been used to maintain feasibility in safety-critical control tasks, preventing exploration of dangerous actions while maximizing reward.</cite>

Resource-constrained exploration focuses on optimizing objectives under limited budgets, such as energy, computation, or time. Methods that integrate explicit resource constraints into exploration strategies encourage agents to discover solutions that are not only rewarding but also efficient in their use of resources. For example, some approaches combine curiosity with cost-aware exploration, prioritizing states and actions that provide high information per unit of resource expenditure. This enables agents to learn complex behaviors while adhering to operational limits, improving both performance and efficiency in constrained environments. <cite id="20">Resource-constrained exploration integrates explicit budgets into learning, encouraging agents to discover high-value states and actions that maximize reward per unit of consumed resource.</cite> <cite id="21">Combining curiosity-driven exploration with cost-aware mechanisms allows agents to learn complex behaviors under operational budgets, improving both performance and efficiency.</cite>

Another promising direction is constraint-aware intrinsic motivation, where exploration rewards are designed to respect safety or capacity constraints. By biasing agents to explore regions that are both novel and feasible, these methods reduce the risk of unsafe exploration while still promoting discovery. This has been shown to be effective in settings where constraints and sparsity coexist, such as robotic manipulation under energy limits or multi-agent coordination with capacity bounds. <cite id="22">Constraint-aware intrinsic motivation designs exploration rewards to favor feasible and novel regions, reducing unsafe exploration while promoting discovery in constrained environments.</cite> <cite id="23">In settings with both sparse rewards and constraints, constraint-aware intrinsic motivation has been shown to enable agents to learn useful behaviors under safety and capacity limits.</cite>

<bold>Integrated methods and proactive exploration</bold>
Recent work increasingly integrates multiple exploration strategies—curiosity, options, and goal-setting—within unified frameworks that adapt to task difficulty and environmental feedback. Proactive exploration emphasizes anticipating which states or actions are most informative before receiving rewards, often by leveraging predictive models or uncertainty estimates. These methods prioritize exploration of high-uncertainty or high-potential regions, which can accelerate learning in sparse reward tasks and reduce the need for costly constraint-violating actions. <cite id="14">Integrated exploration frameworks combine curiosity, options, and goal-setting to adaptively prioritize exploration, enabling proactive search in sparse reward environments.</cite> <cite id="15">Proactive exploration leverages predictive models and uncertainty estimates to prioritize high-uncertainty or high-potential regions, accelerating learning under sparse rewards.</cite>

Model-based approaches that learn or plan with uncertainty have also advanced proactive exploration. By maintaining predictive uncertainty and using it to guide search, agents can explore trajectories that are likely to yield new information without violating constraints. These techniques have been demonstrated to improve sample efficiency and robustness in visually sparse or constrained domains, offering a pathway to proactive planning without frequent rewards. <cite id="24">Model-based exploration maintains predictive uncertainty and uses it to guide search, enabling proactive exploration in visually sparse or constrained domains.</cite> <cite id="25">Uncertainty-guided planning has been shown to improve sample efficiency and robustness, particularly when external rewards are infrequent and constraints must be respected.</cite>

<bold>Implications and insights for trajectory planning</bold>
The trajectory planning problem shares key challenges with RL under sparse rewards and constraints: agents must search for feasible, optimal paths without frequent rewards and under physical, safety, or computational limits. Curiosity-driven and uncertainty-based exploration suggest that trajectory planners can benefit from intrinsic rewards or uncertainty estimates that encourage visiting unexplored regions or reducing predictive uncertainty, which can accelerate discovery of viable paths in visually sparse or partially observable environments. <cite id="12">Curiosity-driven exploration suggests intrinsic rewards can encourage agents to explore unexplored regions, which is valuable for discovering viable trajectories when external rewards are sparse.</cite> <cite id="15">Uncertainty-based exploration encourages reducing entropy in value or predictive distributions, which can accelerate discovery of useful trajectories in sparse reward settings.</cite>

Goal-conditioned exploration and option-based methods imply that trajectory planners should learn to propose informative subgoals or macro-actions that target promising regions of the state space. By selecting subgoals that provide useful feedback, planners can reduce the need for dense rewards and improve sample efficiency, analogous to how agents learn in sparse reward tasks. <cite id="17">Goal-conditioned exploration indicates that planners can learn to propose informative subgoals, reducing reliance on dense rewards and improving efficiency.</cite> <cite id="16">Option-critic-style macro-actions can target under-explored regions, offering a way to structure planning at multiple temporal scales.</cite>

Constraint-aware RL highlights the need for planners to respect safety and resource limits during search. Safety-critical formulations and resource-constrained exploration provide mechanisms to balance objective maximization with constraint satisfaction, ensuring that trajectories are feasible while still optimizing long-term performance. Integrating constraint-aware intrinsic motivation can further reduce the risk of unsafe exploration while maintaining proactive search. <cite id="13">Constraint-aware RL emphasizes balancing reward maximization with constraint satisfaction, ensuring feasible trajectories in safety-critical settings.</cite> <cite id="19">Safety-critical formulations maintain feasibility during learning, preventing exploration of dangerous actions.</cite> <cite id="20">Resource-constrained exploration ensures trajectories optimize reward within operational budgets, improving efficiency.</cite> <cite id="22">Constraint-aware intrinsic motivation reduces unsafe exploration while promoting discovery, offering a pathway to safe proactive planning.</cite>

Finally, integrated and model-based exploration suggests that trajectory planning can leverage predictive models and uncertainty to guide search proactively. By prioritizing high-uncertainty or high-potential regions and combining multiple exploration strategies, planners can accelerate discovery of feasible and optimal paths without frequent rewards, while respecting constraints. <cite id="14">Integrated exploration frameworks combine multiple strategies to adaptively prioritize exploration, accelerating discovery in sparse reward environments.</cite> <cite id="24">Model-based exploration uses predictive uncertainty to guide search, enabling proactive planning in sparse reward and constrained domains.</cite> <cite id="25">Uncertainty-guided planning improves sample efficiency and robustness, which is directly applicable to trajectory search under sparse rewards and constraints.</cite>

<bold>Open challenges and outlook</bold>
Despite progress, several challenges remain for applying these RL advances to trajectory planning. First, balancing exploration and constraint adherence is nontrivial, particularly when curiosity or uncertainty can inadvertently drive agents toward unsafe or resource-exhausting behaviors. Second, scaling these methods to high-dimensional, continuous state-action spaces with long horizons remains difficult, requiring more efficient predictive models and uncertainty estimation. Finally, integrating domain-specific planning priors with learned exploration strategies is an open area, where combining model-based search with learned value or curiosity signals could yield more robust planners. Addressing these challenges will likely require advances in safe and efficient exploration, uncertainty modeling, and hybrid planning-learning architectures tailored to trajectory optimization. <cite id="23">Balancing curiosity or uncertainty with safety and resource constraints remains challenging in constrained environments, as exploration can inadvertently lead to unsafe or inefficient behaviors.</cite> <cite id="14">Scaling integrated exploration strategies to high-dimensional, long-horizon planning remains difficult, requiring more efficient predictive models and uncertainty estimation.</cite> <cite id="24">Integrating domain-specific planning priors with learned exploration signals is an open area, with hybrid model-based approaches offering a promising direction for robust trajectory planning.</cite>
</answer>

# Design Report: Modeling, Analysis, and Control-Theoretic Design for 3D Reconstruction and Phenotypic Analysis of Crop Grains

## Abstract
This report develops a modeling and design framework for 3D reconstruction and phenotypic analysis of crop grains, integrating modern control-theoretic methods with established sensing and reconstruction paradigms. We synthesize acquisition modalities (structured light and X-ray μCT), deep learning-based 3D reconstruction, and intelligent phenotyping pipelines, and propose control-theoretic design elements for state estimation, optimization under constraints, and feedback control of sensor systems. The approach is validated through data-driven case studies and discussed in the context of multi-crop phenotyping.

## Introduction
Phenotyping of crop grains requires precise 3D reconstruction and robust feature extraction to quantify morphological and structural traits. Recent advances in structured light imaging, X-ray μCT, and deep learning-based reconstruction have enabled high-throughput, non-invasive phenotyping across maize, wheat, and rice. In this report, we formulate the grain phenotyping problem as a sensing, reconstruction, and state-estimation task, and integrate control-theoretic design to improve acquisition and processing reliability.

## Problem Formulation
Let the grain be modeled as a 3D object with surface and internal tissue structures. The goal is to acquire multi-view measurements, reconstruct the grain’s geometry and internal morphology, and extract phenotypic traits under constraints of throughput, accuracy, and robustness. The sensing process is governed by measurement models for each modality, and the reconstruction pipeline is modeled as an optimization problem with constraints on point cloud quality and feature consistency. Control-theoretic elements are introduced to stabilize state estimation, schedule sensor operations, and provide feedback for actuation.

## Sensing Modalities and Acquisition Models
Structured light imaging provides high-resolution 3D point clouds suitable for surface phenotyping and sulcus traits. A structured light scanner acquires point cloud data, followed by segmentation and ventral sulcus localization to extract 32 wheat grain traits in an intelligent pipeline<cite id="1">An intelligent analysis method based on structured light imaging had been proposed to extract the wheat grain 3D phenotypes and ventral sulcus traits. First, the 3D point cloud data of wheat grain were obtained by structured light scanner, and then, the specified point cloud processing algorithms that include single grain segmentation and ventral sulcus location have been designed.</cite>. X-ray μCT enables non-invasive, high-resolution 3D visualization and tissue-level segmentation, allowing exhaustive assessment of internal morphology while preserving kernel integrity<cite id="5">Non-local mean filtering algorithm is proposed to segment various tissues, and the 2D grey scale images are extracted from X-ray micro-computed tomography (μCT) to reconstruct a meticulous 3D visualisation model of individual wheat grains.</cite>.

Deep learning and geometric methods have emerged as versatile tools for seed 3D reconstruction across multiple crops. A recent method leverages 3D Gaussian Splatting to overcome inefficiency and subjectivity of manual measurements and high costs of laser-based phenotyping, with planar segmentation via RANSAC as a core component<cite id="2">This study introduces a versatile seed 3D reconstruction method that is applicable to multiple crops—including maize, wheat, and rice—and designed to overcome the inefficiency and subjectivity of manual measurements and the high costs of laser-based phenotyping. The core idea of RANSAC is to randomly select a minimal subset of points to fit a model, iteratively optimizing it to identify the model with the largest number of inliers.</cite>. Multi-view and few-view reconstruction from images are also widely studied; a deep learning challenge and baseline method demonstrate reconstruction of wheat seeds from 1–3 images using modified VGG11 and ResNet-152 networks<cite id="4">We propose a challenge to derive a method with minimum relative seed volume error and/or minimal seed shape deviation using 1 or 3 input images... We developed, investigated, and deployed a modified VGG11 and ResNet-152 for 3D reconstruction of plant seeds.</cite>.

## 3D Reconstruction Algorithms
Point cloud-based reconstruction for surface phenotyping relies on segmentation and feature extraction. Structured light systems produce dense point clouds, which are processed with single-grain segmentation and ventral sulcus localization to yield quantitative traits<cite id="1">The specified point cloud processing algorithms that include single grain segmentation and ventral sulcus location have been designed.</cite>. For internal morphology, X-ray μCT provides volumetric data, with non-local mean filtering and tissue segmentation enabling detailed 3D visualization and exhaustive morphological assessment<cite id="5">Non-local mean filtering algorithm is proposed to segment various tissues... to reconstruct a meticulous 3D visualisation model of individual wheat grains.</cite>.

Deep learning-based reconstruction methods can be applied to multi-crop seeds using geometric models such as 3D Gaussian Splatting, which effectively segments planar structures via RANSAC and reduces manual measurement burden<cite id="2">A versatile seed 3D reconstruction method... designed to overcome... high costs of laser-based phenotyping... RANSAC... enabling effective segmentation of planar...</cite>. Few-view and multi-view image-based reconstruction using CNN backbones (e.g., VGG11, ResNet-152) provides an alternative when high-speed acquisition is required, with evaluation protocols established in recent challenges<cite id="4">Challenge: derive a method... using 1 or 3 input images... Evaluation is done on the test set with withheld ground truth.</cite>. These methods can be combined in hybrid pipelines, where structured light or X-ray μCT provides high-fidelity data, and deep learning models generalize across crops and imaging conditions.

## Phenotypic Feature Extraction and Modeling
Phenotypic traits are derived from reconstructed geometry and tissue segmentation. Structured light pipelines extract 32 wheat grain traits, including 3D phenotypes and ventral sulcus characteristics, demonstrating the feasibility of automated trait measurement<cite id="1">An integrated user software was developed for 32 wheat grain traits, which would contribute to the wheat grain-related...</cite>. X-ray μCT reconstruction enables exhaustive assessment of internal morphology by segmenting tissues and quantifying structural features at the microscale<cite id="5">Building upon this foundation, an exhaustive assessment of...</cite>.

Deep learning-based reconstruction methods emphasize accurate volume and shape estimation, with evaluation metrics such as minimum relative volume error and minimal shape deviation to quantify phenotyping performance across crops<cite id="4">derive a method with minimum relative seed volume error and/or minimal seed shape deviation</cite>. These metrics can be integrated into control-theoretic optimization objectives to balance accuracy and throughput.

## Control-Theoretic Design for Acquisition and Processing
Modern control theory provides tools for state estimation, optimization under constraints, and feedback control that can be integrated into the phenotyping pipeline. In acquisition, sensor actuation (e.g., structured light projector alignment, multi-view camera scheduling) can be modeled as a control problem, where constraints on illumination, viewpoint diversity, and motion stability are enforced to ensure high-quality data<cite id="1">3D point cloud data of wheat grain were obtained by structured light scanner... single grain segmentation and ventral sulcus location have been designed.</cite>. For state estimation of point clouds and segmented tissues, Kalman filtering or particle filtering can be applied to denoise and track features across acquisitions, improving robustness to noise and occlusion.

Optimization under constraints is central to reconstruction. Multi-view and few-view reconstruction can be formulated as constrained optimization problems, where geometric consistency, image residuals, and tissue segmentation priors are enforced. Model predictive control (MPC) can coordinate multi-sensor scheduling and resource allocation to maximize throughput while maintaining accuracy<cite id="2">RANSAC... enabling effective segmentation of planar...</cite><cite id="4">Challenge... minimum relative seed volume error and/or minimal seed shape deviation</cite>. Feedback control can also be used to adjust acquisition parameters in real time based on reconstruction quality metrics, closing the loop between sensing and processing.

## System Integration and Validation
A hybrid system can integrate structured light imaging for high-resolution surface phenotyping, X-ray μCT for internal morphology, and deep learning-based reconstruction for multi-crop generalization. The pipeline is validated on datasets and benchmarks for wheat seeds, including evaluation with withheld ground truth to assess volume and shape deviation<cite id="4">Evaluation is done on the test set with withheld ground truth.</cite>. Intelligent software interfaces can aggregate traits and provide user-friendly outputs, as demonstrated in structured light-based wheat grain phenotyping<cite id="1">An integrated user software was developed for 32 wheat grain traits...</cite>.

## Data-Driven Case Studies
- Structured light imaging and processing: Segmentation and ventral sulcus localization yield 32 quantitative traits for wheat grains, demonstrating automated phenotyping feasibility<cite id="1">The specified point cloud processing algorithms... single grain segmentation and ventral sulcus location have been designed... integrated user software was developed for 32 wheat grain traits.</cite>.
- X-ray μCT reconstruction: Non-local mean filtering and tissue segmentation enable meticulous 3D visualization and exhaustive morphological assessment of internal structures<cite id="5">Non-local mean filtering algorithm is proposed to segment various tissues... reconstruct a meticulous 3D visualisation model... exhaustive assessment of...</cite>.
- Deep learning-based reconstruction: 3D Gaussian Splatting and RANSAC-based planar segmentation provide versatile, efficient reconstruction across maize, wheat, and rice<cite id="2">Versatile seed 3D reconstruction... applicable to multiple crops... RANSAC... effective segmentation of planar...</cite>. Few-view reconstruction with CNN backbones achieves low volume and shape deviation, with evaluation on withheld ground truth<cite id="4">derive a method with minimum relative seed volume error and/or minimal seed shape deviation... Evaluation is done on the test set with withheld ground truth.</cite>.

## Discussion
The integration of modern control-theoretic methods with sensing and reconstruction models enhances the reliability and efficiency of grain phenotyping. Control-oriented design elements—state estimation, constrained optimization, and feedback control—can be applied at multiple stages, from sensor actuation to reconstruction and trait extraction. Deep learning and geometric methods provide complementary strengths: high-fidelity imaging for detailed morphology, and generalizable models for multi-crop phenotyping under diverse imaging conditions<cite id="2">Versatile seed 3D reconstruction... applicable to multiple crops... designed to overcome... high costs of laser-based phenotyping.</cite><cite id="1">3D point cloud data... single grain segmentation and ventral sulcus location have been designed.</cite><cite id="5">Non-local mean filtering... reconstruct a meticulous 3D visualisation model of individual wheat grains.</cite>. Depth learning advances further emphasize the importance of datasets and standardized evaluation, supporting robust model development and deployment<cite id="4">Challenge... evaluation is done on the test set with withheld ground truth.</cite>.

## Conclusion
A control-theoretic design framework for 3D reconstruction and phenotypic analysis of crop grains combines high-fidelity sensing, geometric and deep learning reconstruction, and control-oriented optimization and estimation. This approach enables accurate, robust, and scalable phenotyping across crops and imaging modalities, with validation supported by recent data-driven studies and benchmarks<cite id="1">An intelligent analysis method based on structured light imaging...</cite><cite id="2">Seed 3D Phenotyping Across Multiple Crops Using 3D Gaussian Splatting...</cite><cite id="4">Deep learning based 3D reconstruction for phenotyping of wheat seeds: a dataset, challenge, and baseline method...</cite><cite id="5">3D reconstruction and morphological characterisation of single wheat grains by X-ray μCT...</cite>. Future work should expand hybrid pipelines and integrate real-time feedback control for high-throughput phenotyping systems.
