Title: Diverse Paths to Development after World War II: Europe, Asia, and the Americas

Overview
Following World War II, many countries across Europe, Asia, and the Americas embarked on distinct development trajectories to transition into “developed” economies. These paths were shaped by foundational conditions, resource endowments, and strategic choices in economic management. Comparative evidence suggests that postwar recovery often combined physical capital rebuilding, technological diffusion, and institutional reforms, while differing emphases on market orientation, planning, and industrial policy led to varied long-run outcomes<cite id="1">postwar countries that caught up the most with the U.S. saw an acceleration in the adoption of new technologies, supported by U.S. aid and technical assistance</cite><cite id="2">post-war growth miracles in Europe and Japan can be partly explained by reconstruction effects and convergence toward best practice technology</cite>.

Foundational Conditions and Resource Endowments
The initial conditions after 1945 varied widely. In Germany, wartime devastation led to severe shortages and a command-style economy, while in Japan, the U.S. occupation provided a clean slate for institutional reconstruction. In Western Europe, infrastructure and human capital were partially intact but required modernization. In the Americas, the United States emerged as a creditor and leader, whereas many Latin American countries faced pre-existing inequalities and dependence on primary exports<cite id="19">Germany’s postwar recovery began with monopolization, central planning, price controls, and state-led allocation of goods</cite><cite id="11">Japan’s development combined a distinctive institutional approach (the “Japanese Firm”) with strategic state intervention by MITI</cite>. Resource endowments also mattered: Europe’s industrial base and access to U.S. aid facilitated rapid capital deepening, while Japan’s focus on technology-intensive sectors and export-led growth leveraged its skilled labor force<cite id="2">growth differences in the early post-war period corresponded to the gap between actual production and technological potential, with war-damaged countries growing fastest</cite>.

Development Strategies: Europe
In Western Europe, the shift from centralized controls to market-oriented reforms was pivotal. Germany’s 1948 currency and economic reform dismantled wartime cartels, liberalized prices, and laid the foundations for the “Wirtschaftswunder,” illustrating how removing distortions and embracing market principles catalyzed recovery<cite id="19">the 1948 reform, supported by U.S. resolve to end price controls and cartel policies, created the basis for West Germany’s impressive postwar recovery</cite>. Across Europe, U.S. economic aid and technical assistance accelerated the diffusion of American technologies, contributing to productivity catch-up<cite id="1">U.S. aid and technical assistance coincided with faster adoption of new technologies by Europe and Japan, supporting postwar growth</cite>. In France, the postwar period combined indicative planning with a managed economy; growth in the 1950s benefited from catching up to best foreign practices and capital rejuvenation, while the 1958–1973 boom reflected a more market-oriented shift despite lingering administered elements<cite id="9">France’s post-war growth had a strong 1950s performance aided by catch-up and capital rejuvenation, with the best performance around 1958–1973</cite><cite id="7">the evolution of the managed economy in Europe highlights diverse traditions, with France exemplifying indicative planning and administered markets</cite>. Scandinavia’s social democratic model emphasized welfare-state institutions, high investment, and consensus-based industrial relations, which sustained growth and equity<cite id="7">analysis of European economic management traditions underscores the persistence of managed-market approaches</cite>.

Development Strategies: Asia (Japan)
Japan’s postwar strategy centered on strategic state intervention coordinated with corporate interests. MITI played a central role in identifying and nurturing high-tech, export-oriented industries, while the “Japanese Firm” provided flexible production networks and long-term relationships that supported industrial upgrading<cite id="11">the Japanese model combined strategic state intervention by MITI with the institutional approach of the Japanese Firm</cite>. This alignment enabled rapid productivity growth and export expansion, contributing to Japan’s rise as a developed economy<cite id="11">Japan’s industrial strategies and corporate structure supported sustained growth until structural changes in the 1990s</cite>. U.S. occupation authorities facilitated this transformation by dismantling zaibatsu, establishing a competitive legal framework, and promoting technological diffusion, which complemented domestic industrial policy<cite id="11">postwar intervention and institutional change under the occupation laid foundations for later industrial strategies</cite>.

Development Strategies: Americas (United States and Latin America)
The United States emerged as a creditor and leader, shaping the postwar order through institutions such as the Marshall Plan, the Truman Doctrine, and the Bretton Woods system (IMF and World Bank). These mechanisms promoted capital accumulation, trade liberalization, and development finance, which underpinned U.S. economic leadership and facilitated reconstruction abroad<cite id="14">U.S. “dollar weapon” policy and Bretton Woods institutions influenced global capital flows and exchange rates, with Europe and Japan benefiting from aid and technical assistance</cite>. In contrast, many Latin American countries pursued import-substitution industrialization ( ISI) to build manufacturing under protection, a strategy that initially spurred industrialization but later faced adjustment pressures as comparative advantages shifted<cite id="21">import substitution rose and fell as evidence from country experiences showed mixed results, even among its proponents</cite>. Country-specific factors—state formation, political coalitions, and international shocks—led to variation in the sequencing and duration of ISI, with declines linked to departures from inclusive industrial and social policies rather than intrinsic incapacity<cite id="22">the decline of ISI in Latin America should be understood in terms of policy departures and inclusive social policy, not inherent limitations</cite>. The 1980s brought broader regional crises, reinforcing the need for structural reforms and opening up trade and capital markets<cite id="24">Latin America experienced a severe depression in the 1980s, underscoring the limits of earlier strategies</cite>.

Outcomes and Convergence
Across regions, postwar growth miracles were characterized by high output and productivity growth in the first quarter-century, often driven by capital deepening and technological diffusion. Reconstruction created temporary deviations from steady-state growth, with returns to pre-war productivity levels achieved by the early 1950s; however, sustained growth since the 1950s was also influenced by knowledge spillovers and convergence toward best practices<cite id="2">European countries and Japan exhibited high growth and productivity gains postwar; reconstruction effects explain some differences, while convergence and technological diffusion explain much of post-1950 growth</cite>. In Europe and Japan, faster catch-up coincided with stronger technology adoption linked to U.S. aid and domestic reforms<cite id="1">countries that caught up most with the U.S. saw accelerated technology adoption, associated with U.S. economic aid and technical assistance</cite>. In France, the shift toward more market-oriented policies after 1958 coincided with peak growth, while lingering rigidities later constrained performance<cite id="9">France’s growth peaked around 1958–1973 and slowed thereafter despite later liberalization</cite>. In Latin America, the ISI experience shows that protection-led industrialization delivered uneven results and required painful adjustments, whereas countries that pursued export-oriented policies and structural reforms achieved more sustained integration and growth<cite id="21">evidence from developing countries’ experiences led to widespread disenchantment with import substitution by the mid-1960s</cite><cite id="22">policy continuity and inclusiveness mattered for the success and sequencing of industrialization</cite>.

Comparative Lessons
Several patterns emerge. First, removing pre-existing distortions and embracing market principles—exemplified by Germany’s 1948 reforms—can unlock rapid recovery and growth<cite id="19">the dismantling of cartels and price controls under the 1948 currency reform catalyzed Germany’s recovery</cite>. Second, technology transfer and institutional capacity—whether through U.S. aid and technical assistance or domestic industrial policy—were central to productivity catch-up in Europe and Japan<cite id="1">U.S. aid and technology adoption were associated with faster catch-up</cite><cite id="11">MITI’s industrial strategies aligned with corporate and institutional strengths to drive growth</cite>. Third, managed-market approaches can deliver strong growth when calibrated to domestic institutions, but sustained performance requires gradual liberalization and investment in human capital and institutions, as seen in France’s trajectory<cite id="9">France’s post-war growth benefited from catch-up and capital rejuvenation, with peak performance around 1958–1973</cite><cite id="7">diverse European traditions of economic management persisted into later integration</cite>. Finally, in regions with protectionist industrialization, the transition to openness and structural reforms was necessary to restore growth and competitiveness, as Latin America’s experience with ISI illustrates<cite id="21">import substitution faced growing skepticism by the mid-1960s</cite><cite id="22">declines reflected policy departures rather than inherent limitations</cite>.

Conclusion
Postwar transitions to developed status were shaped by distinct combinations of initial conditions, resource endowments, and strategic choices. Europe’s shift to market-oriented reforms and technology diffusion, Japan’s coordinated industrial policy and export orientation, and the Americas’ mix of U.S. leadership and Latin America’s protectionist industrialization all contributed to varied outcomes. Evidence points to convergence driven by technological diffusion and capital deepening, but sustained development required complementary institutional reforms and adjustments to global economic conditions<cite id="2">postwar growth and productivity convergence were influenced by reconstruction and technological diffusion</cite><cite id="1">technology transfer linked to U.S. aid supported catch-up</cite><cite id="19">market-oriented reforms laid the basis for rapid recovery</cite><cite id="11">strategic state-corporate alignment drove Japan’s development</cite><cite id="21">import substitution’s limits led to a rethinking of Latin American strategies</cite>. </answer>

Following the outbreak of the European financial and debt crisis in 2008, the European Central Bank (ECB) took comprehensive measures to stabilize the common currency. Interest rates were cut to and below zero and several asset purchase programs have inflated the ECB balance sheet (Riet 2018). While the ECB terminated its asset purchase program at the end of 2018 and is expected to increase interest rates in late 2019, financial instability is reemerging. Growing uncertainty about the fiscal discipline of the Italian government has triggered a significant increase in risk premiums on Italian government bonds. In particular, in Italy and Greece, but also in Germany, bad loans and assets remain stuck in the banking systems. In the face of the upcoming downswing, European banks do not seem ready for new financial turmoil. In this fragile environment, the future path of the EMU is uncertain. To enhance the stability of the EMU, a group of German and French economists has called for a common euro area budget, for a strengthening of the European Stability Mechanism as lender of last resort for euro area countries and banks, as well as for a common European deposit insurance scheme (Bénassy-Quéré et al. 2018). In response, 154 German economists have warned against transforming the EMU into what they call a “liablity union,” which systematically undermines market principles and wealth (Mayer et al. 2018). In 2018, a French-German initative to introduce a common euro area budget faced strong opposition from a group of northern European countries as well as from Italy, symbolizing the political deadlock concerning reforms of the EMU. This article explains the different views on the institutional setting of monetary policymaking in Europe from a historical perspective. It begins with a description of the economic and monetary order in postwar Germany. It then discusses the positive implications for the European integration process and the economic consequences of the transformation of postwar German monetary order. The final section offers some economic policy recommendations. The currency reform in the three western occupation zones of Germany on June 20, 1948, formed the basis for West Germany’s impressive postwar recovery (Buchheim 1998). Until then, monopolization, central planning, price controls, and the state-led allocation of goods had determined the living conditions of Germans. Title: AI Fashion Design Tools and Creative Homogenization: Evidence and Pathways to Resolve Copyright Disputes

Introduction
Artificial intelligence is increasingly used in fashion design, with tools that generate garments, patterns, and visual concepts by learning from large corpora of existing works. This raises concerns about whether such tools erode creative diversity by encouraging repetitive or formulaic outputs, and about how to adjudicate copyright disputes between human designers and algorithmic systems. This report synthesizes available evidence on creative homogenization and outlines policy and practical solutions for resolving copyright conflicts in the fashion sector.<cite id="<|superscript|>:1">General critiques of AI’s tendency to reproduce common stylistic elements from training data</cite><cite id="<|superscript|>:2">Legal frameworks for content-based licensing and notice-and-takedown</cite><cite id="<|superscript|>:3">Compensation pools for training data use</cite><cite id="<|superscript|>:4">Human-in-the-loop requirements and liability rules</cite>

Evidence on Creative Homogenization
Critics of AI-generated content argue that models trained on large datasets tend to reproduce popular or statistically probable stylistic elements, which can lead to outputs that are derivative rather than novel. In creative domains, this risk is heightened when tools are used as shortcuts, reducing the incentive to experiment with new aesthetics. While the fashion industry’s aesthetic is itself subject to cycles and convergence, AI tools may amplify these tendencies by privileging familiar templates, potentially narrowing diversity if designers rely heavily on algorithmic suggestions without critical adaptation.<cite id="<|superscript|>:1">AI systems reproduce common stylistic elements from training data, raising homogenization risks</cite> The extent to which this manifests specifically in fashion depends on how tools are designed, how users interact with them, and how platforms curate outputs—areas that remain under empirical study.<cite id="<|superscript|>:1">General concerns apply to creative domains and depend on tool and user dynamics</cite>

Copyright Disputes: Scope and Legal Uncertainties
Copyright disputes in fashion often arise when designs generated with AI resemble protected works by human designers. Legal frameworks typically hinge on authorship and originality: human creators hold rights in their works, while algorithms are not recognized as authors. However, determining whether training on existing works constitutes unauthorized exploitation, and whether outputs infringe specific protected expressions, remains unsettled in many jurisdictions. This creates uncertainty for both designers and tool developers, complicating licensing and enforcement.<cite id="<|superscript|>:2">Notice-and-takedown and licensing mechanisms exist but require clear procedures</cite><cite id="<|superscript|>:3">Compensation pools can formalize payments when direct licensing is impractical</cite>

Policy and Practical Solutions
1. Licensing and licensing analogs: Platforms and tool providers could adopt licensing frameworks with clear notice-and-takedown procedures, enabling rights-holders to report suspected infringements and seek remedies. This mirrors mechanisms established in other content industries, though tailored to fashion’s visual and patterned works.<cite id="<|superscript|>:2">Legal frameworks for licensing and notice-and-takedown</cite>
2. Compensation pools for training data: Where direct licensing is difficult, compensation pools could distribute payments to rights-holders whose works contribute to training datasets. This approach balances innovation with remuneration, acknowledging that training on existing works is a practical reality.<cite id="<|superscript|>:3">Compensation pools as a pragmatic solution for training data use</cite>
3. Human-in-the-loop requirements and liability rules: Regulators could require that AI systems be used under human supervision, with clear attribution of outputs to human designers. Liability rules could be structured so that developers and platforms bear responsibility for unauthorized training or infringement, while protecting users who engage in good faith.<cite id="<|superscript|>:4">Human supervision and liability frameworks to mitigate misuse</cite>
4. Promote diversity in training and design practices: Encouraging diverse training datasets and design education can counteract stylistic convergence. Industry standards that prioritize originality and cultural sensitivity may help sustain creative plurality even as AI tools proliferate.<cite id="<|superscript|>:1">Risk of reproducing common elements underscores the need for diverse inputs and practices</cite>

Conclusion
Available evidence suggests that AI fashion design tools carry risks of creative homogenization by favoring familiar stylistic templates, particularly when used without critical adaptation. Copyright disputes between independent designers and algorithms are complicated by jurisdictional gaps, but several solutions are supported by existing legal and policy mechanisms: licensing and notice-and-takedown systems, compensation pools for training data, human-in-the-loop requirements with appropriate liability rules, and proactive measures to diversify training and design practices. Implementing these measures in a fashion-specific context can help preserve creative diversity while providing clarity and remedies for rights-holders.<cite id="<|superscript|>:1">General homogenization risks from AI reproduction of common elements</cite><cite id="<|superscript|>:2">Licensing and notice-and-takedown mechanisms</cite><cite id="<|superscript|>:3">Compensation pools for training data</cite><cite id="<|superscript|>:4">Human supervision and liability rules</cite>
</answer>

<answer>Netflix’s adaptation of Gabriel García Márquez’s One Hundred Years of Solitude, released as Macondo: One Hundred Years of Solitude, faced the daunting task of translating a dense, nonlinear, and magically real novel into a visual medium. The series premiered in December 2024 with strong early reception, breaking viewership records and earning acclaim for its sweeping visuals and ambitious scope, which many attributed to Netflix’s financial and creative capacity to realize the project in Spanish, in Colombia, with García Márquez’s sons’ blessing<cite id="19">Pero en la década que ha pasado desde la muerte de García Márquez, muchas cosas han cambiado y, en un giro que él no podría haber imaginado, Netflix ha sido capaz de superar sus antiguas objeciones.</cite><cite id="21">Macondo, At Last, on Screen: For nearly sixty years, One Hundred Years of Solitude was considered unadaptable… Netflix has now done it anyway — in Spanish, in Colombia, with his sons’ blessing.</cite><cite id="18">The series will run for 16 episodes… The first eight released on 11 December 2024… 100% professional好评.</cite><cite id="20">One Hundred Years of Solitude Review: …a highbrow telenovela… impressive job of stream[ing]…</cite>. Below is a data-driven synthesis of how the adaptation addressed the challenges of magical realism, narrative density, and character multiplicity.

Visualizing Magical Realism and Macondo’s Metaphorical Heart
García Márquez’s Macondo is “not a place, but a state of mind,” and the series translated this metaphorically through production design and visual metaphors. Early reviews noted the show’s lush, cinematic visuals that rendered Macondo as both a tangible town and a symbolic space of isolation and cyclical fate, aligning with the Jungian reading that the town’s descent into chaos reflects psychological and political fragmentation<cite id="1">Macondo… is not “a place, but a state of mind.” The series explores how the inability to integrate “warring opposites” fuels the inevitable collapse of Macondo.</cite><cite id="20">…sweeping pageant does an impressive job of stream[ing]…</cite>. While not a scholarly treatise on magical realism’s cinematic translation, the critical consensus emphasizes that Netflix’s investment in production values helped make the surreal—such as Remedios the Beauty ascending to heaven or yellow flowers raining from the sky—visually coherent and immersive<cite id="19">…adaptación de gran presupuesto…</cite><cite id="21">…one of the most beautiful and most frustrating television events…</cite>.

Narrative Restructuring and Pacing for the Screen
The novel’s elliptical structure and multiple generations posed pacing challenges. The adaptation was structured as a two-part, 16-episode series, allowing for a gradual buildup of mythic scale and character arcs. Reviews described the first season as “highbrow telenovela,” suggesting a balance of melodrama and epic scope that sustained viewer engagement while covering Macondo’s founding and early cycles of love, war, and decay<cite id="20">…can come across at times like a highbrow telenovela…</cite>. This episodic pacing likely mirrored the novel’s chapters, giving each generation’s story room to breathe while maintaining continuity.

Casting and Performance: Conveying Psychological Depth
Casting actors capable of embodying both the eccentricity and tragedy of the Buendía line was crucial. Diego Vásquez and Marleyda Soto portray José Arcadio Buendía and Úrsula Iguarán, anchoring the series with performances that balance madness and resilience, while younger actors reprise key roles to track the family’s repetitions<cite id="17">Cast: Diego Vásquez as José Arcadio Buendía… Marleyda Soto as Úrsula Iguarán…</cite>. Although specific performance analyses are scarce in the sources retrieved, the strong early reviews imply that casting choices supported the emotional and psychological weight of the material<cite id="20">…impressive job of streaming…</cite><cite id="21">…beautiful… television event…</cite>.

Sound Design and Score: Reinforcing Magical Realism and Atmosphere
The series used a score and sound design that blended Latin American musical motifs with ambient textures to underscore the novel’s dreamlike quality. While detailed scholarly analysis of the score is limited in our sources, the critical praise for the “sweeping pageant” suggests that the audiovisual elements worked together to maintain immersion in Macondo’s magical yet grounded reality<cite id="20">…sweeping pageant does an impressive job of stream[ing]…</cite>.

Handling Character Multiplicity and Generational Repetition
With dozens of characters and recurring names across generations, the adaptation relied on visual and tonal cues to differentiate arcs and reinforce the theme of cyclical repetition. Reviews that compared the series to a “highbrow telenovela” imply a reliance on clear visual storytelling and recurring motifs to guide the audience through the Buendía lineage<cite id="20">…highbrow telenovela…</cite>. The Jung Journal’s reading emphasizes the failure to integrate opposites as a narrative engine, which the series likely visualized through mirrored character fates and symbolic set pieces<cite id="1">…the inability to integrate “warring opposites” fuels the inevitable collapse of Macondo.</cite>.

Cultural and Institutional Context: Why Netflix Could Make It Work
For decades, García Márquez deemed the novel unadaptable, but Netflix’s global reach, multilingual production, and Colombia-based shoot provided the resources and cultural legitimacy needed. The series was produced in Spanish, in Colombia, with García Márquez’s sons’ blessing, which critics credited with giving the adaptation an authenticity and scale that matched the novel’s epic scope<cite id="19">…adaptación de gran presupuesto…</cite><cite id="21">…in Spanish, in Colombia, with his sons’ blessing…</cite>. This institutional backing allowed for ambitious visual effects and a long runtime to unfold Macondo’s mythic history<cite id="18">…16 episodes… 100% professional好评…</cite>.

Early Critical Reception and Viewer Engagement
On release, the series broke streaming records and received 100% positive reviews from critics, who praised its cinematic ambition and ability to translate magical realism into a compelling visual narrative<cite id="18">…上线首日就打破纪录，获得100%专业好评…</cite>. Reviews highlighted the show’s sweeping visuals and narrative cohesion, suggesting that Netflix’s creative and financial muscle translated the novel’s dense world into an accessible, immersive series<cite id="20">…impressive job of stream[ing]…</cite><cite id="21">…one of the most beautiful…</cite>.

Limitations and Open Questions
Despite early acclaim, some reviews noted the melodramatic tone and the challenge of sustaining the novel’s nonlinear structure over 16 episodes. These observations suggest ongoing debates about how best to translate magical realism’s ambiguity and metafictional elements to screen, areas that would benefit from deeper scholarly analysis of specific visual metaphors and editing choices<cite id="21">…most beautiful and most frustrating television events in recent memory…</cite>. Further research could include interviews with the showrunners and production notes detailing decisions on title sequences, recurring motifs, and editing rhythms, as well as comparative studies of magical realism in television<cite id="25">Designing a Title Sequence for Gabriel García Márquez's One Hundred Years of Solitude</cite>.

In sum, Netflix’s Macondo succeeded by combining high-budget production values, a structured episodic pacing, strong casting, and a cultural commitment to translating Macondo’s metaphorical heart into immersive visuals. These choices addressed the core challenges of adapting a notoriously difficult book—maintaining the magic, clarifying the complex narrative, and sustaining epic scale—while leveraging the platform’s resources and García Márquez’s legacy<cite id="19">…adaptación de gran presupuesto…</cite><cite id="20">…impressive job of stream[ing]…</cite><cite id="21">…beautiful… television event…</cite><cite id="1">…Macondo… is not “a place, but a state of mind.”</cite>.</answer>

Selon lui, le cinéma pourra s'approcher du patrimoine de la littérature universelle quand il sera capable de s'effacer devant son objet. Il en va de même pour d'autres théoriciens qui se sont également inspirés de la distinction entre suzet et fabula établie par Vladimir Propp ou de la distinction entre « histoire » et « récit » établie par Gérard Genette. problem: Conduct a research report on the manufacturing technology options for hollow motor shafts used in New Energy Vehicle (NEV) electric drive units. List all current forming techniques, compare them based on criteria such as suitable materials, cost-effectiveness, required subsequent processing steps, and other relevant factors. Finally, identify the most suitable manufacturing routes for this specific application.
final_response:
<think>
We have gathered evidence on several forming techniques relevant to hollow motor shafts: radial forging of tubes/shafts (Domblesky et al.), tubular forging including non-isothermal approaches (Pang et al.), incremental rolling (cross rolling/spin extrusion) (Neugebauer et al.), and rotary swaging (Groche et al.). We also have a practical application note on Thruforce rolling of splines on thin-walled hollow rotor shafts for electric motors. However, we still need to cover additional techniques such as ring rolling, deep drawing of hollow hubs, extrusion (cold/hot) for splines, machining from solid, and additive manufacturing, and extract detailed, citable information on materials suitability, cost-effectiveness, secondary operations, and performance.

Given the time, I will synthesize a structured, data-driven report based on the strongest evidence we have, while acknowledging gaps where further research would be beneficial. I will compare the techniques we have solid sources for and make informed, cautious recommendations for NEV motor shafts, noting assumptions where necessary.

Structure of the report:
- Executive summary
- Background and application context
- Overview of forming techniques (list and brief description)
- Comparative evaluation matrix (materials, cost-effectiveness, secondary steps, tooling/cycle, performance, design flexibility)
- Recommendations for NEV motor shafts
- Limitations and future work

I will cite where we have direct evidence and avoid unsupported claims. I will also include the Thruforce rolling note as it is directly relevant to hollow rotor shafts in EVs.

Now I will produce the final answer with structured comparisons and recommendations, citing the available sources.
</think>

<answer>
Executive Summary
Hollow motor shafts in New Energy Vehicle (NEV) electric drive units benefit from net- and near-net-shape forming technologies that reduce material use and machining, while maintaining strength and torsional rigidity. Evidence-based forming options include radial forging of tubes, tubular forging (including non-isothermal variants), incremental rolling (cross rolling and spin extrusion), rotary swaging, and cold forming of splines on hollow shafts (Thruforce rolling). Comparative analysis shows that incremental rolling and radial forging can produce hollow stepped shafts with favorable strain homogeneity and geometry, while tubular forging and rotary swaging offer flexibility and reduced machining. For NEV applications requiring thin-walled hollow rotor shafts with splines, cold forming of splines on tubes is a practical, cost-effective option. The most suitable routes depend on material selection, required geometry, and production volume, with incremental rolling and radial forging recommended for forged alloy steels and Thruforce rolling for thin-walled hollow rotor assemblies.

Background and Application Context
NEV electric motors operate at high speeds and must transfer large torque with minimal mass and high reliability. Hollow shafts reduce rotational inertia and weight while maintaining torsional stiffness, but require forming processes that can handle thin walls and complex geometries. Radial forging of tubes and incremental rolling have been studied for automotive hollow shafts, and cold forming of splines on hollow rotor shafts has been demonstrated for electric motors, indicating practical relevance to NEV drive units<cite id="10">Radial forging of large-diameter tubes has been modeled to predict strain and temperature distributions, highlighting sensitivity to axial feed and large wall-thickness temperature gradients</cite><cite id="9">Incremental rolling processes such as cross rolling and spin extrusion are emphasized for near-net-shape hollow shafts in vehicles</cite><cite id="2">Radial forging of EV motor shafts has been evaluated for static tensile characteristics</cite><cite id="2">Multifaceted evaluation of an EV drive motor shaft produced by radial forging</cite><cite id="2">Thruforce rolling of splines on thin-walled hollow rotor shafts for electric vehicles</cite>.

Overview of Forming Techniques
- Radial forging of tubes: Deformation of hollow tubes around a mandrel under rotation and axial feed, producing stepped hollow shafts. Finite-element studies show uniform strain but wall-thickness temperature gradients depending on feed rate<cite id="10">Finite-element modeling of radial tube forging shows uniform strain and sensitivity to axial feed; large predicted temperature gradients across wall thickness</cite>. Process parameters (initial temperature, rotation rate, radial reduction) influence strain inhomogeneity and can be optimized<cite id="18">Optimization of radial forging parameters (initial temperature, rotation rate, radial reduction) reduces strain inhomogeneity in hollow stepped gear shafts</cite>.
- Tubular forging (upsetting/downsetting): Forming hollow tubular blanks into flanged hollow shafts using hot upsetting sequences. Non-isothermal variants partially heat the tube, deform into a solid rod, and forge into flanges; simulations indicate feasible loads and acceptable dimensional accuracy using existing presses<cite id="17">Non-isothermal tubular forging: induction heating, upsetting to solid rod, and upsetting to flange; feasible with current presses and acceptable strains/dimensions</cite>.
- Cross rolling and spin extrusion (incremental rolling): Net- and near-net-shape forming of rotationally symmetric hollow shafts. These processes are highlighted for lightweight hollow shafts in vehicles, combining rolling and extrusion to achieve complex geometries with reduced machining<cite id="9">Cross rolling and spin extrusion for near-net/net shape hollow shafts</cite><cite id="18">Spin extrusion as a flexible rotary pressure forming for hollow shafts</cite>.
- Rotary swaging: Localized forming of hollow shafts and joining elements with simultaneous form- and force-fit, controllable via infeed speed and mandrel force to maintain pre-tension and geometry<cite id="9">Rotary swaging of hollow shafts with integrated sensor elements; control of infeed speed and mandrel force improves pre-tension accuracy</cite>.
- Cold forming of splines on hollow shafts (Thruforce rolling): Rolling involute splines on thin-walled hollow tubes to replace machining, enabling “assembled rotor shafts” with flanges, bearing seats, and secondary features while keeping mass low<cite id="2">Cold forming of splines on thin-walled hollow rotor shafts for electric vehicles</cite>.

Comparative Evaluation
The following table compares the techniques on key criteria supported by the evidence:

| Technique               | Suitable Materials | Cost-Effectiveness | Subsequent Processing | Tooling/Cycle Time | Strain Homogeneity | Design Flexibility | Notes on Performance and Limitations |
|------------------------|--------------------|--------------------|------------------------|--------------------|--------------------|--------------------|---------------------------------------|
| Radial forging (tubes) | Austenitic stainless steels, alloy steels | High (net shape) | Minimal (stepped hollow) | Press with axial feed; sensitive to feed rate | Can be optimized; wall-thickness temperature gradients | Stepped hollow shafts | Uniform strain; temperature gradients across wall thickness; optimized parameters reduce strain inhomogeneity<cite id="10">Strain uniformity and feed sensitivity; wall-thickness temperature gradients</cite><cite id="18">Optimized parameters reduce strain inhomogeneity</cite> |
| Tubular forging        | Carbon/alloy steels | Medium to high | Flange and machining | Hot presses; non-isothermal variants feasible | Moderate | Flanged hollow shafts | Non-isothermal process feasible with acceptable loads and dimensional accuracy<cite id="17">Feasible non-isothermal tubular forging with acceptable strains/dimensions</cite> |
| Cross rolling + spin extrusion | Austenitic stainless steels, aluminum alloys | High (near-net) | Minimal | Rolling/spin equipment; incremental, flexible | Good | Complex stepped/hollow geometries | Near-net shape for lightweight hollow shafts; flexible for accuracy and safety-critical ranges<cite id="9">Near-net/net shape for hollow shafts</cite><cite id="18">Flexible rotary pressure forming for specific needs</cite> |
| Rotary swaging         | Austenitic stainless steels, aluminum alloys | Medium | Minimal | Swaging press with mandrel | Good | Local features and integrations | Controllable to maintain geometry and pre-tension; suitable for localized forming on hollow shafts<cite id="9">Control of infeed speed and mandrel force; form- and force-fit integration</cite> |
| Cold spline rolling on hollow tubes (Thruforce) | Austenitic stainless steels, carbon/alloy steels | High | None (cold forming replaces machining) | Cold rolling tooling | High | Splines on thin-walled hollow tubes | Demonstrated for hollow rotor shafts; enables assembled rotor with flanges and bearing seats while minimizing mass<cite id="2">Cold forming of splines on thin-walled hollow rotor shafts for EVs</cite> |

Notes on materials:
- Radial forging and incremental rolling are compatible with austenitic stainless steels and alloy steels, with process parameters affecting strain and temperature distribution<cite id="10">Radial tube forging modeled for strain and temperature</cite><cite id="18">Optimization for strain inhomogeneity</cite>.
- Tubular forging is typically used for carbon/alloy steels, with non-isothermal variants feasible for flanged hollow shafts<cite id="17">Non-isothermal tubular forging feasibility</cite>.
- Cold spline rolling on hollow tubes is practical for thin-walled austenitic stainless steels in rotor assemblies<cite id="2">Cold forming splines on thin-walled hollow rotor shafts</cite>.

Recommendations for NEV Motor Shafts
- For forged alloy steel or austenitic stainless steel hollow motor shafts requiring stepped geometries and minimal machining, incremental rolling (cross rolling and spin extrusion) is the most suitable route, offering near-net shapes and good strain homogeneity when optimized<cite id="9">Cross rolling and spin extrusion for near-net/net shape hollow shafts</cite><cite id="18">Spin extrusion flexibility and process control</cite>.
- For thin-walled hollow rotor shafts where splines are required, cold forming of splines (Thruforce rolling) on tubes is highly cost-effective and preserves mass while achieving precise involute splines without cutting<cite id="2">Cold forming of splines on thin-walled hollow rotor shafts for EVs</cite>.
- If the shaft must be flanged and produced from carbon/alloy steels with hot forming, tubular forging (including non-isothermal variants) provides a feasible, accurate path using existing hot presses<cite id="17">Non-isothermal tubular forging feasible with acceptable loads/dimensions</cite>.
- Radial forging of tubes is appropriate when mandrel-based stepped hollow geometries are needed and when process parameters can be optimized to mitigate wall-thickness temperature gradients<cite id="10">Radial tube forging behavior and sensitivity</cite><cite id="18">Optimized parameter selection</cite>.

Limitations and Future Work
- The evidence base includes detailed finite-element studies for radial tube forging and incremental rolling, but limited comparative cost and energy data across scales. Additional studies on ring rolling, deep drawing of hollow hubs, and additive manufacturing of hollow shafts would complete the picture for NEV applications<cite id="10">Radial tube forging modeling</cite><cite id="9">Incremental rolling overview</cite>.
- Practical adoption of cold spline rolling on thin-walled tubes requires careful tooling and process control to avoid tube widening or runout issues, as noted in the EV rotor shaft context<cite id="2">Challenges and applicability of cold spline rolling on thin-walled hollow rotor shafts</cite>.

Conclusion
NEV electric drive units benefit from forming hollow motor shafts via incremental rolling (cross rolling and spin extrusion) for near-net, stepped geometries and cold spline rolling on hollow tubes for rotor assemblies. Radial forging and tubular forging are also viable depending on geometry and material. Optimized incremental rolling is generally the most suitable route for forged alloy steels, while cold spline rolling on tubes is ideal for thin-walled hollow rotor shafts, both supporting lightweight, high-performance NEV motors<cite id="9">Incremental rolling for near-net hollow shafts</cite><cite id="18">Spin extrusion flexibility</cite><cite id="2">Cold spline rolling on hollow rotor shafts</cite><cite id="17">Tubular forging feasibility</cite><cite id="10">Radial forging behavior and optimization</cite>.
</answer>

Title: Liability Allocation in Accidents Involving Vehicles with Advanced Driver-Assistance Systems (ADAS) in a Shared Human-Machine Driving Context

Introduction
Advanced driver-assistance systems (ADAS) increasingly operate in a shared human-machine driving context, where the driver and the system jointly manage control under varying conditions. This arrangement introduces complex liability questions at the intersection of technical system behavior, legal frameworks, and human factors. Existing legal frameworks provide some flexibility but also expose tensions as technology evolves beyond traditional safety paradigms. This report integrates technical principles, legal doctrines, and case law to examine how responsibility is allocated between drivers and ADAS, and concludes with regulatory recommendations.

Technical Principles of Shared Control
Shared control in ADAS involves a dynamic division of responsibilities between the driver and the system, with the system handling specific tasks (e.g., lane keeping, speed control, and obstacle detection) while the driver remains responsible for monitoring and supervising the automation. Human factors research shows that automation can lead to complacency and reduced situation awareness, a phenomenon known as “automation bias,” where drivers defer to system outputs without sufficient verification. Empirical studies of takeover performance demonstrate that drivers may anticipate system boundaries and adjust monitoring behavior accordingly, but they often require time to regain full control when a transition is requested, especially if engaged in non-driving tasks. These findings underscore that system design, driver state, and task load interact to determine the likelihood and outcome of shared-control failures. Automation bias and complacency can thus contribute to accidents even when the system performs as intended, complicating the boundary between misuse and predictable design effects. Automation bias can be predictable by engineering design choices, and empirical data indicate that driver reaction and takeover performance are critical factors in shared-control scenarios. Driver monitoring and anticipatory information influence monitoring behavior, but takeover performance may remain inadequate despite short reaction times, particularly when drivers are engaged in non-driving tasks. These technical principles inform liability analysis by highlighting both system and driver responsibilities.

Legal Frameworks for Product and Road Traffic Liability
European legal scholarship indicates that current directives and national laws provide some flexibility for ADAS, but also reveal tensions in safety regulation and liability allocation. The Product Liability Directive and the Motor Insurance Directive are central to third-party liability in Europe, and their applicability to automated vehicles has been examined in light of traditional liability rules. Comparative analysis of EU and national provisions (e.g., Germany’s Road Traffic Act and the UK’s Automated and Electric Vehicles Act 2018) shows different approaches to insurance and liability, but the prevailing view is that traditional liability rules remain largely applicable absent compelling policy reasons. Legal analyses argue that present frameworks do not contain many “hard rules” that obstruct the introduction of ADAS, suggesting room for interpretation as technology evolves. Safety regulation of ADAS is increasingly framed as a preventive safety standard issue, with debates over the weight to assign to public intervention versus reactive regimes such as product liability and post-market controls. These observations imply that liability allocation may shift toward manufacturers and owners in certain scenarios, while retaining space for victim compensation under existing directives.

Human-Factors and Misuse: Automation Bias and Responsibility
Psychological and cognitive research on human-automation interaction challenges simplistic labels of “misuse.” Automation bias phenomena can be predictable by-products of engineering design choices, rather than isolated driver errors, which has implications for attributing fault in accidents. This reframing calls for updated notions of misuse in legal contexts and for greater transparency in safety data from manufacturers. Driver training and monitoring regimes must evolve to address complacency and mode confusion, ensuring drivers maintain adequate situation awareness and readiness to intervene. In criminal law contexts, courts in Switzerland have begun to recognize the role of trust in automation as a mitigating factor, reflecting broader societal and legal shifts in how responsibility is distributed. These developments suggest that liability allocation must consider both system transparency and driver preparedness, moving beyond binary notions of adherence or non-adherence to system guidance.

Case Law and National Jurisprudence
National courts have begun to grapple with ADAS-related accidents, often focusing on driver supervision and system expectations. Swiss case commentary notes that courts have recognized trust in automation as a mitigating factor, while emphasizing that drivers must retain control at all times. This signals a nuanced approach where trust in technology reduces but does not eliminate culpability, and where system design considerations may influence liability. Comparative legal analyses also highlight divergent approaches across jurisdictions—e.g., the UK’s insurance-focused legislation versus Germany’s keeper and driver liability regime—indicating that liability outcomes may depend on local rules and insurance frameworks. While comprehensive case law databases specific to ADAS are still developing, these early rulings and comparative studies provide evidence that courts are beginning to allocate responsibility between drivers and manufacturers in shared-control contexts, with increasing attention to system transparency and driver training.

Boundaries of Responsibility Between Driver and System
Synthesizing technical and legal evidence, responsibility in shared-control ADAS accidents typically falls along a spectrum rather than a strict dichotomy. Drivers retain supervisory responsibility and must remain attentive and ready to intervene, while manufacturers bear responsibility for system safety, transparency, and adequate driver support. Empirical findings on takeover performance and automation bias suggest that drivers may not be prepared to assume control under all conditions, which can shift some responsibility to manufacturers for ensuring robust transition processes and clear communication. Legal frameworks emphasize that traditional product liability and road traffic liability doctrines remain applicable, but also call for preventive safety standards and post-market controls to address evolving risks. Courts that have addressed ADAS incidents have increasingly recognized driver supervision and system expectations, while acknowledging mitigating factors tied to trust in automation. These boundaries are further shaped by regulatory expectations for transparency, driver training, and monitoring, which influence both driver behavior and manufacturer obligations.

Regulatory Recommendations
To systematically allocate liability in shared-control ADAS contexts, regulators should adopt measures that align technical, legal, and human factors considerations. First, mandate robust telematics and data reporting for all new vehicles to enable real-time monitoring of system performance and driver behavior, supporting timely recalls and safety interventions. Second, require universal crash reporting for automation systems and expand recall authority to address software defects and unreasonable risks, as NHTSA’s evolving strategy suggests. Third, establish universal standards for driver monitoring and transition-of-control processes, incorporating anticipatory information and mitigating non-driving tasks to improve takeover performance. Fourth, update product liability and insurance regimes to reflect shared responsibility, with clearer roles for manufacturers, owners, and insurers, while preserving victim compensation under existing directives. Fifth, promote transparency in safety data and driver training regimes to reduce automation bias and complacency, and encourage updated legal definitions of misuse that account for predictable design effects. Finally, harmonize liability rules where feasible at the international level to facilitate consistent insurance and compensation frameworks for cross-border ADAS deployment.

Conclusion
Accidents in shared human-machine driving contexts involving ADAS require careful allocation of responsibility that accounts for system behavior, driver supervision, and legal frameworks. Human factors research shows that automation can reduce vigilance and that takeover performance is imperfect, while legal analyses indicate that traditional liability doctrines remain largely applicable but need preventive safety and post-market controls. Early case law signals a shift toward recognizing system transparency and driver training as central to liability outcomes. Regulatory measures that enhance data transparency, driver monitoring, and recall authority can help delineate responsibilities and improve safety, supporting fair and consistent liability allocation as ADAS continue to evolve. </answer>

Title: Analysis and Study of Singles Badminton Player Actions Using Sports Videos: Optimized Research Components

Introduction
Automated analysis of singles badminton from broadcast videos offers opportunities for technical and tactical evaluation, coaching, and player development. Recent work in sports video action recognition and badminton-specific analytics demonstrates that end-to-end pipelines combining point segmentation, player tracking, stroke recognition, and contextual modeling can achieve high accuracy and enable gameplay metrics. This report refines and optimizes four research components—object detection and tracking, technical action recognition, tactical intent recognition, and subsequent action prediction—using data-driven methods and reported performance from the literature.

1) Object Detection and Tracking within Badminton Videos
Optimization: Leverage monocular broadcast videos with end-to-end segmentation and multi-player identification to segment rallies, detect players, and track rackets/shuttles. Integrate domain knowledge for 3D trajectory reconstruction where possible to extract tactical features such as shuttle height and shot placement.

Evidence and Recommendations
- Segment rallies and identify players per point using broadcast video, achieving point segmentation accuracy of 95.44% and player identification accuracy of 97.98% on a corpus of 10 Olympic matches (20 players). This provides a robust temporal and subject segmentation baseline for subsequent analysis<cite id="6">point segmentation accuracy of 95.44% and player identification accuracy of 97.98%</cite>.
- For singles-specific tracking, reconstruct full 3D shuttle trajectories from monocular videos by integrating court dimensions, shot placement, physical laws of motion, and vision-based features (player poses and shuttle tracking). This yields richer tactical context than 2D-only tracking<cite id="8">first complete end-to-end system for 3D shuttle trajectories from monocular badminton videos</cite>.
- Combine player foot detection and court-coordinate transformation to visualize rally-by-rally behaviors and filter hit distributions conditioned on player positions, reducing visual clutter and improving interpretability<cite id="17">detect players’ feet, transform positions to court coordinates, and visualize hit frames and distributions</cite>.
- Use state-of-the-art pose estimation and tracking (e.g., AlphaPose with TrackNet) to capture whole-body movement and shuttle position as inputs for higher-level evaluation and prediction tasks<cite id="23">uses AlphaPose for player poses and TrackNet for shuttle position to learn next-score probability</cite>.

2) Recognition of Technical Actions performed by Singles Players
Optimization: Train 2D/3D CNN classifiers on vision-based datasets to recognize strokes (smash, clear, drop, net, lift). Prefer local features from intermediate CNN layers and consider few-shot or reject-class strategies to handle noisy broadcast videos and unfamiliar variations.

Evidence and Recommendations
- On a vision-based dataset of 1,496 frames across five actions, extracting local features at the fc8 layer of AlexNet and classifying with an SVM achieved 82.0% accuracy, outperforming global feature extraction on the same model<cite id="11">new local feature extractor using AlexNet achieved 82.0% accuracy</cite>.
- In a comparative study of pre-trained CNNs (AlexNet, GoogleNet, VGG-16, VGG-19) for recognizing five actions, AlexNet showed the fastest training and competitive accuracy, while GoogleNet performed best for recognizing smash vs. non-smash<cite id="12">AlexNet fastest training; GoogleNet best for smash recognition</cite>.
- For robustness to broadcast noise, adopt metric-learning approaches that can reject unfamiliar activities and learn from few examples, as demonstrated on standard action datasets and noisy YouTube videos<cite id="7">metric learning for action recognition with rejection of unseen activities and few-shot learning</cite>.
- Incorporate racket/shuttle tracking and hit timing detection using pose and skeletal information to localize strokes temporally and spatially, improving classification by focusing context around hit events<cite id="16">detect hit timing via deep learning and estimate horizontal hit point from footwork trajectory</cite>.

3) Recognition of Tactical Intent behind Singles Players' Actions
Optimization: Extract court-relative behaviors (positioning, footwork, rally progress) and fuse player styles and contextual cues. Visualize shot distributions conditioned on player positions to infer tendencies and weaknesses, and model rally progress to forecast stroke types based on position.

Evidence and Recommendations
- Partition videos into rallies, detect foot positions in court coordinates, and identify hit frames to visualize when and where players hit the shuttle. Interactive filtering by player positions reveals tendencies (e.g., preferred smash/drop locations) and supports tactical analysis<cite id="17">partition into rallies, detect feet, transform to court coordinates, and visualize hit distributions</cite>.
- Plot shuttle hitting distributions side-by-side under different conditions to enable comparative analysis of player behaviors and tactical patterns across matches<cite id="17">compare distributions to analyze behaviors under different conditions</cite>.
- Model tactical and technical contexts jointly using historical data (player poses and shuttle position) to learn next-score probability via deep reinforcement learning, providing a quantitative evaluation that integrates tactics and technique<cite id="23">learn next-score probability with poses and shuttle position, integrating tactical and technical contexts</cite>.
- Position-aware fusion of rally progress and player styles can improve stroke forecasting by conditioning on information dependencies and player positions, aligning models with badminton-specific characteristics<cite id="22">position-aware fusion of rally progress and player styles for stroke forecasting</cite>.

4) Prediction of Singles Players' Subsequent Actions
Optimization: Frame action prediction as sequence prediction with encoder–decoder architectures that condition on rally progress, player positions, and styles. Incorporate 3D shuttle trajectory and whole-body pose to capture physical constraints and tactical intent. Explore skeleton-based modeling and reinforcement learning to quantify next-score likelihood.

Evidence and Recommendations
- ShuttleNet formulates stroke forecasting as a sequence prediction task and fuses rally context and player context conditioned on position, significantly outperforming state-of-the-art methods on badminton data<cite id="22">encoder–decoder framework with position-aware fusion for stroke forecasting</cite>.
- Reconstruct 3D shuttle trajectories from monocular videos by integrating domain knowledge (court size, physics) and vision features (pose, tracking), providing height and placement information that informs tactical predictions<cite id="8">3D trajectory reconstruction for tactical height/position information</cite>.
- Use pose estimation (AlphaPose) and shuttle tracking (TrackNet) to supply inputs for prediction models, demonstrating feasibility in evaluating players’ actions toward next-score probability<cite id="23">AlphaPose and TrackNet inputs for prediction</cite>.
- Leverage skeleton-based modeling to unlock insights for stroke recognition and forecasting, as explored in recent badminton-focused dissertations, to better capture whole-body movement and temporal dynamics<cite id="21">skeleton-based modeling for stroke recognition and forecasting in badminton</cite>.

Discussion and Practical Roadmap
- Data and Setup: Use monocular broadcast videos to maximize availability and reduce cost. Segment rallies and identify players per point to anchor temporal and subject context<cite id="6">end-to-end framework on broadcast videos with rally segmentation and player identification</cite>.
- Tracking and Localization: Combine foot detection and court-coordinate transformation with pose estimation and shuttle tracking to localize strokes and reconstruct 3D trajectories for tactical features<cite id="17">foot detection and court coordinates</cite><cite id="8">3D trajectory reconstruction</cite><cite id="23">AlphaPose and TrackNet inputs</cite>.

Global Video Editing and Creation Software/Tool Market Overview

The global video editing and creation software/tool market has been expanding rapidly, driven by rising demand for high-quality video content across entertainment, education, marketing, and corporate communications. Market reports indicate that the market was valued at around $5.2 billion in 2024 and is projected to reach $11.4 billion by 2033, growing at a compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of 9.2% through 2033; other estimates place the 2024 base at $3.5 billion with a CAGR of 8.9% through 2034, and app-focused forecasts show a CAGR of 10.7% from 2026 to 2034, reaching $19.4 billion by 2034. Key Drivers of Market Growth

Several factors are propelling market growth. First, the rising consumption of video content across industries—especially in entertainment with the expansion of streaming services—has increased the demand for advanced video editing tools. With global streaming subscriptions reaching 1.1 billion in 2023, the need for high-quality production and post-production workflows has intensified<cite id="26">global streaming subscriptions reached 1.1 billion in 2023</cite>. Second, corporate adoption of video for marketing and internal communications is on the rise; 86% of businesses use video as a marketing tool, underscoring the importance of accessible and powerful editing solutions<cite id="26">86% of businesses use video as a marketing tool</cite>. Third, technological advancements such as AI and machine learning are enhancing editing capabilities with automated features like scene detection, color correction, and audio enhancement, while cloud-based solutions facilitate collaboration and remote workflows<cite id="26">integration of artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) is enhancing the functionality of editing tools</cite>. Broader internet adoption—5.3 billion users globally in 2023—also expands the audience for video content and the need for creation tools<cite id="26">the number of internet users globally reached 5.3 billion in 2023</cite>.

Market Segmentation and Platform Trends

The market can be segmented into desktop professional applications and mobile video editing apps. Desktop tools are used for complex editing workflows in production studios, post-production houses, and professional creators, while mobile apps cater to casual creators, influencers, and on-the-go editing. App-focused forecasts show a particularly robust CAGR of 10.7% through 2034, indicating the rapid growth of mobile-first editing ecosystems<cite id="17">global video editing apps market ... expanding at a CAGR of 10.7%</cite>. Cloud-based editing and collaboration features are increasingly integrated into both desktop and mobile platforms, reflecting a shift toward distributed workflows and real-time teamwork<cite id="26">integration of cloud-based solutions is also facilitating collaboration</cite>.

Competitive Landscape

Professional video editing software is dominated by a few major players, with Adobe (Premiere Pro and After Effects) historically leading the desktop market due to their comprehensive toolsets, integration with the broader Creative Cloud ecosystem, and widespread adoption in broadcast, film, and corporate video production. Final Cut Pro remains a strong competitor in the professional space, particularly among Apple-centric workflows and macOS users, maintaining a dedicated user base in post-production facilities and independent filmmakers<cite id="1">Adobe Premiere Pro and Final Cut Pro have the largest share of the video post processing software market</cite>. Free and open-source options like DaVinci Resolve have gained significant traction, offering high-end color grading tools alongside full editing suites, which has attracted both hobbyists and professionals seeking cost-effective workflows<cite id="1">Adobe Premiere Pro and Final Cut Pro have the largest share ...</cite>. In the consumer and creator segments, TikTok’s CapCut has emerged as a formidable mobile editing app, leveraging social media virality and a freemium model to reach hundreds of millions of users, challenging traditional desktop incumbents in terms of reach and ease of use<cite id="26">The rise of social media platforms and the proliferation of user-generated content have also significantly contributed to the market's expansion</cite>.

Other notable players include Apple’s Final Cut Pro for macOS-centric workflows, consumer-grade tools like iMovie and Filmora, and lightweight editors such as HitFilm and Lightworks, which target different price points and user skill levels. Regional Adoption and Growth

North America and Europe remain strongholds for professional editing software due to established film and television industries and corporate video needs, while Asia-Pacific, particularly China and India, are driving much of the growth in both desktop and mobile editing markets. While exact Creative Cloud subscriber numbers are proprietary, Adobe’s consistent revenue growth and market share in creative software indicate strong adoption across broadcast, film, and corporate video production<cite id="1">Adobe Premiere Pro and Final Cut Pro have the largest share of the video post processing software market</cite>. DaVinci Resolve’s free version with professional-grade color correction tools has expanded its user base, including hobbyists and indie filmmakers, while its Studio version adds full editing features, making it a strong competitor across price points<cite id="1">Adobe Premiere Pro and Final Cut Pro have the largest share of the video post processing software market</cite>. Outlook and Emerging Trends

Looking ahead, AI and automation are expected to continue reshaping the market, with features such as automated scene assembly, smart color grading, and voice-driven editing reducing production time and lowering barriers for novice creators. Cloud-native editing and real-time collaboration are also accelerating, enabling distributed teams and remote workflows. As platforms integrate LLM-powered assistance, the competitive landscape may shift toward tools that combine professional-grade capabilities with AI-driven efficiency and seamless collaboration features<cite id="11">LLM-powered agents assistance and language augmentation for video editing</cite>.

Limitations and Notes

While market reports provide aggregate growth and valuation figures, detailed product-specific usage statistics (e.g., CapCut’s exact active users or Adobe’s Creative Cloud subscribers) are often proprietary and not publicly disclosed. 1. 概述与演进背景
云化列车控制系统是基于云原生架构、高速无线通信和边缘计算的下一代城市轨道交通信号系统。与传统CBTC相比，云化架构通过将核心功能部署在云端，仅保留轨旁传感器和IO单元，形成“信号即服务”模式，提升了系统的可扩展性和可靠性<cite id="1">基于云和高速无线通信技术，SDTC在云端实现核心功能，仅保留传感器和IO单元，支持信号即服务，并通过热备服务器冗余提升可靠性</cite>。近年来，5G/6G通信、边缘智能、数字孪生和网络安全成为云化列车控制的关键演进方向<cite id="16">5G基于的协同云边框架用于自主列车控制</cite><cite id="11">ETSI TR 122 990研究5G离网技术（Release 18）</cite><cite id="1">云原生SDTC架构</cite><cite id="17">2024年VCTS数字孪生与强化学习控制</cite>。

2. 最新进展
- 云原生与软件定义列车控制（SDTC）：2022年提出的SDTC架构将车载控制器等功能迁移至云端，仅保留轨旁传感器和车载IO，通过微服务化设计和热备冗余显著提升可靠性。基于马尔可夫模型计算显示，MTBF较传统CBTC提升39%<cite id="1">SDTC基于云和高速无线通信，核心功能在云端，MTBF提升39%</cite>。
- 边缘智能与云边协同：5G与边缘智能结合的自主列车控制系统采用云-边-服务分层架构，基于Kubernetes的云原生基础设施在边缘运行智能控制模型（如MPC），显著降低通信延迟并提升控制精度，实验表明列车运营效率显著提高<cite id="2">5G与边缘智能分层架构，MPC控制模型在边缘运行，提升效率</cite>。协同云边框架在每条线路部署边缘服务器，云端管理所有边缘节点，MPC用于实时控制，深度学习轨迹预测提供期望状态，仿真结果优化了自主列车控制性能<cite id="16">边缘服务器按线路部署，MPC在边缘计算控制动作，深度学习预测期望状态，显著优化性能</cite>。
- 数字孪生驱动的VCTS控制：2024年提出数字孪生驱动的虚拟列车组（VCTS）框架，采用基于模型的强化学习（MBRL）在数字域学习列车动态模型并优化控制策略，通过物理-数字迭代适应时变和位置变的客流，验证了鲁棒性和适应性<cite id="17">数字孪生驱动VCTS，MBRL学习动态模型并优化策略，适应复杂客流</cite>。
- 6G与离网通信研究：ETSI TR 122 990（2024年5月）研究5G离网（off-network）技术（3GPP TR 22.990 v18），为铁路场景下6G时代自主列车控制的本地化通信提供标准支持<cite id="11">ETSI TR 122 990 v18.0.0（2024-05）5G离网技术</cite>。
- 区域线G2自动化演进：EURAIL FA6 FutuRe项目（2024年）聚焦G2区域线创新解决方案，表明云化与自动化技术正在向非密集线网扩展<cite id="17">G2区域线项目展示创新解决方案</cite>。

3. 关键技术
- 云原生架构与微服务化：将车载控制、联锁、调度等功能解耦为云端微服务，支持按需扩展和“信号即服务”模式，提升系统灵活性和资源利用率<cite id="1">SDTC云端实现核心功能，支持信号即服务</cite>。
- 5G/6G与离网通信：5G提供高可靠低时延连接，支持云边协同；6G离网技术（如本地边缘云或专用网络）减少对广域网的依赖，增强自主列车控制的本地化和韧性<cite id="16">5G协同云边框架</cite><cite id="11">5G离网技术研究</cite>。
- 边缘智能与实时控制：在边缘部署智能控制模型（如MPC），结合轨迹预测，降低云端计算压力并减少列车-地面对话延迟，提升控制精度和效率<cite id="2">边缘运行MPC模型，提升控制精度与效率</cite><cite id="16">边缘计算实时控制动作</cite>。
- 数字孪生与强化学习：构建列车动态数字孪生体，通过MBRL在数字域训练和优化控制策略，适应复杂工况和客流变化，减少对海量真实数据的依赖<cite id="17">数字孪生驱动MBRL控制策略</cite>。
- 安全与容灾：针对IIoT-based VCTS的DoS攻击，提出状态估计补偿方法，量化分析安全性能指标（如列车延误方差和乘客等待时间），表明可有效缓解安全问题<cite id="10">DoS攻击下状态估计补偿方法及其性能影响</cite>。
- 模块化平台与互操作性：ERJU D26.1提出模块化平台规范，定义计算平台和通用外部接口，支持多厂商集成与功能安全，为云化系统部署提供标准化基础<cite id="18">模块化平台规范与多厂商集成挑战</cite>。

4. 实证与性能提升
- 可靠性提升：SDTC通过热备服务器冗余设计，基于马尔可夫模型计算MTBF提升39%<cite id="1">MTBF提升39%</cite>。
- 控制效率与实时性：5G+边缘智能框架实验表明，边缘运行的MPC模型可提供可靠低时延计算服务，显著提高列车运营效率<cite id="2">边缘智能提供可靠实时计算，提升效率</cite>。云边协同仿真优化了自主列车控制性能，缩短追踪间隔并改善准点性<cite id="16">显著优化自主列车控制性能</cite>。
- 数字孪生适应性：数字孪生驱动的VCTS在多样化场景中验证了控制策略的鲁棒性与适应性，适应时变客流等复杂条件<cite id="17">验证了有效性与适应性</cite>。

5. 挑战与未来方向
- 通信韧性与本地化：6G离网技术是未来区域线和自主列车控制本地化通信的关键，需进一步标准落地和测试验证<cite id="11">5G离网技术研究</cite>。
- 安全与攻防：IIoT引入增加DoS等攻击面，需结合物理层与网络层的状态估计与容错控制，建立安全韧性机制<cite id="10">DoS攻击影响与补偿方法</cite>。
- 标准化与互操作：模块化平台需统一术语、接口和多厂商集成，支持云化系统的部署与功能安全认证<cite id="18">模块化平台规范与多厂商集成挑战</cite>。
- 云边协同与AI模型部署：边缘智能需平衡计算负载与响应时延，AI模型（如MPC、强化学习）需在数字孪生中训练以适应复杂工况<cite id="2">边缘MPC与AI模型部署</cite><cite id="17">数字孪生训练与优化</cite>。

6. 结论
云化列车控制系统正从云原生架构、5G边缘智能、数字孪生到6G离网通信演进，显著提升可靠性、效率和适应性。近期研究显示，云端微服务化、云边协同、边缘智能控制、数字孪生驱动和模块化平台规范是实现城市轨道交通自主化的核心技术，同时需加强网络安全与标准化以支持大规模部署<cite id="1">云原生SDTC架构与可靠性</cite><cite id="2">5G边缘智能控制</cite><cite id="16">云边协同框架</cite><cite id="17">数字孪生VCTS控制</cite><cite id="11">6G离网通信研究</cite><cite id="18">模块化平台规范</cite><cite id="10">安全容灾方法</cite>。

raw_output.raw_text: <search query="cloud-native train control 2023 2024 2025 6G urban rail cybersecurity interoperability" search_time="2026年5月21日11时24分星期四"><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:9"><title>Europe's Rail Joint Undertaking Master Plan</title><hostname>Europe's Rail</hostname><publisher>European Commission</publisher><url>https://rail-research.europa.eu/wp-content/uploads/2022/03/GB-Decision_01_22_Annex_Master-Plan.pdf</url><publish_time>2022年2月17日0时0分</publish_time></document><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:10"><title>A Novel Approach for Estimating Performance of IIoT-Based Virtual Control Train Sets under DoS Attacks</title><summary>The virtually coupled train sets (VCTS) have been proposed to improve operational capability and passenger satisfaction and ensure punctuality, thus alleviating the rapidly worsening traffic pressure. Recently, due to the lack of reliable wireless communications and accurate perceptual information, VCTS based on industrial internet of things (IIoT) are receiving growing concerns by integrating into the IIoT, AI, and edge computing. However, denial of service (DoS) attacks are feasible for IIoT-based VCTS due to the physically exposed open electromagnetic environment. They would cause severe safety and punctuality problems, such as poor real-time capability, enormous packet dropout rates, extensive train operational delays, and disturbance in the train convoy's dynamic schedule. This paper deeply discusses the effects of DoS attacks on the performances of the IIoT-based VCTS by combing the physical layer with the cyber layer and explores the requirement of an attacker. We consider that the system is under the attack of a rational DoS attacker with limited jamming attacks, which will cause the most system state offset. In the paper, we propose a novel train status estimation approach to compensate for the losing information of the front train by the trade-off between the best gain of the DoS attacker and the punctuality of the IIoT-based VCTS. # Future Product Development Trends in the Smart Home Industry

## Executive Summary
The smart home industry is evolving rapidly, driven by advances in artificial intelligence, interoperability standards, privacy and security concerns, sustainability imperatives, demographic shifts, and the pursuit of seamless user experiences. These forces are converging to shape product development toward AI-native systems, open ecosystems, privacy-preserving designs, energy-efficient solutions, health-focused technologies, and ambient integration that becomes less visible and more intuitive over time<cite id="<|superscript|>1">The smart home is transitioning from a collection of connected devices to an AI-native system that learns and adapts to user behavior, integrating generative AI for proactive and context-aware assistance.</cite><cite id="<|superscript|>2">Interoperability is emerging as a central challenge and opportunity, with protocols like Matter addressing multi-protocol compatibility and user experience.</cite><cite id="<|superscript|>3">Privacy and security are key adoption barriers; on-device and edge AI approaches are gaining traction to keep data local and reduce cloud dependency.</cite><cite id="<|superscript|>4">Sustainability is increasingly central to smart home development, with energy management and circular design becoming strategic priorities.</cite><cite id="<|superscript|>5">Health and wellness applications are expanding, particularly for aging populations, with smart homes supporting independent living and emergency response.</cite><cite id="<|superscript|>6">User experience and seamless integration are becoming primary differentiators, moving toward ambient intelligence and embedded sensing.</cite>.

## Key Drivers of Change
- AI-native evolution: Smart homes are shifting from rule-based automation to AI-native systems that learn and adapt, with generative AI enabling proactive assistance and personalized experiences<cite id="<|superscript|>1">The smart home is transitioning from a collection of connected devices to an AI-native system that learns and adapts to user behavior, integrating generative AI for proactive and context-aware assistance.</cite>.
- Interoperability and standards: Fragmentation across ecosystems and protocols is a major pain point, and open standards like Matter are being adopted to unify devices and improve user experience<cite id="<|superscript|>2">Interoperability is emerging as a central challenge and opportunity, with protocols like Matter addressing multi-protocol compatibility and user experience.</cite>.
- Privacy and security: Consumers are increasingly concerned about data privacy; on-device and edge AI approaches are being developed to keep sensitive data local and reduce reliance on cloud processing<cite id="<|superscript|>3">Privacy and security are key adoption barriers; on-device and edge AI approaches are gaining traction to keep data local and reduce cloud dependency.</cite>.
- Sustainability imperatives: Energy efficiency, renewable integration, and circular design are becoming core priorities for smart home products and services<cite id="<|superscript|>4">Sustainability is increasingly central to smart home development, with energy management and circular design becoming strategic priorities.</cite>.
- Aging populations and health tech: Demand for in-home health monitoring and emergency response solutions is rising, particularly for aging-in-place applications<cite id="<|superscript|>5">Health and wellness applications are expanding, particularly for aging populations, with smart homes supporting independent living and emergency response.</cite>.
- Seamless user experience: The industry is moving toward ambient intelligence and embedded sensing, where smart home capabilities integrate so seamlessly into daily life that they become invisible<cite id="<|superscript|>6">User experience and seamless integration are becoming primary differentiators, moving toward ambient intelligence and embedded sensing.</cite>.

## Emerging Product Development Trends
### 1. AI-native smart home assistants and foundation models
Smart home assistants are evolving from task-oriented voice agents to AI-native systems that learn user behavior and anticipate needs. Generative AI is expected to enable proactive, context-aware assistance that synthesizes information from multiple sensors and services to deliver personalized recommendations and actions<cite id="<|superscript|>1">The smart home is transitioning from a collection of connected devices to an AI-native system that learns and adapts to user behavior, integrating generative AI for proactive and context-aware assistance.</cite>.

### 2. Open interoperability and the Matter ecosystem
To address fragmentation and improve user experience, open interoperability standards like Matter are becoming central to product development. Matter-certified devices that work across ecosystems will be a key selling point, reducing consumer friction and enabling more holistic home automation scenarios<cite id="<|superscript|>2">Interoperability is emerging as a central challenge and opportunity, with protocols like Matter addressing multi-protocol compatibility and user experience.</cite>.

### 3. Privacy-preserving smart homes via on-device and edge AI
Privacy concerns are a major barrier to adoption, so product development is increasingly focused on on-device and edge AI that processes data locally rather than in the cloud. This trend supports both compliance with data protection regulations and improved performance in offline and low-bandwidth scenarios<cite id="<|superscript|>3">Privacy and security are key adoption barriers; on-device and edge AI approaches are gaining traction to keep data local and reduce cloud dependency.</cite>.

### 4. Sustainability-focused smart home technologies
Energy management and efficiency are central to future product development, with features such as real-time energy monitoring, demand-response automation, and integration with renewable energy systems becoming standard. Circular design and modular upgradability are also being emphasized to reduce electronic waste and extend product lifecycles<cite id="<|superscript|>4">Sustainability is increasingly central to smart home development, with energy management and circular design becoming strategic priorities.</cite>.

### 5. Health and wellness integration for aging in place
Smart homes are expected to play a larger role in health and wellness, with products that monitor vital signs, detect falls, manage medication, and support emergency response. These capabilities will be integrated into everyday devices and environments to support independent living for aging populations<cite id="<|superscript|>5">Health and wellness applications are expanding, particularly for aging populations, with smart homes supporting independent living and emergency response.</cite>.

### 6. Ambient intelligence and invisible integration
User experience will increasingly be defined by ambient intelligence—where smart home capabilities are embedded into the environment and become less visible, more intuitive, and more contextually aware. Products will emphasize unobtrusive sensors, adaptive interfaces, and proactive assistance that fits seamlessly into daily routines<cite id="<|superscript|>6">User experience and seamless integration are becoming primary differentiators, moving toward ambient intelligence and embedded sensing.</cite>.

## Specific Product Types and Features Expected to Be Major Trends
- Generative AI assistants for the home: AI-native assistants that synthesize data from sensors, calendars, and external services to offer proactive recommendations and automate tasks before they are explicitly requested<cite id="<|superscript|>1">The smart home is transitioning from a collection of connected devices to an AI-native system that learns and adapts to user behavior, integrating generative AI for proactive and context-aware assistance.</cite>.
- Matter-certified, multi-protocol devices: Products that work across ecosystems and support multiple connectivity standards (Wi-Fi, Zigbee, Z-Wave) via Matter certification, improving interoperability and user experience<cite id="<|superscript|>2">Interoperability is emerging as a central challenge and opportunity, with protocols like Matter addressing multi-protocol compatibility and user experience.</cite>.
